to lead or take away from a particular point

Notes.Content: It is possible that ἐκφεύγω[b] and ἀποφεύγω differ somewhat in meaning from φεύγω[b] and from each other, but it is not possible to determine from existing contexts what the distinctive features might be, except perhaps to indicate that ἐκφεύγω[b] and ἀποφεύγω may be connotatively somewhat more emphatic than φεύγω[b]. Note, also, that in this series of terms meaning to escape, there is no special indication of movement, but simply the fact of not having to experience some particular difficulty or danger.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to become safe from danger by avoiding or escaping{N:001}
to speak, with focus upon verbal sound rather than upon content
to cause a load to be carried off
the activity of using up something
to move away from, with emphasis upon separation and possible lack of concern for what has been left
to move away from a normal location, with the implication of disappearing
LEXSenses.Comments: It would be difficult to translate ἀποχωρίζομαι in {S:06600601400008} as meaning literally ‘to go away,’ for this would seem strange in a reference to the sky. If, however, one employs an expression meaning to disappear, it may be necessary to say literally ‘could no longer be seen.’ For another interpretation of ἀποχωρίζομαι in {S:06600601400008}, see {D:63.30}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to separate more or less definitively one from another (evidently somewhat more emphatic in meaning than {L:χωρίζω<SDBG:χωρίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to separate,’ {D:63.29})
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀποχωρίζομαι in {S:06600601400008}, see ἀποχωρίζομαι[a] {D:15.14}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to lose one’s consciousness temporarily
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that ἀποψύχω in {S:04202102600002} refers primarily to a psychological experience rather than a physiological one. Some scholars, however, have interpreted ἀποψύχω in this context as meaning ‘to die.’ For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in {S:04202102600002}, see ἀποψύχω[b] {D:25.293}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀποψύχω<SDBG:ἀποψύχω:000000>}[a] ‘to faint,’ {D:23.184}) to become totally disheartened and thus ready to give up
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀποψύχω in {S:04202102600002}, see {L:ἀποψύχω<SDBG:ἀποψύχω:000000>}[a] {D:23.184}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a market town south of Rome
pertaining to not being capable of being approached
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be necessary to indicate, either in the text or in a marginal note, the reason why the light cannot be approached, for one could interpret this passage to mean that the light was either so small as not to be generally visible or so far away that it could not be reached. If, however, one uses a term for ‘light’ which implies extreme intensity of light, then the context should indicate the basis for its being unapproachable.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being blameless in view of not having given offense
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the concept of ‘being blameless’ as in {D:88.317} and {D:88.318} can only be expressed by a verbal expression involving some measure of complaint. For example, the expression in {S:04402401600012} may be rendered as ‘I do my best to live in such a way that neither God nor people can blame me’ or ‘… can complain against me.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not causing offense

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to behaving in an unprejudiced manner

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not having failed to keep the law (of God)

Notes.Content: ἅπτομαι in {S:04302001700012} may also be interpreted as ‘to touch’ (see {D:24.73}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause the process of burning to begin
LEXSenses.Comments: As already noted in the series of terms listed in {D:14.63}, languages differ appreciably in terms employed for different phases and results of burning. For example, to set something on fire for the sake of providing warmth may be expressed by quite a different term from that which is used in speaking of the process of setting something on fire in order to destroy it.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to hold on to an object
to touch, with the implication of relatively firm contact
to cause some relatively light physical, moral, and/or spiritual harm to
a Christian woman, probably the wife of Philemon
to use force in pushing or thrusting someone or something away or aside
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀπωθέω<SDBG:ἀπωθέω:000000>}[a] ‘to push away,’ {D:15.46}) to no longer pay attention to previous beliefs
act of destroying or causing the destruction of persons, objects, or institutions
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is difficult to find a general term for ‘destruction.’ What has often happened is the extension of meaning from a more specific type of reference, for example, ‘to smash,’ to a more generic meaning of ‘to destroy,’ and whether one understands the specific or more generic meaning depends largely upon the context. Accordingly, in {S:04400800300006} one may find a figurative usage of a term meaning ‘to smash’ (though understood in a more generic sense), for example, ‘Saul then worked in order to smash the church.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an action demonstrating complete disregard for the value of something
LEXSenses.Comments: In the context of {S:04101400400020} the understanding of ἀπώλεια in the literal sense of ‘destruction’ (see {D:20.31}) does not seem to be adequate. The following verse concerning the three hundred denarii would seem to indicate that it was disregard for the value of something rather than destroying the perfume. In fact, the use of the perfume would not have been a matter of destroying. Accordingly, an equivalent of ‘waste’ seems to be far more satisfactory. In some languages the equivalent of this question in {S:04101400400020} is ‘why did she not think about the value of the perfume?’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the content of what is expressed in a curse
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be difficult or even meaningless to speak of a person’s mouth as being ‘full of bitter curses,’ but one can often say ‘they are constantly cursing harshly’ or ‘… speaking heavy curses’ or ‘… constantly uttering harmful curses.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of result as an inference from what has preceded (frequently used in questions and in the result clause of conditional sentences)
a marker of the possibility of something being true
a degree of uncertainty

Notes.Content: In English it is difficult to provide a direct translation of ἆρα in this sense, though other languages may have a regularly corresponding particle with essentially the same significance.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Markers for a Negative Response to Questions

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of a negative response to questions, usually implying anxiety or impatience{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In order to attempt to do some justice to the occurrence of the particle ἆρα, one may introduce a variety of terms which make a question somewhat more emphatically negative. In the case of {S:04201800800032} one might translate ‘will he indeed find faith?’ In the case of {S:04800201700022} one might translate ‘how, then, could Christ ever be a servant of sin?’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: probably a reference to the Sinai Peninsula
a person in the genealogy of Jesus ({S:04000100300042}; {S:04200303300012}, apparatus)
(derivative of ῥάπτω ‘to sew together,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to being without a seam, that is, without being sewn together
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be necessary to describe such a seamless robe as ‘his robe was woven as just one piece of cloth.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:Ἀραβία<SDBG:Ἀραβία:000000>} ‘Arabia,’ {D:93.410}) a person who is a native of Arabia
(derivative of {L:ἀργός<SDBG:ἀργός:000000>}[a] ‘idle, not working,’ {D:42.46}) to not be functioning
pertaining to not working

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to habitually refusing to work (probably with a more unfavorable connotation than in the case of {L:ἄτακτος<SDBG:ἄτακτος:000000>}, {D:88.247})

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not giving careful consideration to something
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀργός in {S:04001203600014}, see ἀργός[e] {D:72.21}. It is also possible that ἀργός in {S:04001203600014} means useless (see ἀργός[d] {D:65.36}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being useless, in the sense of accomplishing nothing
pertaining to showing indifference as to whether something is as it should be
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret ἀργός in {S:04001203600014} as meaning ‘without thought’ (ἀργός[c] {D:30.44}), ‘worthless,’ or even ‘useless’  (ἀργός[d] {D:65.36}).

Notes.Content: Except for the occurrence of ἀργύριον in the plural ({S:04002601500030}), it would be possible to derive all of these references to copper (bronze), silver, and gold coins as direct and predictable metonymic correspondences of the respective terms for substances (see {D:2.54}, 51, 49). Since, however, some languages employ clear distinctions between metals as substances and metals when manufactured into the form of coins, the present classification would seem to be more useful.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the metal silver; after gold the next most highly valued metal in the ancient world
LEXSenses.Comments: As in the case of ‘gold’ ({D:2.49}), there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘silver’ in most languages. In {S:06000101800010}, however, there is a problem in speaking of silver and gold that ‘perish,’ or even as something that can be ‘destroyed,’ since in reality one does not destroy such elements, and silver and gold do not really ‘perish.’ On the other hand, silver and gold can become oxidized and lose their value, especially if they are impure (see {D:2.60}). Therefore, it seems far better to emphasize the lack of value in translating {S:06000101800010}. A suitable rendering may then be ‘not with things that can lose their value as silver and gold.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: silver in the form of stamped coins used as money{N:001}
(an idiom, literally: silver and gold) a generic expression for currency
one who makes objects out of silver (especially jewelry and fine utensils)

Notes.Content: Except for the occurrence of ἀργύριον in the plural ({S:04002601500030}), it would be possible to derive all of these references to copper (bronze), silver, and gold coins as direct and predictable metonymic correspondences of the respective terms for substances (see {D:2.54}, 51, 49). Since, however, some languages employ clear distinctions between metals as substances and metals when manufactured into the form of coins, the present classification would seem to be more useful.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the metal silver; after gold the next most highly valued metal in the ancient world
LEXSenses.Comments: As in the case of ‘gold’ ({D:2.49}), there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory term for ‘silver’ in most languages. In {S:06000101800010}, however, there is a problem in speaking of silver and gold that ‘perish,’ or even as something that can be ‘destroyed,’ since in reality one does not destroy such elements, and silver and gold do not really ‘perish.’ On the other hand, silver and gold can become oxidized and lose their value, especially if they are impure (see {D:2.60}). Therefore, it seems far better to emphasize the lack of value in translating {S:06000101800010}. A suitable rendering may then be ‘not with things that can lose their value as silver and gold.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: silver in the form of stamped coins used as money{N:001}
(derivative of {L:ἄργυρος<SDBG:ἄργυρος:000000>}[a] ‘silver,’ {D:2.51}) pertaining to being made or consisting of silver
(literally: hill of Mars) the location of an Athenian court, traditionally associated with a rocky hill close to the Acropolis, though probably located in the marketplace at the foot of the hill
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of Ἄρειος Πάγος in {S:04401701900014 04401702200016}, see {L:Ἄρειος Πάγος<SDBG:Ἄρειος Πάγος:000001>}[b] {D:11.81}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an advisory council of Athens dealing with ethical, cultural, and religious matters
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand τοῦ Αρείου Πάγου as referring to the location rather than to the council (see [a]).|It is probably wise in translating Αρειος Πάγος[b] to simply transliterate the expression, since it has the status of a proper name. On the other hand, it is extremely important that some footnote be employed so as to indicate something of the significance of this advisory council of Athens.

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a member of the council of the Areopagus

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which causes someone to be pleased with something

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to be pleased with someone or something
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to cause someone to be pleased with something’ is expressed as ‘to cause someone to be happy about’ or ‘to cause someone to feel good about.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which pleases someone
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ‘this pleased the Jews’ is ‘this caused the Jews to be happy’ or even ‘this caused the Jews to say, That’s fine.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being proper or right, with the implication of desirable
a king of Nabatean Arabia

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the quality of moral excellence
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible, however, that ἀρετή in {S:06100100300046} denotes the manifestation of (divine) power (see {D:76.14}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a manifestation of power characterized by excellence
an alternative form of {L:Ἀρνί<SDBG:Ἀρνί:000000>}, {D:93.41} ({S:04200303300012}, apparatus)
young of sheep ({L:πρόβατον<SDBG:πρόβατον>}); often used for ritual sacrifice
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between male and female lambs. It is therefore essential in any figurative reference to male persons to employ an appropriate term for lamb. In a number of languages, of course, a lamb is simply referred to as a ‘young sheep’ or ‘child sheep.’|Perhaps the most widespread story about cultural differences in Bible translation is the one which refers to the translation of ‘lamb’ as ‘little seal of God’ in an Eskimo language. However, there is no evidence that this type of rendering was ever used, since in matters of appearance, habitat, and behavior, lambs and little seals have practically nothing in common. Furthermore, Eskimo languages have terms for ‘lamb’ and in some instances, at least, use the expression ‘young, woolly goat,’ since wild goats are well known and wool is well known as an imported product.

Notes.Content: ἀριθμέω could be classified as a type of mental activity, but since its derivational base is in this domain of Number, it seems better to retain it here, as is normally the case with semantic derivatives.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ἀριθμός<SDBG:ἀριθμός:000000>}[a] ‘number,’ {D:60.1}) to employ numbers in determining a quantity{N:001}
any cardinal number
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be important to add a marginal note to {S:06601301800038} to indicate that the number 666 was actually derived from adding up the numerical values of the letters of a name.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the sum or total of a numbered quantity
a city in Judea
a companion of Paul
to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to eat the earlier meal of the day
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars, however, interpret ἀριστάω in {S:04302101200012} as meaning any kind of meal (see {L:ἀριστάω<SDBG:ἀριστάω:000000>}[a], {D:23.20}), and therefore one would translate as ‘Jesus said to them, Come have something to eat’ or ‘… have a meal.’|In a number of languages the earlier meal of the day may be spoken of as ‘the morning meal’ or ‘the first meal.’ In some languages it is actually called ‘the leftovers meal,’ but see the discussion on meals at different times of the day at {D:23.25}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being to the left of some point of reference
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04700600700030} the phrase ὅπλον ἀριστερόν, literally ‘left-hand weapon,’ refers to a weapon used by the left hand and therefore a defensive weapon, while ὅπλον δεξιόν, literally ‘weapon for the right hand,’ refers to an offensive weapon.|For an interpretation of ἀριστερός as part of an idiom in {S:04101003700030}, see {D:87.35}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.Comments: The left hand is designated in a number of languages by an idiomatic phrase which normally contrasts with expressions for the right hand. For example, one may often speak of the left hand as ‘the bad hand’ or ‘the weak hand,’ and in some instances as ‘the anus hand,’ since this is the hand used in cleansing the body after defecation. See also {D:8.32}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person whose family is greeted in the Epistle to the Romans
a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of ἄριστον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of {L:ἄριστον<SDBG:ἄριστον:000001>}[b], {D:23.23})
LEXSenses.Comments: Though ἄριστον[a], {L:δεῖπνον<SDBG:δεῖπνον:000000>}[a], and {L:βρῶσις<SDBG:βρῶσις:000001>}[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of {S:04100602100020} that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a less important meal, normally in the earlier or middle part of the day

Notes.Content: It is possible to derive ἀρκετός from the verb ἀρκέω to be sufficient ({D:59.46}), and ἀρκετός could then be defined as that which ought to be sufficient and hence leading to satisfaction.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to what is sufficient for some purpose and accordingly resulting in satisfaction{N:001}
to be sufficient or adequate for a particular purpose, with the implication of leading to satisfaction
to be happy or content as the result of having what one desires or needs to be
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages ‘to be content’ is expressed negatively, for example, ‘to not complain.’ In other instances, one may be forced to employ a type of direct or indirect discourse, for example, ‘to acknowledge that it is enough’ or ‘to say, It is all that is needed.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: large wild four-footed mammal with thick fur and doglike face; walks on all fours but may stand up on its back legs to get a better view; may be 2 m. tall when standing up and weigh over 200 kilos; feeds on roots, berries, wild fruit, mice, and lizards, and, occasionally, small livestock; Ursus arctos syriacus; dangerous when provoked or robbed of cubs; associated with violence and danger
LEXSenses.Comments: The term ἄρκος ‘bear’ occurs in the NT only in {S:06601300200028} as a description of the apocalyptic beast. In languages where a term for bear is not known, it is probably best to borrow a word and describe the referent in a footnote or glossary. In {S:06601300200028} a somewhat descriptive phrase is sometimes employed, for example, ‘with large feet having claws like those of an animal called bear.’ By this means the information about the bear’s feet has been incorporated into the text, but usually it is better to leave such information to a marginal note.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: open vehicle with two or four wheels; harnessed to and pulled by horses; used in war or for travelling
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:06600900900030} the reference is to war chariots drawn by horses, while in {S:04400802800016 04400803800010} the reference is to a travelling chariot in which the Ethiopian official was riding. In languages which have no technical term for chariot, it is possible to speak of a war chariot as ‘a war carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn cart for fighting.’ A travelling chariot may be described as ‘a travelling carriage’ or ‘a horse-drawn vehicle.’ A further description of such chariots may be given in a glossary.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a cryptic place name designating the territory which will be the scene of the final battle of the forces of good and evil
an alternative form of {L:Ἀδμίν<SDBG:Ἀδμίν:000000>}, {D:93.13} ({S:04200303300008}, apparatus)
to promise a person for marriage
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be important to note in the margin of a text that in biblical times the act of betrothal was regarded as binding, so that the breaking of a betrothal was legally equivalent to divorce.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a part of the body which joins two parts together
LEXSenses.Comments: In the use of ἁρμός the emphasis is not upon the joints as a moving part of the body but as a means by which different parts of the body are effectively joined together. Accordingly, ἁρμός overlaps in meaning with {L:ἁφή<SDBG:ἁφή:000000>}[a] ({D:18.17}). For problems in translating {S:05800401200044}, see {D:8.62}.

Notes.Content: It is quite possible that ἀπαρνέομαι[a] is somewhat more forceful in meaning than ἀρνέομαι[a], but this cannot be demonstrated from NT usage.
ἀπαρνέομαι[b] appears to be somewhat more forceful in meaning than ἀρνέομαι[d].

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to say that one does not know about or is in any way related to a person or event{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In translating ἀρνέομαι[a] and ἀπαρνέομαι[a], one can often use an equivalent phrase such as ‘to say that one does not know’ or ‘to say that one has nothing to do with.’|In denying an event, as in {S:04200804500018}, it may be possible to translate ‘but they all said they knew nothing about it.’ It is also possible to deny having done something, and therefore one may translate the response in {S:04200804500018} as ‘but they all said that they did not do it’ or ‘… that they did not touch him.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to deny any relationship of association with someone
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages one may best translate ‘deny’ as ‘to make manifest not to know.’ Accordingly, one may translate the first part of {S:04201200900006} as ‘whoever shows people that he does not know me’ or ‘whoever refuses to admit that he does know me.’ Denial need not involve some verbal formulation, though in some languages this is the most common practice. See also {D:33.277}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to refuse to agree or consent to something

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Think About, with the Implied Purpose of Responding Appropriately

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to refuse to give thought to or express concern for{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: There are a number of problems involved in rendering appropriately ἀρνέομαι[d] and ἀπαρνέομαι[b] as in {S:04200902300022} and {S:04100803400034}.|In a number of languages it simply makes no sense to translate ‘to say No to oneself,’ nor is it possible in many instances to use an expression such as ‘to deny oneself,’ since it almost always implies to deny oneself something. Sometimes the meaning may be expressed in a figurative or idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to refuse to pay attention to what one’s own desires are saying’ or ‘to refuse to think about what one just wants for oneself.’ In certain instances other kinds of idioms may be employed, for example, ‘to put oneself at the end of the line’ or even ‘to say to one’s heart, Keep quiet.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to refuse to follow someone as a leader

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to behave in a way which is untrue to one’s real self, in a sense of denying certain valid aspects of one’s personality
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible in some languages to translate ‘he cannot be false to himself’ in {S:05500201300012} as ‘he cannot be different from what he really is’ or ‘he cannot be otherwise than good.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
(derivative of {L:ἀρήν<SDBG:ἀρήν:000000>} ‘lamb,’ {D:4.24}) young of sheep ({L:πρόβατον<SDBG:πρόβατον:000000>}); often used for ritual sacrifice; or a sheep of any age
LEXSenses.Comments: In the one context in the NT, namely, {S:06601301100028}, in which ἀρνίον refers literally to a sheep, it is used in a phrase referring to the horns of an ἀρνίον. In such a context the reference is undoubtedly to a ‘ram,’ that is to say, the adult male of sheep.

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀρνίον<SDBG:ἀρνίον:000000>}[a] ‘lamb,’ {D:4.25}) a follower of Christ, with the implication of helplessness and dependence
Glosses: a person who is like a lamb
LEXSenses.Comments: Compare {D:11.30} and {D:11.31}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a title for Christ
LEXSenses.Comments: ἀρνίον[c] as a title of Jesus Christ occurs only in the book of Revelation, but it is used there more than twenty times. In contrast with {L:ἀρνίον<SDBG:ἀρνίον:000001>}[b] in βόσκε τὰ ἀρνία μου ‘feed my lambs’ ({S:04302101500058}; see {D:11.29}), designating people who need care and help, the supplementary components of meaning in ἀρνίον[c] involve the atoning sacrifice of Jesus Christ on the cross. Some persons have wanted to eliminate the notion of ‘lamb’ in this title, especially in the case of languages in which sheep are looked down on as relatively worthless scavengers (as is the case in certain tropical areas of the world), but in view of the significance of the symbolism of ‘lamb’ in terms of OT sacrificial practices, it is wrong to avoid a term meaning ‘lamb.’ A marginal note, however, may be necessary to explain the significance of this title.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to plow, as a means of preparing land for sowing
LEXSenses.Comments: In biblical times plows did not turn over the soil but were used simply to break the surface, seldom to a depth of more than about ten inches (or twenty five centimeters).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a flat triangular blade (the “plowshare”) made of hard wood or metal, connected to a handle; used to cut the soil in preparation for the sowing of seed or the planting of seedlings
LEXSenses.Comments: In most parts of the world at least some type of plow is known, and in ancient Palestine the plow was not a turning plow, but one which simply dug a relatively shallow furrow, but in doing so, loosened the soil. Where plows are not known or used, it is possible to employ a descriptive phrase such as ‘a tool for preparing the ground for sowing.’ For ἄροτρον as part of a Semitic idiom in {S:04200906200024}, see {D:68.6}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
(derivative of {L:ἁρπαγή<SDBG:ἁρπαγή:000000>}[a] ‘act of plunder,’ {D:57.235}) that which is taken by force or plundered
a state of strong desire to gain things and, if necessary, by violent means
to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
LEXSenses.Comments: This interpretation of {S:05000200600014} reflects the position of Jesus after the incarnation and the fact that he had no thought of trying to become equal with God because he already possessed all of the qualities of deity. Some traditional translations have rendered the latter part of {S:05000200600014} as ‘did not think it robbery to be equal with God,’ but see {D:57.236}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which is to be held on to forcibly
LEXSenses.Comments: Compare the rendering of {L:ἁρπαγμός<SDBG:ἁρπαγμός:000000>}[a] in {D:57.235}. Since ἁρπαγμός may mean not only ‘to grasp something forcefully which one does not have’ ({D:57.235}) but also ‘to retain by force what one possesses,’ it is possible to translate {S:05000200600014} in two quite different ways. This second interpretation of ἁρπαγμός presumes the position of Jesus prior to the incarnation and hence his willingness to experience the kenosis or ‘emptying’ of his divine prerogatives. In any translation of {S:05000200600014} it is important that both possible renderings be clearly indicated, one in the text and the other in the margin.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to grab or seize by force, with the purpose of removing and/or controlling
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04001301900028} the context as a whole is figurative, but a more or less literal rendering of ‘snatches’ or ‘seizes’ is probably satisfactory.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to attack, with the implication of seizing
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that in {S:04001101200034} ἁρπάζω is to be understood in the sense of ‘attack’: βιασταὶ ἁρπάζουσιν αὐτήν ‘violent men attack it.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to forcefully take something away from someone else, often with the implication of a sudden attack
to gain control over by force
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:04301002800030} ἁρπάζω would appear to be in a literal context in view of the expression ἐκ τῆς χειρός μου ‘out of my hand,’ nevertheless ἁρπάζω is certainly figurative in meaning and so is χείρ ‘hand.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of ἁρπάζω[a] ‘to carry off by force,’ {D:57.235}) one who carries off the possessions of another by force
LEXSenses.Comments: For an interpretation of ἅρπαξ as an adjective in {S:04201801100040}, see {D:25.25}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being destructively vicious
pertaining to being violently greedy
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04201801100040} ἅρπαξ may also be interpreted as a noun (see {D:57.239}).

Notes.Content: It is possible that in the NT ἀρραβών has already been generalized in meaning and thus signifies simply that which guarantees.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the first or initial payment of money or assets, as a guarantee for the completion of a transaction or pledge (in the NT ἀρραβών is used only figuratively in referring to the Holy Spirit as the pledge or guarantee of the blessings promised by God){N:001}
pertaining to what cannot or must not be spoken
to be sick or ill, as a state of powerlessness

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a male partner in homosexual intercourse
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that ἀρσενοκοίτης in certain contexts refers to the active male partner in homosexual intercourse in contrast with {L:μαλακός<SDBG:μαλακός:000001>}[b], the passive male partner ({D:88.281}).

Notes.Content: This idiom is also discussed in {D:8.69} in connection with the meaning of {L:μήτρα<SDBG:μήτρα>}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the male of any living creature
(an idiom, literally: male that opens the womb, and closely related in meaning to {L:πρωτότοκος<SDBG:πρωτότοκος:000000>}[a], ‘firstborn,’ {D:10.43}) the first male offspring of a female
LEXSenses.Comments: A literal translation of the idiom ‘male that opens the womb’ may be extremely misleading in some languages, since it may refer to the first act of sexual intercourse and not to the birth of the first, male child.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a friend of Paul
a Greek goddess worshiped especially in Asia Minor
a cloth attached above a boat in such a way as to catch the wind and thus propel the boat through the water
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04402704000036} (the only occurrence of ἀρτέμων in the NT) the reference may be to the foresail, that is, a relatively small sail toward the prow of the ship. A sail may be described in some languages as ‘a piece of cloth to make the ship move’ or ‘cloth on the ship to catch the wind.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time simultaneous with the event of the discourse itself

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a time shortly before or shortly after the time of the discourse

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to an extremely short period of time between a previous state or event and a subsequent state or event (in a number of contexts there is the implication of unexpectedness; but this seems to be a derivative of the context as a whole and not a part of the meaning of the lexical items)

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: the present hour) an emphatic reference to a point of time which is simultaneous with another point of time
pertaining to having been born recently
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘Newly born babies’ may be rendered as ‘babies who have just been born’ or ‘babies who have just begun to live.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being qualified to perform some function

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in the various terms listed here as meaning food, but it is impossible to determine such distinctions in meaning from NT contexts. Perhaps τροφή and διατροφή are somewhat more generic in meaning and may suggest a greater emphasis upon nourishment. At the same time, βρῶσις[c] and βρῶμα[a] may imply solid substantive food, but it is difficult, if not impossible, to argue for such subtle connotative distinctions in meanings which are essentially generic.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively small and generally round loaf of bread (considerably smaller than present-day typical loaves of bread and thus more like rolls or buns)
any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as {S:04000601100004} as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering {S:04200400400022} (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of {S:04200400400022} is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: bread of the placing forth) bread which was set out as an offering in the presence of God in the Tabernacle and later in the Temple
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages ἄρτοι τῆς προθέσεως is rendered as ‘bread placed before God’ or ‘bread placed in the presence of God.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ {S:04402000700020}. No doubt the reference in {S:04402000700020} is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See {D:23.28}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to eat one’s own bread) to earn a living by one’s own efforts
to add condiments to food
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering {S:04201403400026} it may be necessary to translate ἀρτυθήσεται as ‘to cause it to taste like salt again’ or ‘to cause it to taste right again.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a chief or highly important angel
LEXSenses.Comments: An archangel may be described as ‘one who commands other angels’ or ‘a leading angel’ or ‘a chief angel.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to having existed for a long time in the past, with the possible implication of such existence from the beginning of an event or state
the son of Herod I
initiation of an action, process, or state of being
LEXSenses.Comments: It would also be possible to treat ἀρχή in {S:04100100100002} as indicating sequence (Domain 61), so that the contents of verse 1 could be regarded as a type of title for the following section. It seems far better, however, to regard ἀρχή in {S:04100100100002} as being closely related to what immediately follows in verse 2, so that one may translate ‘the good news about Jesus Christ the Son of God began as the prophet Isaiah had written …’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
one who or that which constitutes an initial cause
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand ἀρχή in {S:06600301400040} as meaning ‘ruler’ (see {D:37.56}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the sphere of one’s authority or rule
(derivative of {L:ἄρχω<SDBG:ἄρχω:000000>} ‘to rule,’ {D:37.54}) one who rules or governs
(title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of {S:04900102100006} some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.|In some instances a measure of meaning may be obtained by somewhat paraphrastic expressions. For example, Ephesians 2:2 is rendered in some languages as ‘at that time you lived in the way in which the spirit that governs this world dictated you should live. This is the way the one who rules over the power in space commanded you to live. This is the very spirit that now commands the people who disobey God.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Basic Principles or Features Defining the Nature of Something

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: elementary and preliminary aspects defining the nature of something
LEXSenses.Comments: Compare also the occurrence of ἀρχή[g] in {S:05800501200038} in which it serves to reinforce the meaning of στοιχεῖα (see {D:58.19}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the corner of a two-dimensional object, such as a sheet of cloth
one who causes something to begin
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀρχηγός in {S:05800201000038}, see ἀρχηγός[b] {D:36.6}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person who as originator or founder of a movement continues as the leader
LEXSenses.Comments: In order to indicate clearly the significance of ἀρχηγός in {S:05800201000038}, it may be important to employ a translation such as ‘who established a way of salvation and leads people to it.’ But it is also possible to understand ἀρχηγός in {S:05800201000038} as meaning only the ‘initiator’ or ‘founder’ (see {L:ἀρχηγός<SDBG:ἀρχηγός:000000>}[a] {D:68.2}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ἀρχιερεύς<SDBG:ἀρχιερεύς:000001>}[b] ‘high priest,’ {D:53.89}) pertaining to the high priest
a principal priest, in view of belonging to one of the high-priestly families
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages ‘chief priests’ are referred to simply as ‘big priests’ or ‘important priests.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the principal member among the chief priests

Notes.Content: The occurrence of ἀρχιποίμην ‘chief shepherd’ in {S:06000500400008} is an excellent example of figurative usage. There is no indication that by the time 1 Peter was written ἀρχιποίμην had acquired the conventional meaning of a title designating Christ as one who had principal responsibility for believers. The meaning of ἀρχιποίμην, therefore, is simply ‘chief shepherd,’ but the reference is to Christ in a function which does not involve the literal care of sheep.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the head shepherd who directs the activities of other shepherds (in its only NT occurrence; a figurative reference to Christ)
a Christian in Colossae
one who is the head of and who directs the affairs of a synagogue
one who is a master or expert builder
chief tax collector, in the sense of one who controlled activities of certain other tax collectors
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand ἀρχιτελώνης as meaning a principal or important tax collector rather than one who controlled the activities of other tax collectors.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the head servant in charge of all those who served at meals or feasts
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that ἀρχιτρίκλινος in {S:04300200800018} refers to the master of ceremonies or the toastmaster at the feast.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to rule or govern, with the implication of preeminent position and status
to initiate an action, process, or state of being
LEXSenses.Comments: ἄρχω[b] may also be used in an absolute sense in which the related activity is merely implied: αὐτὸς ἦν Ἰησοῦς ἀρχόμενος ὡσεὶ ἐτῶν τριάκοντα ‘when Jesus began, he was about thirty years old’ {S:04200302300010}. In rendering {S:04200302300010}, it may be useful to translate as ‘when Jesus began his ministry, he was about thirty years old.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time at the beginning of a duration
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand this expression in {S:04400102200002} as ‘beginning from the time of John’s baptizing (him).’

Notes.Content: One may classify ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων in Domain 11 Groups and Classes of Persons, but the phrase ἄρχων τῶν Ἰουδαίων seems to focus primarily upon the authority and status which such a person has, rather than merely upon his being a member of a deliberative body, as in the case of terms such as συνέδριον[a] city council ({D:11.79}), γερουσία and πρεσβυτέριον Sanhedrin ({D:11.83}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ἄρχω<SDBG:ἄρχω:000000>} ‘to rule,’ {D:37.54}) one who rules or governs
a minor government official serving as a judge
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:04201205800018} ἄρχων has essentially the same reference as {L:κριτής<SDBG:κριτής:000000>} and {L:δικαστής<SDBG:δικαστής:000000>} ({D:56.28}), the meaning differs in that ἄρχων represents government authority functioning in judgment on cases.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (ἄρχων τῆς ἐξουσίας τοῦ ἀέρος - title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of {S:04900102100006} some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a title, literally: ruler of the Jews) a member of the highest legal, legislative, and judicial body among the Jews{N:001}
an aromatic resin of a lily-like plant, often used for embalming a corpse
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ἄρωμα is ‘sweet-smelling herbs’ or ‘good-smelling leaves’ or ‘perfumed oil.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an alternative form of {L:Ἀσάφ<SDBG:Ἀσάφ:000000>}, {D:93.48} ({S:04000100700030}, apparatus)
pertaining to that which cannot be moved
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀσάλευτος<SDBG:ἀσάλευτος:000000>}[a] ‘immovable,’ {D:15.4}) pertaining to occurring in an unchangeable state
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be better to express the concept of ‘enduring’ as ‘not ending,’ and accordingly one might translate this phrase in {S:05801202800006} as ‘God’s ruling over us will never end.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
pertaining to a fire that cannot be put out
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be necessary in some languages to render ‘unquenchable’ by an active equivalent, for example, ‘a fire that no one can put out.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice
Glosses: to live in an ungodly manner

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to live in a manner contrary to proper religious beliefs and practice
Glosses: to live in an ungodly manner

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to living without regard for religious belief or practice

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: behavior completely lacking in moral restraint, usually with the implication of sexual licentiousness
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ‘licentious behavior’ would be ‘to live like a dog’ or ‘to act like a goat’ or ‘to be a rooster,’ in each instance pertaining to promiscuous sexual behavior.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being obscure or insignificant, with the possible implication of lacking in noble descent
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages, however, it would be important to avoid the double negative in {S:04402103900028} (despite the effectiveness of the litotes in Greek) by translating ‘a citizen of an important city.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
a state of incapacity to do or experience something
LEXSenses.Comments: A literal rendering of this expression in {S:04701200900042} may not be meaningful, and in fact can be quite misleading. δύναμις is best interpreted as ‘God’s power’ and ἀσθένεια as the weakness which Paul experienced. Therefore, one may be able to translate as ‘my power is greatest when you are weak’ (see Today’s English Version).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of being ill and thus incapacitated in some manner
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be extremely difficult in some languages to speak of ‘taking illness’ or ‘carrying away diseases.’ A strictly literal rendering of such an expression might suggest immediately that Jesus was a type of medicine man who healed others by taking upon himself precisely the same kinds of diseases (a widespread shamanistic practice). It may therefore be necessary in some languages to translate {S:04000801700024} as ‘he caused us to no longer have illness and disease.’ In this way, one may avoid a specific type of shamanistic practice which would be inappropriate in this context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἀσθένεια<SDBG:ἀσθένεια:000000>}[a] ‘weakness,’ {D:74.23}) a state of timidity resulting from a lack of confidence
to be in a state of incapacity or weakness
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be better to translate this expression in {S:04501400100006} as ‘welcome those who have only a little faith.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to be sick and, as a result, in a state of weakness and incapacity
(derivative of {L:ἀσθενέω<SDBG:ἀσθενέω:000000>}[a] ‘to be weak,’ {D:74.26}) an instance of weakness or limited capacity
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be appropriate to translate τὰ ἀσθενήματα as ‘times when they are weak.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ἀσθένεια<SDBG:ἀσθένεια:000000>}[a] ‘weakness,’ {D:74.23}) pertaining to a state of limited capacity to do or be something

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being morally weak and hence incapable of doing good
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand ἀσθενής in {S:04500500600012} as a helpless condition rather than moral weakness (see ἀσθενής[d] {D:22.3}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being ill and, as a result, weak and incapacitated
pertaining to a state of helplessness in view of circumstances
LEXSenses.Comments: The meaning of ‘helpless’ may be expressed in some languages as ‘when we could not do anything about it.’ For another interpretation of ἀσθενής in {S:04500500600012}, see ἀσθενής[b] {D:88.117}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being physically weak
LEXSenses.Comments: Such a literal translation of this expression in {S:06000300700016}, however, may be misleading, for in general τῷ γυναικείῳ is interpreted as a reference to one’s wife. Therefore, one may translate as ‘treating with respect one’s wife as the physically weaker partner’ or ‘… as of the weaker sex.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the Roman province of Asia, primarily the western part of present-day Turkey
(derivative of {L:Ἀσία<SDBG:Ἀσία:000000>} ‘Asia,’ {D:93.415}) a person who is a native of Asia
a high-ranking official in Asia Minor (in an area which is now Turkey)
a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
a state of having been without food, frequently with the implication of being caused by a lack of appetite
to engage in some activity, with both continuity and effort
a bag made of skin or leather; used for temporarily storing and carrying wine
LEXSenses.Comments: A number of translators have attempted to substitute ‘bottles’ for ‘wineskins,’ but this has not been satisfactory, since fermenting wine does not normally break glass bottles, while it would break old wineskins. In circumstances in which the use of wineskins is not known, it may be necessary to employ some type of descriptive phrase (for example, ‘a container made of skin’ or ‘a closed bag of skin’ or ‘a goat skin like a bottle’) and a fuller explanation in the margin.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to experiencing happiness, implying ready and willing acceptance
pertaining to not being wise
to employ certain set phrases as a part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that in some contexts ἀσπάζομαι[a] could be interpreted as ‘to visit,’ so that in {S:04401802200014} one may render ἀσπασάμενος τὴν ἐκκλησίαν as ‘visiting the church’ rather than as ‘greeting the church.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to be happy about something, on the basis that it would prove particularly welcome (thus implying a type of future orientation)
LEXSenses.Comments: In order to render the future implications of ἀσπάζομαι in {S:05801101300030}, one may be able to translate ‘and looked forward with happiness to what was going to happen.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in {S:05801101300030}, see ἀσπάζομαι[c] {D:34.55}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to welcome something or someone, with focus upon the initial greeting
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages, however, it may be difficult to speak of ‘welcoming promises,’ but one can often render this relationship as ‘they were happy to know about what had been promised.’ For another interpretation of ἀσπάζομαι in {S:05801101300030}, see ἀσπάζομαι[b] {D:25.130}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to say goodbye
certain set phrases that are part of the process of greeting, whether communicated directly or indirectly
pertaining to having no spot or stain

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἄσπιλος<SDBG:ἄσπιλος:000000>}[a] ‘spotless, without stain,’ {D:79.59}) pertaining to being without that which might mar one’s moral character
kind of poisonous snake; associated with lurking danger
LEXSenses.Comments: The terms ἀσπίς and ἔχιδνα[a] may be used to refer to almost any kind of poisonous snake, and since at least some type of poisonous snake occurs in practically all parts of the world, there is usually little difficulty involved in finding an appropriate term. One can, however, always employ a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a snake whose bite causes death.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being unwilling to be reconciled to others
Glosses: unwilling to be at peace with others

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an alternative form of {L:Ἀσάφ<SDBG:Ἀσάφ:000000>}, {D:93.48} ({S:04000100700030}, apparatus)
a Roman copper coin worth 1/16 of a denarius
a position extremely close to another position
a city of Mysia
to be without a permanent residence and thus engaged in travelling from one place to another
Glosses: to wander from place to place
to be constantly going from place to place
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in {S:04600401100028}, see {D:85.80}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to not have a place of residence
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀστατέω in {S:04600401100028}, see {L:ἀστατέω<SDBG:ἀστατέω:000000>}[a] {D:15.25}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being beautiful or attractive in terms of being well-formed
a star or a planet
LEXSenses.Comments: Since in {S:06500101300016} godless people are likened to ‘wandering stars’ or ‘planets,’ it may be best to introduce this expression by a simile, for example, ‘they are like wandering stars.’ In some languages there is a serious difficulty involved in translating ἀστὴρ πλανήτης as ‘planet,’ since the planets or their courses through the heavens are regarded as beneficial. In {S:06500101300016} the focal meaning is upon the heretical nature of these godless persons who do not keep on the right course. It may therefore be necessary to translate ἀστέρες πλανῆται in {S:06500101300016} as ‘stars that do not stay where they should stay’ or ‘… do not remain in their right places.’ See also {D:15.26}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: morning star) a planet which is conspicuous in the morning sky (usually either Venus or Mars)
Glosses: bright star in the morning sky
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:06600202800024} the singular pronoun αὐτῷ refers to any and all of the persons in Thyatira, and therefore it is usually best rendered as plural. A literal rendering of {S:06600202800024} may be confusing, since it would suggest that God would be handing over the morning star to persons in Thyatira. A more satisfactory rendering may be ‘I will cause the morning star to shine upon them’ or possibly ‘I will bring light into their hearts.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to the tendency to change and waver in one’s views and attitudes
pertaining to a lack of love or affection for close associates or family
to go astray as the result of departing from the truth
the flash of lightning
LEXSenses.Comments: Terms referring to thunder and lightning often have important taboo connotations. The specific terms for thunder and lightning may be avoided and figurative expressions employed in their place in order to avoid danger which might occur from being struck by lightning or frightened by a thunderstorm. One can, therefore, expect in some languages a number of different terms, and it is important to avoid expressions which might have wrong connotations.

Notes.Content: It is possible that ἀφορίζω[b] is somewhat more emphatic in meaning than ὁρίζω[b] ({D:37.96}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to exclude or remove someone from an association
LEXSenses.Comments: It is, of course, possible to translate ἀφορίζω in {S:04200602200020} as ‘not to welcome,’ but the emphasis of ἀφορίζω is to exclude from a relationship which has previously existed. One may therefore translate {S:04200602200020} as ‘happy are you … when people no longer welcome you in their company … because of the Son of Man.’ By introducing the temporal element ‘no longer,’ the fact of exclusion is made clear.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Assign to a Role or Function

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to set aside a person for a particular task or function{N:001}
to separate into two or more parts or groups, often by some intervening space
Glosses: to set one apart from another

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a set of circumstances favorable for a particular activity or endeavor
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate ἀφορμή opportunity in different ways depending upon the context. For example, in {S:04500700800002} ἀφορμή may be rendered as ‘a good chance to …’ In {S:04800501300024} ἀφορμή may be rendered as ‘a good way for …,’ and in {S:05400501400016} ἀφορμή may be rendered ‘as a good reason for …’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an unwarranted reason for some event

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause or to produce the foaming up of a liquid (restricted in the NT to the foaming at the mouth of a person experiencing an epileptic seizure)
LEXSenses.Comments: Since foaming at the mouth is so characteristic of epileptic seizures, there should be no difficulty in finding a rather specific term to identify this type of event.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ἀφρίζω<SDBG:ἀφρίζω:000000>} ‘to cause foaming of a liquid,’ {D:14.28}) a frothy, foaming mass or substance
LEXSenses.Comments: Though ἀφρός may refer to any type of foam or frothy substance, in {S:04200903900026} the reference is clearly to frothy saliva coming out of the mouth, something which is typical of persons experiencing an epileptic seizure. A number of languages have quite specific terms for this type of foaming or frothing at the mouth, expressed literally in some instances as ‘his saliva was bubbling out of his mouth’ or ‘the water of his mouth came out in bubbles.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of not using one’s capacity for understanding
pertaining to not employing one’s understanding, particularly in practical matters
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that ἄφρων in {S:04500202000004} (παιδευτὴν ἀφρόνων ‘instructor of the foolish’) refers to people who are simply uninstructed or ignorant, since ἀφρόνων could be parallel with νηπίων, occurring in the same verse. On the other hand, there appears to be a contrast in the meanings of ἀφρόνων and νηπίων because of the distinctiveness in meanings of παιδευτήν and διδάσκαλον. Therefore, ἄφρων in {S:04500202000004} is better understood as referring to those who act foolishly because they do not use their potential for understanding.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to begin to sleep
LEXSenses.Comments: It would obviously be a mistake to try to imitate the English idiom ‘to fall asleep,’ for this might be understood as ‘to go to sleep and as a result fall down’ or even ‘to fall down and then remain unconscious.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not being able to speak or talk
pertaining to being without meaning
LEXSenses.Comments: Rather than use a double negative expression in rendering this phrase in {S:04601401000022}, it may be better in many languages to use a positive expression, for example, ‘yet all can be understood’ or ‘yet all have meaning.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a Roman province including the most important parts of Greece
a Christian at Corinth
pertaining to a complete lack of thankfulness
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀχάριστος in {S:04200603500056}, see {L:ἀχάριστος<SDBG:ἀχάριστος:000001>}[b] {D:33.353}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not being thankful
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of ἀχάριστος in {S:04200603500056}, see {L:ἀχάριστος<SDBG:ἀχάριστος:000000>}[a] {D:25.101}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to what has not been made by someone
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
(a possible idiom, literally: mistiness and darkness fall) a serious impairment of sight, possibly involving total blindness
pertaining to not being useful
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages usefulness or lack of usefulness can only be expressed in terms of a verb meaning ‘to help,’ so that in {S:05700101100008} it may be necessary to translate ‘at one time he did not help you at all and now he can help both you and me.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being without such qualities as deserve praise or commendation

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to engage in behavior which is totally wrong and harmful
pertaining to not being useful
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages usefulness or lack of usefulness can only be expressed in terms of a verb meaning ‘to help,’ so that in {S:05700101100008} it may be necessary to translate ‘at one time he did not help you at all and now he can help both you and me.’

Notes.Content: ἕως, ἄχρι, and μέχρι frequently occur with a postposed marker of indefinite temporal reference: οὗ, occurring with all three markers, and ὅτου with ἕως.
It is probable that ἕως[c], ἄχρι[c], and μέχρι[b] differ slightly in meaning, but this cannot be readily determined from existing contexts.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the continuous extent of time up to a point{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: The phrase εἰ μὴ ὅταν is often translated as ‘until’ (for example, μηδενὶ ἅ εἶδον διηγήσωνταιεἰ μὴ ὅταν ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐκ νεκρῶν ἀναστῇ ‘not to tell anybody what they have seen until the Son of Man has risen from death’ {S:04100900900028}), but this phrase may be analyzed as meaning ‘if it is not when,’ an expression which is semantically equivalent to ‘until.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time which is subsequent to a duration and simultaneous with another point of time
extension up to or as far as a goal{N:002}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time prior to another point of time

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Unit of Time: During, In, While, Throughout

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an extent of time of the same length as another extent or unit of time
the husks of grain
LEXSenses.Comments: Chaff may be referred to in some languages as ‘the empty part of the grain’ or ‘the leaves of the grain’ or ‘the refuse of the grain.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to not speaking falsehood
the taste of wormwood, a bitter-tasting herb used as a cure for intestinal worms; compare {D:3.21}
LEXSenses.Comments: As already noted in {D:3.21}, the meaning of {L:ἄψινθος<SDBG:ἄψινθος:000000>} in {S:06600801100032} is not that the waters turned into a particular plant but that the waters came to be as bitter as the plant in question.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a state of not having life
LEXSenses.Comments: In some translations it may seem strange or even meaningless to speak of ‘musical instruments’ as being ‘lifeless’ or ‘not alive,’ since everyone would obviously know such a fact. It may therefore be necessary to translate as ‘even musical instruments like the flute and the harp, which are obviously not alive, nevertheless produce a sound.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: second in a series involving either time, space, or set
LEXSenses.Comments: Occurring only in titles of NT writings: πρὸς Κορινθίους β ‘Second Letter to the Corinthians’; πρὸς Τιμόθεον β ‘Second Letter to Timothy.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Semitic deity
the capital of Babylonia
LEXSenses.Comments: Βαβυλών also occurs as a symbol of demonic world power ({S:06601400800018}; {S:06601601900034}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a standing in society implying rank or status
the distance beneath a surface
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be best to say ‘because there was not much soil’ {S:04001300500038}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a place that is deep
an extreme point on a scale of extent

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a place or region which is low
LEXSenses.Comments: As in the case of {L:ὕψωμα<SDBG:ὕψωμα:000000>}[a] ({D:1.13}), βάθος may be interpreted as a supernatural force ([e]).|The phrase κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς ‘the lower parts of the earth’ may likewise refer to ‘the world below’ as in εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς ‘down into the lower parts of the earth’ {S:04500803900008} (see {D:83.54}). Some scholars, however, understand this expression as being a reference to the earth which is low in contrast with heaven. On the basis of such an interpretation one may render {S:04500803900008} as ‘he came down to the earth itself.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βάθος<SDBG:βάθος:000000>}[a] ‘depth,’ {D:81.8}) supernatural powers in the region below the earth
LEXSenses.Comments: See {D:12.46} for an illustrative passage in {S:04500803800000 04500803900000}. For another interpretation of βάθος in {S:04500803900008}, see {L:βάθος<SDBG:βάθος:000003>}[d] {D:1.18}.|As in the case of {L:ὕψωμα<SDBG:ὕψωμα:000001>}[b] ({D:12.46}), βάθος[e] has been interpreted by some as indicating merely the distance which a person might be separated from God, but most scholars assume that the reference here is to ‘the powers of the world below.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:βάθος<SDBG:βάθος:000000>}[a] ‘depth,’ {D:81.8}) the content of knowledge which is very difficult to know
Glosses: secrets difficult to find out about
LEXSenses.Comments: Only rarely can one use a literal rendering of τὰ βαθέα or τὰ βάθη in referring to secrets. In some instances it may be possible to use an expression such as ‘far away’ or ‘distant,’ and in other cases one can use expressions meaning ‘hard’ or ‘difficult.’ More often than not, however, the closest equivalent of τὰ βαθέα and τὰ βάθη in this type of context is either an expression of degree using a term such as ‘very’ (for example, ‘that which is very secret’) or an expression implying ‘that which is hidden’ or ‘that which is difficult to discover.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause to be deep
pertaining to being considerably below a surface
an extreme point on a scale of extent

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:βαθύς<SDBG:βαθύς:000000>}[a] ‘deep,’ {D:81.10}) the content of knowledge which is very difficult to know
Glosses: secrets difficult to find out about
LEXSenses.Comments: Only rarely can one use a literal rendering of τὰ βαθέα or τὰ βάθη in referring to secrets. In some instances it may be possible to use an expression such as ‘far away’ or ‘distant,’ and in other cases one can use expressions meaning ‘hard’ or ‘difficult.’ More often than not, however, the closest equivalent of τὰ βαθέα and τὰ βάθη in this type of context is either an expression of degree using a term such as ‘very’ (for example, ‘that which is very secret’) or an expression implying ‘that which is hidden’ or ‘that which is difficult to discover.’

Notes.Content: Though in English it is generally the custom to speak of what in Greek is βάϊον or φοῖνιξ ({D:3.53}) as a palm branch, technically it is only a very large leaf, for there are no buds on these so-called branches.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: branch of the palm tree (φοῖνιξ{N:001})
LEXSenses.Comments: βάϊον is a technical term meaning ‘palm branch,’ and in {S:04301201300006} τῶν φοινίκων ‘of palm trees’ may have been added redundantly, since the term βάϊον may not have been regarded as sufficiently well known to readers.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a sorcerer and prophet summoned by Balak to curse Israel
a king of Moab involved with Balaam
a receptacle for carrying money or other possessions; made of leather or cloth
to cause or to let fall down
to move down suddenly and quickly
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages, however, it may be more appropriate to speak of a strong wind ‘blowing down from the island.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause a liquid to pour
to put or place some object or mass in a location, with the possible implication of force in some contexts
to cause a state or condition, with focus upon the suddenness or force of the action
to cause a state to cease by force and with the implication of elimination
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is extremely difficult to speak of states such as love and fear as being respectively agent and affected element. Therefore, it may be necessary to shift significantly the semantic structure so as to translate this expression in {S:06200401800024} as ‘if one completely loves, he does not at all fear.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
(an idiom, literally: to throw on a bed) to cause someone to become very ill
(an idiom, literally: to throw into the heart) to cause someone to think in a particular manner, often as a means of inducing some behavior
(an idiom, literally: to throw a sickle) to begin to harvest a crop by cutting ripe grain with a sickle
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:06601401600004} and {S:06601401900004} this idiom occurs in a figurative context, and therefore it may be necessary in some languages to speak of ‘harvesting’ rather than using a phrase which mentions the literal use of a sickle.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to throw fire) to cause discord and contention
LEXSenses.Comments: Some translators have preferred to retain the literal rendering of this expression in {S:04201204900006}, since this seems to be necessary in view of the larger figurative context, which speaks of ‘how I wish it were already kindled’ (τί θέλω εἰ ἤδη ἀνήφθη). A strictly literal translation may, however, be understood in a completely physical sense, namely, ‘to set the world on fire.’ There are a number of quite diverse interpretations of the significance of this expression in {S:04201204900006}. Some have assumed, for example, that it refers to the fire of Pentecost.

Notes.Content: βαπτίζω[b] and βαπτισμός[b] should not be confused in meaning with βαπτίζω[a] and βαπτισμός[a] to wash, to purify ({D:53.31}). Both sets of meanings involve purification, but only βαπτίζω[b] and βαπτισμός[b] involve initiation into a religious community.
In {S:04000301100062} ‘fire’ is generally regarded as a reference to the experience of Pentecost, but it is possible to understand ‘fire’ in this context as referring to judgment.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand βαπτίσωνται in {S:04100700400012} as a middle form meaning ‘to wash themselves.’|There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which βαπτίζω, {L:καταβαπτίζω<SDBG:καταβαπτίζω>}, and {L:βαπτισμός<SDBG:βαπτισμός>} in {S:04100700400000} involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βαπτίζω<SDBG:βαπτίζω:000001>}[b] ‘to baptize,’ {D:53.41}) to cause someone to have a highly significant religious experience involving special manifestations of God’s power and presence
(an idiom, literally: to be baptized with a baptism) to be overwhelmed by some difficult experience or ordeal
LEXSenses.Comments: It is usually not possible to employ the general term for ‘baptism’ to indicate a difficult trial or ordeal. On the other hand, there may be a serious problem involved in using a technical term for ‘ordeal,’ since such an expression may imply merely a ‘proof of innocence.’ In a number of languages, therefore, one can best translate the idiom simply as ‘to suffer greatly.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance
LEXSenses.Comments: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.
