LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to wash (in some contexts, possibly by dipping into water), with a view to making objects ritually acceptable
LEXSenses.Comments: There is some doubt as to the precise extent to which {L:βαπτίζω<SDBG:βαπτίζω>}, {L:καταβαπτίζω<SDBG:καταβαπτίζω>}, and βαπτισμός in {S:04100700400000} involve ritual cleansing, but the context would seem to imply this, particularly in view of the relationship of such washing to the rules followed by Jews in general and Pharisees in particular.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to employ water in a religious ceremony designed to symbolize purification and initiation on the basis of repentance{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: According to the Didache (early second century) different forms of baptism were practiced in the early church, but with evident preference given to immersion.|The baptism practiced by John the Baptist would seem to reflect far more the Jewish pattern of ritual washing than the type of baptism employed by Christians, which constituted a symbol of initiation into the Christian community on the basis of belief in and loyalty to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. There seems, however, to be no reason to employ a different expression for baptism in the case of John than in the case of the early Christians. Most translators actually employ a transliterated form of the Greek term βαπτίζω, but in some languages this is both awkward as well as inappropriate, especially if another term or expression has already been employed and is widely accepted by groups practicing various types or forms of baptism. In some languages, for example, one may employ an expression such as ‘to enter the water’ or ‘to undergo the ritual involving water.’ Such expressions do not necessarily imply the quantity of water nor the particular means by which water is applied.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βαπτίζω<SDBG:βαπτίζω:000001>}[b] ‘to baptize,’ {D:53.41}) one who baptizes

Notes.Content: It is possible that ἐμβάπτω differs in meaning from βάπτω in specifying somewhat more clearly the factor of something being in something else.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to dip an object in a liquid{N:001}
a prisoner released by Pilate at the request of the Jews during the trial of Jesus
an Israelite general
the father of a man killed in the Temple

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person not participating in Greek culture and civilization (βάρβαρος contrasts with {L:Ἕλλην<SDBG:Ἕλλην:000000>}[a] ‘Greek,’ {D:11.90}, with the focus on culture rather than on language; see {S:04601401100024} at {D:11.94})
LEXSenses.Comments: It would be a mistake in the case of {S:04500101400008} to speak merely of ‘Greeks and barbarians’ or ‘Greeks and savages.’ By NT times {L:Ἕλλην<SDBG:Ἕλλην:000000>} (see {D:11.90}) would have included most of those who participated in one way or another in the culture of the Greco-Roman world. Accordingly, one may render the contrast in {S:04500101400008} as ‘the civilized and the uncivilized.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the native people of an area in which a language other than Greek or Latin was spoken (such persons would be regarded as being outside the civilized world of NT times)
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering this expression in {S:04402800200006} it would be possible in some languages to translate ‘the people there who spoke a strange language were friendly to us’ or ‘the local inhabitants of that island were kind to us.’ ἔσομαι τῷ λαλοῦντι βάρβαρος καὶ ὁ λαλῶν ἐν ἐμοὶ βάρβαρος ‘I will be a foreigner to the one who speaks, and the one who speaks will be a foreigner to me’ {S:04601401100036}. In {S:04601401100036} βάρβαρος implies being a foreigner from a country outside of the so-called civilized world.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a pattern of behavior associated with a low cultural level
LEXSenses.Comments: Regardless of the level of culture or civilization, each ethnic group seems to be able to point to some other group regarded as being uncivilized. In some languages such a group is identified as ‘those who live far away’ or ‘those who do not live in towns’ or ‘those who are very strange.’ In {S:05100301100020} {L:Σκύθης<SDBG:Σκύθης:000000>} ‘Scythian’ ({D:93.583}) may represent a state of civilization even lower than that implied by βάρβαρος ‘barbarian.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to experience difficulty by burdensome and troublous obligations
(an idiom, literally: to be burdened by sleep) to be in a state of deep sleep
(an idiom, literally: their eyes were weighed down) to become excessively or exceedingly sleepy
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ἦσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ βεβαρημένοι (or καταβαρυνόμενοι) would be ‘they could no longer keep their eyes open’ or ‘they could not drive sleep away.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to hear heavily with the ears) to be mentally slow or dull in comprehending
one of the twelve apostles
a false prophet
the ‘family name’ of the apostle Simon Peter
an additional name of a certain Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus who was an associate of Paul
hardship which is regarded as particularly burdensome and exhausting
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04002001200032} βάρος refers not to difficulties in general but to the specific hardship of working for the entire day.|In a number of languages hardship resulting from work may be expressed in terms of the effect upon the workers, for example, ‘to get tired from working’ or ‘to become weak as the result of working.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a high point on a scale of extent and often implying importance and value
the family name of a certain Joseph (often called Justus) who was one of two candidates for the place of Judas Iscariot
the family name of a certain Judas who was appointed as a companion of Paul
a blind man
pertaining to being relatively heavy
LEXSenses.Comments: Although the meaning of βαρύς in {S:04002300400008} is literal, the entire expression is figurative, and so it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘they fix up heavy loads, so to speak, and tie them on people’s backs.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which is difficult in view of its being burdensome
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering ‘his commandments are not burdensome,’ it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘it is not difficult to do what he has commanded.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being important in view of substantive character
pertaining to one who is vicious and cruel
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a strictly literal translation of {S:04402002900020} might be misunderstood. It may therefore be important to translate the last part of this expression as ‘people like cruel wolves will come among you.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being of great value or worth, implying in some contexts a monetary scale
to punish by physical torture or torment
severe pain associated with torture and torment
LEXSenses.Comments: A strictly literal translation of ὁ καπνὸς τοῦ βασανισμοῦ αὐτῶν may be seriously misleading, for it might imply that it is the smoke which causes the suffering, but it is clearly the fire which torments them (as indicated in {S:06601401000000}). Therefore, ir may be necessary to translate ‘and the smoke of the fire that torments them.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βασανίζω<SDBG:βασανίζω:000000>} ‘to torture,’ {D:38.13}) a person serving as a guard in a prison, whose function was to torture prisoners as a phase of judicial examination
LEXSenses.Comments: It is difficult to know in the case of {S:04001803400018} if βασανιστής is to be understood in the specific sense of ‘torturer’ (in which case it could be classified after {D:38.13}) or only in terms of ‘prison guard.’ The use of βασανιστής in {S:04001803400018} may simply be an instance of literary hyperbole. As such it may be possible to translate the expression in {S:04001803400018} as ‘his master was very angry and handed him over to prison guards to torture him until he should pay back the whole amount.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: severe pain associated with torture and torment
the action of ruling as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
LEXSenses.Comments: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an area or district ruled by a king
LEXSenses.Comments: Since in many areas of the world kingship is not known (that is to say, the succession of rulers within a family and by inheritance), it may not be possible to find a technical term meaning ‘kingdom.’ Usually, however, one may employ an expression which is roughly equivalent in meaning to ‘domain,’ so that, for example, the last part of {S:04100602300030} may be rendered as ‘up to a half of the region which I rule.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a king
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (ου n) the dwelling of a king or ruler; usually larger and more elaborate than the dwelling of an average person
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04200702500040} βασίλειον may be rendered as ‘the home of a king’ or ‘the home of a ruler.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who has absolute authority within a particular area and is able to convey this power and authority to a successor (though in NT times, certain kings ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities and had no power to pass on their prerogatives)
to rule as a king, with the implication of complete authority and the possibility of being able to pass on the right to rule to one’s son or near kin
LEXSenses.Comments: It is generally a serious mistake to translate the phrase ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the kingdom of God’ as referring to a particular area in which God rules. The meaning of this phrase in the NT involves not a particular place or special period of time but the fact of ruling. An expression such as ‘to enter the kingdom of God’ thus does not refer to ‘going to heaven’ but should be understood as ‘accepting God’s rule’ or ‘welcoming God to rule over.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βασιλεύω<SDBG:βασιλεύω:000000>}[a] ‘to rule, to reign as a king,’ {D:37.64}) to be in control in an absolute manner
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages, however, it may be impossible to personify death as being capable of ‘reigning’ or ‘ruling.’ Sometimes the equivalent meaning may be expressed as ‘from the time of Adam to that of Moses there was no way for people to escape death’ or ‘… to die was certain’ ({S:04500501400004}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a king
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘his royal robes’ may be rendered as ‘his clothing which he had as king,’ and the phrase ‘the royal priesthood’ may be rendered as ‘priests who are like kings.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an official directly responsible to a king

Notes.Content: In certain contexts outside of the NT, βασίλισσα is employed to refer to the wife of a king.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a female ruler who has absolute authority within a particular area and who is able to pass on the power to rule to a successor{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: For an analysis of the use of {L:Κανδάκη<SDBG:Κανδάκη:000000>} in {S:04400802700022}, see {D:37.77}. See also {D:93.209}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the part of the leg below the ankle on which a person or animal stands and moves
LEXSenses.Comments: βάσις is a more technical term for the foot than is πούς.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to bewitch a person, frequently by use of the evil eye and with evil intent
LEXSenses.Comments: βασκαίνω[a] differs from {L:μαγεύω<SDBG:μαγεύω:000000>} to practice magic ({D:53.96}) in that the former involves the use of so-called black magic, but for a different interpretation of βασκαίνω in {S:04800300100012}, see {D:88.159}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to deceive a person by devious and crafty means, with the possibility of a religious connotation in view of the literal meaning ‘to bewitch’ (see {D:53.98})
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that {L:βασκαίνω<SDBG:βασκαίνω:000000>} in {S:04800300100012} is to be understood literally in the sense of bewitching by means of black magic (see {D:53.98}).

Notes.Content: It is possible to interpret βαστάζω in {S:04501101800024} in a more or less literal sense, namely ‘to carry’ or ‘to bear’ (see {D:15.188}), but the overall context of {S:04501101800024} is figurative.

It is difficult to know the extent to which βαστάζω στίγματα should be regarded as an idiom. It is possible to understand this expression to mean that Paul had the scars from wounds which were similar to those of Jesus, but it seems far better to understand this in a more figurative sense, despite the fact that one cannot determine precisely the extent to which such a phrase had become a standardized idiom.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to bear or carry a relatively heavy or burdensome object
to carry away from a place, with the probable implication of something that is relatively heavy

(similar in meaning to {L:ὑποφέρω<SDBG:ὑποφέρω:000000>} ‘to endure,’ {D:25.175}, but probably somewhat more emphatic in meaning) to continue to bear up under unusually trying circumstances and difficulties
to provide continuous and possibly prolonged assistance and help by supplying the needs of someone
to undergo a grievous, difficult experience
to accept, but with the implication of the truth being difficult to comprehend or to respond to properly
(an idiom, literally: to carry a name) to spread information extensively about a person
(an idiom, literally: to bear marks) to undergo experiences which mark one as the slave of some master
Glosses: to bear the marks of a slave
to experience being the slave of
LEXSenses.Comments: See also {D:8.55} and {D:33.481}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a productive idiomatic expression, literally: to carry one’s cross) to be prepared to endure severe suffering, even to the point of death
Glosses: to be prepared to suffer even unto death
LEXSenses.Comments: The idiom ‘to carry one’s cross’ or ‘to take up one’s cross’ involves a number of important features of meaning. Unfortunately, this expression is frequently not understood correctly by many people who hear it or even use it. One reason for this is the actual absence of crucifixion in modern society. If a literal translation is to be employed, then some marginal note will probably be necessary in order to indicate clearly the full implications of such a statement.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
LEXSenses.Comments: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render {S:04201102700042} as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of plant with sharp projections on its stem and/or branches; regarded as useless; symbol of hardship
LEXSenses.Comments: The reference to the passage of Scripture in {S:04202003700000} is supplied from the context.|Except for {S:04200604400034}, all occurrences of βάτος in the NT are to the burning bush of {S:00200300200000}, in which the reference may very well be to a ‘burning thorn bush.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Hebrew liquid measure of between eight and nine gallons or approximately thirty-five liters
LEXSenses.Comments: Because of the possible symbolic numerical values used in the Parable of the Dishonest Steward, it is important to retain the numerals, while making some adjustment in the case of the term βάτος. Accordingly, one may speak of ‘one hundred barrels of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred containers of olive oil’ or ‘one hundred large jars of olive oil.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: tailless amphibian with a squat body, moist smooth skin, and long hind legs for jumping; about 70 mm long; brown or olive-green; develops from tadpole; Rana esculenta (Edible frog) or Rana punctata (Spotted frog)
LEXSenses.Comments: In this only reference to frogs in the NT, the connotation is of something unclean and abhorrent. In a number of societies, however, frogs are regarded as very valuable and worthwhile animals, since they are often an important source of food. On the other hand, in such areas there are usually certain types of frogs or toads which are particularly poisonous and whose names, therefore, do carry bad connotations.

Notes.Content: βατταλογέω in the sense of ‘to babble’ or ‘to utter senseless sounds’ is treated in {D:33.89}. The justification for βατταλογέω in the sense of ‘to speak much’ is probably to be found in the context of {S:04000600700008}, where the term πολυλογία ({D:33.87}) appears to be an explanation of the meaning of βατταλογέω.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to speak much or extensively, with a possible added implication of meaningless words
Glosses: to speak for a long time
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in {S:04000600700008}, see βατταλογέω[b] {D:33.89}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to utter senseless sounds or to speak indistinctly and incoherently
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βατταλογέω in {S:04000600700008}, see {L:βατταλογέω<SDBG:βατταλογέω:000000>}[a] {D:33.88}.|In some languages the equivalent of ‘to babble’ is ‘to speak like a baby’ or ‘to speak sounds that make no sense.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βδελύσσομαι<SDBG:βδελύσσομαι:000000>}  ‘to abhor,’ {D:25.186}) that which is utterly detestable and abhorrent

(a fixed phrase derived from Hebrew, literally: the detestable thing of desolation) an abomination (either an object or an event) which defiles a holy place and thus causes it to be abandoned and left desolate
LEXSenses.Comments: In translating βδέλυγμα, it may be necessary in some languages to use a phrase such as ‘that which God detests’ or ‘that which God hates’ or even ‘that which causes God’s anger.’ The term ἐρημώσεως may then be translated as ‘that which causes people to abandon’ or ‘that which causes something to be deserted.’ The entire phrase may then be translated in some languages as ‘that which God detests and which causes something to be abandoned’ or ‘… left desolate.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to one who or that which is or should be detested or regarded as abhorrent
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages ‘detestable’ may be rendered as ‘thought to be extremely bad’ or even ‘that which should never even be seen.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to strongly detest something on the basis that it is abominable
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that in {S:06602100800014} ἐβδελυγμένοις refers to sexual perverts.

Notes.Content: The meanings of βέβαιος[c] ({D:28.43}), βεβαιόω[b] and βεβαίωσις ({D:28.44}) involve two quite distinct sets of semantic features. There is the obvious element of that which is confirmed, verified, and true (meanings which could be classified in Domain 72 True, False) as well as the process of making such information known. These meanings could therefore be treated in either domain.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being certain, on the basis of being well established
pertaining to being able to be relied on or depended on
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βέβαιος in {S:05800200200018}, see βέβαιος[c] {D:28.43}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which is known with certainty{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βέβαιος in {S:05800200200018}, see βέβαιος[b] {D:31.90}.

Notes.Content: The meanings of βέβαιος[c] ({D:28.43}), βεβαιόω[b] and βεβαίωσις ({D:28.44}) involve two quite distinct sets of semantic features. There is the obvious element of that which is confirmed, verified, and true (meanings which could be classified in Domain 72 True, False) as well as the process of making such information known. These meanings could therefore be treated in either domain.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βέβαιος<SDBG:βέβαιος:000001>}[b] ‘dependable, reliable,’ {D:31.90}) to cause someone to be firm or established in belief
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βεβαιόω in {S:04101602000024}, see βεβαιόω[b] {D:28.44}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to be known as certain{N:001}
Glosses: to prove to be true and certain
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βεβαιόω in {S:04101602000024}, see {L:βεβαιόω<SDBG:βεβαιόω:000000>}[a] {D:31.91}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to increase in inner strength, with the implication of greater firmness of character or attitude
Glosses: to be strengthened in one’s heart

Notes.Content: The meanings of βέβαιος[c] ({D:28.43}), βεβαιόω[b] and βεβαίωσις ({D:28.44}) involve two quite distinct sets of semantic features. There is the obvious element of that which is confirmed, verified, and true (meanings which could be classified in Domain 72 True, False) as well as the process of making such information known. These meanings could therefore be treated in either domain.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to be known as certain{N:001}
Glosses: to prove to be true and certain
LEXSenses.Comments: {S:05000100700056} βεβαίωσις may denote either the process of making known something in such a way as to confirm its truth or the process of causing people to think about something and to accept it as trustworthy, in which case βεβαίωσις might also be classified in Domain 31 Hold a View, Believe, Trust, Subdomain G Accept as True.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being profane in the sense of worldly or godless

Notes.Content: βεβηλόω may differ significantly from κοινόω[a] in denoting a more serious degree of defilement, but this cannot be readily determined from existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to become unclean, profane, or ritually unacceptable{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to translate literally the concept of ‘unclean,’ for physical cleanliness and ritual acceptability are completely unrelated. In some languages it is necessary to translate κοινόω[a] or βεβηλόω as ‘to take away its holiness’ or ‘to make something unacceptable to God.’ In many cultures one must express this concept as involving so-called negative taboo.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the name of the Devil as the prince of the demons
an alternative form of {L:Βηθζαθά<SDBG:Βηθζαθά:000000>}, {D:93.430} ({S:04300500200026}, apparatus)
a name given to the Devil or to the Antichrist
a small, slender instrument, pointed on one end and with a hole at the other end, used in passing thread through cloth in sewing
LEXSenses.Comments: There is no convincing evidence that the expression ‘eye of a needle’ in {S:04001902400020} and {S:04201802500014} is a figurative name for a narrow gate. The reference to a camel passing through the eye of a needle is a case of rhetorical hyperbole, that is to say, a purposeful exaggeration to point out the extreme difficulty of the event referred to.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: thin straight rod with a sharp point; may be propelled by a bow (arrow) or by hand (dart); used as a weapon in hunting or battle
LEXSenses.Comments: In the NT βέλος occurs only in a highly figurative context: τὰ βέλη … πεπυρωμένα flaming arrows (or darts) {S:04900601600026}, referring to temptations by the Devil.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to events which measure up to their intended purpose
LEXSenses.Comments: In the {D:65.23} contexts, βελτίων, {L:καλῶς<SDBG:καλῶς:000001>}[b], {L:εὖ<SDBG:εὖ:000001>}[b], and {L:εὖγε<SDBG:εὖγε:000000>} occur in highly elliptical constructions.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
the daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Herod Agrippa II
a city in Macedonia
(derivative of {L:Βέροια<SDBG:Βέροια:000000>} ‘Beroea,’ {D:93.422}) a person who lives in or is a native of Beroea
a person mentioned in some manuscripts of {S:04402000400012}
an alternative form of {L:Βεώρ<SDBG:Βεώρ:000000>}, {D:93.74} ({S:06100201500022}, apparatus)
the father of Balaam ({S:06100201500022}, apparatus). Most manuscripts read {L:Βοσόρ<SDBG:Βοσόρ:000000>} ({D:93.80}) in {S:06100201500022}
an alternative form of Βηθσαϊδά, {D:93.432} ({S:04300500200026}, apparatus)
an alternative form of {L:Βηθζαθά<SDBG:Βηθζαθά:000000>}, {D:93.430} ({S:04300500200026}, apparatus)
a place of uncertain location ({S:04300102800006}, apparatus)
a village on the Mount of Olives
a place on the east side of the Jordan where John baptized
an alternative form of {L:Βηθαβαρά<SDBG:Βηθαβαρά:000000>}, {D:93.426} ({S:04300102800006}, apparatus)
an alternative form of {L:Βηθζαθά<SDBG:Βηθζαθά:000000>} ({D:93.430}) ({S:04300500200026}, apparatus)
a pool in the northeast part of Old Jerusalem
a town south of Jerusalem
a place northeast of the Lake of Galilee
a village near Jerusalem, perhaps east of Bethany

Notes.Content: Despite certain differences in size, in some languages the closest natural equivalent of the phrase βῆμα ποδός is simply ‘a square foot,’ while in other languages employing the metric system, a phrase such as ‘a square meter’ would be more appropriate. Some languages, however, may employ expressions such as ‘the measure of an arm’s length’ or ‘the ground of one stride.’ The focal point in {S:04400700500018} is not so much the specific measurement, but rather the very limited space.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a raised platform mounted by steps and usually furnished with a seat; used by officials to address an assembly, often on judicial matters, with a focus on judgement
LEXSenses.Comments: The association of a βῆμα with judicial procedures means that there is almost always an important component of judicial function associated with this term. Therefore in translating βῆμα, it is often best to use a phrase such as ‘a place where a judge decides’ or ‘a place where decisions are made’ or ‘a judge’s seat.’ The focus upon judgment is particularly important in those passages which refer to the judgment seat of God ({S:04501401000040}) and of Christ ({S:04700501000018}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: a step of a foot (a distance of approximately two and a half feet or a little less than a meter)) an extremely limited or restricted space
a person greeted in {S:04501601500010} (apparatus)

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: beryl, usually bluish green or green in color (see {D:2.29})
an alternative form of Βηθσαϊδά, {D:93.432} ({S:04300500200026}, apparatus)
a strong, destructive force
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is difficult, if not impossible, to find a term such as ‘violence,’ but one may describe the effects of violence by expressions which indicate the harm that is done. For example, {S:04400502600024} may be translated ‘they did not wish to harm anyone, for they were afraid of the people,’ and similarly in {S:04402704100044}, one may translate ‘the waves did great damage to the stern.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to experience a violent attack
LEXSenses.Comments: In many languages it may be difficult, if not impossible, to speak of the kingdom of heaven ‘suffering violent attacks,’ but generally some active form may be employed, for example, ‘and violently attack the kingdom of heaven’ or ‘ … the rule of God.’ See comment at βιάζω[b] {D:20.10}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to employ violence in doing harm to someone or something
LEXSenses.Comments: Since there are a number of different interpretations of this expression (πᾶς εἰς αὐτὴν βιάζεται) in {S:04201601600038} as well as for the parallel expression in {S:04001101200028} (ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν βιάζεται; see βιάζω[a]); it is important to consult various commentaries before undertaking a translation. Probably the most widely held interpretation of these difficult expressions is based on the fact that many people did not hesitate to employ violence or military force in order to establish what they regarded as the rule of God on earth.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to the use of violent or strong force
(derivative of βιάζομαι[b] ‘to use violence,’ {D:20.10}) a person who employs violence in order to accomplish his purpose
LEXSenses.Comments: See the comment at {D:20.10} for a discussion of some of the problems involved in the interpretation of this type of expression.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a diminutive derivative of βιβλίον[a], thus, a scroll of small size

Notes.Content: As noted in the case of ἐπιστολή[b] ({D:33.48}), there is an intimate semantic relationship between letter, document, and book as physical objects and the contents of such writings. For book as an object, see βίβλος[a] and βιβλίον[b] ({D:6.64}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a document consisting of a scroll or book
the contents of a book{N:001}
relatively short statements in written form

Notes.Content: As noted in the case of ἐπιστολή[b] ({D:33.48}), there is an intimate semantic relationship between letter, document, and book as physical objects and the contents of such writings. For book as an object, see βίβλος[a] and βιβλίον[b] ({D:6.64}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a document consisting of a scroll or book
LEXSenses.Comments: The books referred to in {S:04401901900018} consisted of sheets of parchment or of papyrus sewn together in the form of long scrolls or bound in the form of a book.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the contents of a book{N:001}
relatively short statements in written form
to consume solid food
an alternative form of {L:Βηθαβαρά<SDBG:Βηθαβαρά:000000>}, {D:93.426} ({S:04300102800006}, apparatus)
a province in northern Asia Minor
to conduct oneself, with focus upon everyday activity
(semantic derivative of {L:βίος<SDBG:βίος:000000>}[a] ‘life,’ {D:41.18}) the resources which one has as a means of living
to conduct oneself, with focus upon everyday activity
to conduct oneself, with focus upon everyday activity
(derivative of {L:βιόω<SDBG:βιόω:000000>} ‘to live,’ {D:41.18}) pertaining to daily life or existence
pertaining to that which causes harm
LEXSenses.Comments: There is no indication in {S:05400600900030} as to the specific nature of the harm, but the extent of it is made clear in the following clause which speaks of complete destruction. This could be physical, moral, and/or spiritual.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause harm or injury to someone or something (a highly generic meaning involving a wide range of harm and injury)
LEXSenses.Comments: In translating terms meaning ‘to harm’ or ‘to injure,’ it may be necessary to specify suffering, for example, ‘to cause people to suffer’ or ‘to cause people to have pain.’

Notes.Content: By setting up certain highly generic meanings for βλαστάνω, δίδωμι, ἀποδίδωμι, and ποιέω, it would be possible to treat the phrase compounds in this series as being semantically endocentric. However, it seems more satisfactory to regard them as what might be called low-grade idioms with specialized meanings of the semantically head expressions.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to begin vegetative growth, with special emphasis upon the sprouting of leaves
LEXSenses.Comments: The initial stages of growth, either of a plant as a whole or in the renewal of foliage after a winter or dry season, may be expressed in a number of ways, for example, ‘to become green again,’ ‘to show leaves,’ ‘to see leaves begin,’ or ‘when leaves unfold.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to produce fruit or seed (of plants){N:001}
a court official of Herod Agrippa I
to speak against someone in such a way as to harm or injure his or her reputation (occurring in relation to persons as well as to divine beings)
LEXSenses.Comments: One way in which βλασφημέω and βλασφημία[a] were used in speaking of defaming God was by claiming some kind of equality with God. Any such statement was regarded by the Jews of biblical times as being harmful and injurious to the nature of God.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to speak against someone in such a way as to harm or injure his or her reputation (occurring in relation to persons as well as to divine beings)
LEXSenses.Comments: One way in which βλασφημέω and βλασφημία[a] were used in speaking of defaming God was by claiming some kind of equality with God. Any such statement was regarded by the Jews of biblical times as being harmful and injurious to the nature of God.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βλασφημέω<SDBG:βλασφημέω:000000>} ‘to blaspheme,’ ({D:33.400}) the content of a defamation
(derivative of {L:βλασφημέω<SDBG:βλασφημέω:000000>} ‘to blaspheme,’ {D:33.400}) pertaining to being insulting and slanderous
(derivative of {L:βλέπω<SDBG:βλέπω:000000>}[a] ‘to see,’ {D:24.7}) that which is seen or that which one becomes aware of

Notes.Content: On the basis of existing contexts, it is not possible to distinguish clearly between the meanings of ὁράω[a] ({D:24.1}) and βλέπω[a] ({D:24.7}). Especially in the Gospel of John, the two terms are used in some instances for what appears to be merely stylistic variation.

It is possible that ἐμβλέπω[b] differs somewhat in meaning from βλέπω[d] in focusing the thought processes on some particular object or matter, but it is difficult to determine this on the basis of existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to see, frequently in the sense of becoming aware of or taking notice of something{N:001}
to have the faculty of sight

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:βλέπω<SDBG:βλέπω:000000>}[a] ‘to see,’ {D:24.7}) to be ready to learn about future dangers or needs, with the implication of preparedness to respond appropriately
to process information by giving consideration to various aspects{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the concept of thinking is closely related to terms referring to perception. For example, in some languages one may speak of thinking as ‘to see with the heart’ or ‘to look at with the liver.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to come to understand as the result of perception
to take responsibility for causing something to happen
Glosses: to see to it that something happens
to arrange for something to happen

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βλέπω<SDBG:βλέπω:000000>}[a] ‘to see,’ {D:24.7}) to be oriented in a particular direction

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Distinguish, To Evaluate, To Judge

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to see into the face) to judge on the basis of external appearances
Glosses: to judge on the basis of appearance
to pay no attention to a person’s status
to judge on the basis of reputation
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages an equivalent of this expression in {S:04002201600064} may be ‘when you judge, you look into a man’s heart’ or ‘when you judge you see more than a person’s face’ or ‘when you judge a person, who he appears to be doesn’t count.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being obligatorily put or placed
a nickname given by Jesus to the sons of Zebedee
to cry or shout with unusually loud volume
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
an alternative form of {L:Βόες<SDBG:Βόες:000000>}[a] ({D:93.78})
the sound of shouting or crying out

Notes.Content: The various terms noted in {D:35.1} (ἀντιλαμβάνω[a], ἐπιλαμβάνομαι[d],  ὑπολαμβάνω[c], συμβάλλω[e], παρίστημι[l], ἀντέχω[c], ἐπαρκέω[a], βοηθέω, βοήθεια[a]) with a generic meaning of ‘help’ no doubt possess certain contrastive features of meaning, at least of a connotative type, but there is no specific evidence of this in NT usage.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: assistance in supplying what may be needed{N:001}
(derivative of {L:βοηθέω<SDBG:βοηθέω:000000>} ‘to help,’ {D:35.1}) an object which provides help or support
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be important to render βοήθεια[b] by something more specific, for example, 'ropes,´ as in 'they fastened some ropes tightly around the ship,´ since ropes may be the most likely reference in {S:04402701700006}.

Notes.Content: The various terms noted in {D:35.1} (ἀντιλαμβάνω[a], ἐπιλαμβάνομαι[d],  ὑπολαμβάνω[c], συμβάλλω[e], παρίστημι[l], ἀντέχω[c], ἐπαρκέω[a], βοηθέω, βοήθεια[a]) with a generic meaning of ‘help’ no doubt possess certain contrastive features of meaning, at least of a connotative type, but there is no specific evidence of this in NT usage.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to assist in supplying what may be needed{N:001}
(derivative of {L:βοηθέω<SDBG:βοηθέω:000000>} ‘to help,’ {D:35.1}) one who provides help or assistance
Glosses: patron (in the sense of one who supports a person or endeavor)

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a hole, trench, or pit, natural or dug
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a distinction is made between ditches dug by people for presumably agricultural purposes and those which are natural depressions in the ground. There is no way to determine from the NT contexts which type of ditch is involved.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βάλλω<SDBG:βάλλω:000000>}[a] ‘to throw,’ {D:15.215}) the distance which one would normally throw some object
to use a rope with a lead weight attached to it in order to measure the depth of water
watery mud, with an additional feature of filth and uncleanness

LEXSenses.Comments: In most languages east and west are related to the rising or setting sun, although in some languages there may be some local geographical feature which serves as a marker of direction, for example, the location of a particular mountain, the ocean, or a river. For north, some languages employ ‘to the left of the rising sun,’ that is to say, the direction is oriented in terms of the left hand of a person facing toward the rising sun. Similarly, south would be ‘to the right of the rising sun.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause animals to eat, particularly pasturing animals
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible to interpret βόσκω in {S:04302101500054} as meaning ‘to tend’ or ‘to take care of,’ especially since βόσκω occurs in a figurative context referring to people. Such an interpretation may be classified in Domain 35 Help, Care For Subdomain D Care For, Take Care Of, as a figurative meaning. However, it seems more likely that βόσκω in {S:04302101500054} should be understood as an instance of figurative usage, and as such it may also be interpreted as βόσκω[b] ‘to take care of,’ {D:44.1}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to herd animals so as to provide them with adequate pasture and to take care of what other needs may be involved
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of βόσκω in {S:04302101500054}, see {L:βόσκω<SDBG:βόσκω:000000>}[a] {D:23.10}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: eating by animals
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages a distinction is made in terms relating to eating by animals on the basis of the type of food involved, for example, animals which graze on grass in contrast with those who eat refuse, roots, acorns, etc. An additional distinction is sometimes made in the case of animals which are largely meat-eating in contrast with those that are predominantly plant-eating.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the father of Balaam
LEXSenses.Comments: Βοσόρ is the reading in most NT manuscripts for {L:Βεώρ<SDBG:Βεώρ:000000>} ({S:00402200500014}); see {D:93.74}. Βοσύρ is an incidental variant spelling ({S:06100201500023}, apparatus)

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any of the smaller green plants (in Hellenistic Greek often used in contexts referring to plants as fodder for animals)
LEXSenses.Comments: βοτάνη is more generic in meaning than {L:χόρτος<SDBG:χόρτος:000000>}[a], {D:3.15}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the small round fruit, sweet and juicy, of a creeping plant that develops a woody stem when it matures; Vitis vinifera; symbol of blessing, prosperity, and happiness
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars have contended that βότρυς means primarily a bunch of grapes, while σταφυλή designates individual grapes. In {S:06601401800068} this difference might seem plausible, but there is scarcely any evidence for such a distinction, since both words may signify grapes as well as bunches of grapes.|In some languages it is necessary to borrow a term for ‘grapes’ from a dominant language and then employ some kind of classifier, for example, ‘fruit called grapes.’ In other languages grapes may be known as ‘wine fruit,’ since wine may be more widely known than a term for grapes.

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a councilor as a member of the Sanhedrin (see {D:11.80})

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.|This meaning is also found as a variant reading: Οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες διεπρίοντο καὶ ἐβούλοντο ἀνελεῖν αὐτούς ‘but when they heard this they were furious, for they were planning to put them to death’ {S:04400503300012} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to think over carefully in an attempt to make a decision

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000001>}[b] and βουλεύομαι[a] ‘to purpose, to plan, to intend,’ {D:30.56}) that which has been purposed and planned
(an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action

Notes.Content: It is also possible to understand βούλημα in {S:04500901900020} as ‘what God desires or wills’ (see {D:25.4}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to desire,’ {D:25.3}) that which is desired, with the implication of accompanying planning and will

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βούλομαι<SDBG:βούλομαι:000001>}[b] and {L:βουλεύομαι<SDBG:βουλεύομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to purpose, to plan, to intend,’ {D:30.56}) that which has been purposed and planned
to desire to have or experience something, with the implication of some reasoned planning or will to accomplish the goal

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to think, with the purpose of planning or deciding on a course of action
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are two quite distinct sets of terms for planning depending upon the purpose involved in such planning. If the planning is constructive, either for oneself or someone else, one set of terms is likely to be used, while if the planning is harmful (usually against someone else), another set of terms would be used.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively low elevated land formation, in contrast with {L:ὄρος<SDBG:ὄρος:000000>} ‘mountain’ ({D:1.46}), which refers to something higher
general word for individual cattle; may be male (bull or ox) or female (cow); plural: cattle
LEXSenses.Comments: In most contexts βοῦς (masc. gender) would seem to refer to an ox (in contrast with {L:ταῦρος<SDBG:ταῦρος:000000>} ‘bull,’ {D:4.16}). In the plural form βοῦς may be translated simply as a collective ‘cattle.’|Though in a number of languages a very special distinction is made between ‘bulls’ and ‘oxen’ (or ‘steers’), no such marked difference occurs in NT usage, and there appears to be no need of introducing any artificial distinction in particular passages.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a gift received as a prize or reward as the result of having won in a competition
LEXSenses.Comments: In some contexts βραβεῖον refers not to a physical prize or reward but to a spiritual benefit, as in {S:05000301400012} (τὸ βραβεῖον τῆς ἄνω κλήσεως τοῦ θεοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ‘the prize which is God’s call through Jesus Christ to the life above’).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to control the activity of someone, based presumably upon correct judgment and decision
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘the peace of Christ’ as ‘controlling.’ In some instances one may translate this expression in {S:05100301500012} as ‘the peace that Christ provides should show you what you should think.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βραδύς<SDBG:βραδύς:000000>} ‘slow,’ {D:67.123}) to extend a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay
to move slowly by boat

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to an extended period of time, with the implication of being slow to do something

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βραδύς<SDBG:βραδύς:000000>} ‘slow,’ {D:67.123}) extending of a period of time, with the implication of slowness and/or delay

Notes.Content: It is possible that χείρ[c], βραχίων[a], and δάκτυλος[b] in the figurative sense of power of an individual differ somewhat in meaning one from the other, but it is impossible to determine this on the basis of existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of βραχίων ‘arm,’ not occurring in the NT) power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: exalted arm, or: lifted up arm) great power, with the implication of an exalted quality

Notes.Content: The series of expressions indicating relative shortness of time may very well differ slightly, at least in connotative meaning, but on the basis of existing NT contexts it is not possible to determine significant denotative differences. The phrases in this series may be technically regarded as idioms, but functionally they are better classed as frozen phrases, which act essentially like morphological units.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively small number of objects or events, probably implying less than expected
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of a small or limited number of objects is expressed by a negative attribution to an expression of large quantity, so that ‘few’ becomes ‘not many.’ For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in {S:05801302200026}, see {D:67.106}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively small quantity or extent, probably implying less than expected
a degree of indefinite approximation
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05800200700006} (a quotation from Psalm {D:8.6}) the expression βραχύ τι as a lexical unit refers to rank. However, {S:05800200800000} suggests that the writer of Hebrews probably interpreted βραχύ as meaning a small quantity (see {D:59.14}) and as referring to time in the sense of ‘a little (while).’ For this interpretation of τι, see {D:92.12}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05801302200026} the phrase διὰ βραχέων may refer to the act of sending the communication or the amount of time required to receive the communication, that is to say, to read the communication or to hear it read. For another interpretation of διὰ βραχέων in {S:05801302200026}, see {D:59.4}.

Notes.Content: The meanings of terms in {D:67.152}-{D:67.158} could almost be treated equally well in Domain 23 Physiological Processes and States, since these could be regarded as simply derivatives of physiological states. However, the focus of meaning in the respective contexts seems to be more upon a particular period of time rather than upon a physiological state or condition.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a very small child, even one still unborn
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages one must make a clear distinction between a baby after its birth and one before birth, that is, a fetus. Hence, in such languages the term employed in {S:04200104100026} must be quite different from the term used in {S:04200201200014}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the period of time when one is very young{N:001}
Glosses: childhood (probably implying a time when a child is still nursing)

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: rain, whether light or torrential
LEXSenses.Comments: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see {D:2.10}). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause rain to fall
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages one cannot say literally ‘to send rain,’ for this would seem to imply that someone was carrying the rain to some destination. It may be more appropriate, therefore, to speak of ‘causing rain to fall’ or ‘causing rain to come down.’ It may be necessary, however, in some languages to indicate whether the occurrence of rain is for the detriment or the benefit of persons involved, and therefore it may be necessary to say in some instances ‘to cause rain to come down upon for the benefit of’; otherwise the reader might infer that the rain was some kind of punishment.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to make something wet or moist
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made in the use of terms which imply different quantities of moisture, and one must make certain that the choice of a term in {S:04200703800024} is in keeping with this context of crying and moistening by means of tears.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the loud sound that accompanies a flash of lightning
LEXSenses.Comments: See {L:ἀστραπή<SDBG:ἀστραπή:000000>}[a] lightning ({D:14.16}) for further discussion.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: rain, whether light or torrential
LEXSenses.Comments: Though most languages have a general term for rain, the event of raining is more frequently referred to by a verb rather than by a noun, since rain is something which takes place and is not regarded as a thing or mass, unless, of course, one is referring to the water which comes down as rain, that is to say, ‘rain water’ (see {D:2.10}). In some languages the event of raining is generally expressed idiomatically as ‘God is urinating.’ This might appear unduly crude and anthropomorphic, but to the speakers of such a language the expression is often quite acceptable and has no undesirable connotations.|Though in English one may use an impersonal subject with the verb ‘to rain,’ for example, ‘it is raining,’ many languages require some kind of personal agent, for example, ‘God is raining,’ or an impersonal agent such as ‘the sky is raining’ or ‘the clouds are raining.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to throw a bridle on) to place restrictions upon someone’s behavior
LEXSenses.Comments: It may, however, be important in some languages to express more clearly the intent involved, and therefore one might wish to translate this clause in {S:04600703500022} as ‘my purpose is not to try to control you’ or ‘… to tell you just what you must do.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering
LEXSenses.Comments: Though it is possible to interpret βρυγμὸς τῶν ὀδόντων as an idiom denoting suffering, it is probably better to understand this in a some what more literal sense (especially in view of biblical views current at that time concerning the next world). It may be important, however, to suggest the significance of this symbolic action, namely, ‘gnashing their teeth in suffering’ or ‘to of suffer so much as to gnash the teeth.’ As in the case of {S:04400705400018}, it is important to avoid an expression for ‘gnashing the teeth’ which will suggest ‘gritting the teeth’ in the sense of determination or courageous resistance.

Notes.Content: It is possible to interpret the phrase βρύχω τοὺς ὀδόντας as being simply an idiom meaning ‘to show anger against,’ but the context suggests that the persons actually did grind their teeth as a symbol of their anger. See also {D:88.184}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Processes Involving the Mouth, Other Than Eating and Drinking

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the grinding or the gnashing of the teeth, whether involuntary as in the case of certain illnesses, or as an expression of an emotion such as anger or of pain and suffering
LEXSenses.Comments: In translating ‘they ground their teeth at him’ ({S:04400705400018}) it may be necessary to indicate the type of emotion which is involved in such an action, for example, ‘in anger they ground their teeth at him’ or ‘they showed their anger by grinding their teeth.’ It is essential to avoid an expression such as ‘to grit the teeth,’ which in English is a symbol of determination, not of anger.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to grind one’s teeth) to express and manifest intense anger
LEXSenses.Comments: As noted in {D:23.41}, it is possible to understand the expression βρύχω τοὺς ὀδόντας in both a literal as well as a figurative sense. The persons may very well have ‘ground their teeth’ as a sign of their anger and fury, so that a statement about what such persons did could be true in a literal as well as in a figurative sense.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause a forceful and abundant supply of a liquid
LEXSenses.Comments: This flow from a spring may be referred to in some languages as ‘to cause to come out’ or ‘to cause to flow out.’

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in the various terms listed here as meaning ‘food,’ but it is impossible to determine such distinctions in meaning from NT contexts. Perhaps τροφή and διατροφή are somewhat more generic in meaning and may suggest a greater emphasis upon nourishment. At the same time, βρῶσις[c] and βρῶμα[a] may imply solid substantive food, but it is difficult, if not impossible, to argue for such subtle connotative distinctions in meanings which are essentially generic.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as {S:04000601100004} as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering {S:04200400400022} (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of {S:04200400400022} is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any type of solid food, particularly meat
(derivative of {L:βρῶσις<SDBG:βρῶσις:000000>}[a] ‘eating,’ {D:23.3}) pertaining to what can be eaten

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in the various terms listed here as meaning ‘food,’ but it is impossible to determine such distinctions in meaning from NT contexts. Perhaps τροφή and διατροφή are somewhat more generic in meaning and may suggest a greater emphasis upon nourishment. At the same time, βρῶσις[c] and βρῶμα[a] may imply solid substantive food, but it is difficult, if not impossible, to argue for such subtle connotative distinctions in meanings which are essentially generic.

It would also be possible to classify βρῶσις καὶ πόσις in {S:04501401700016} as referring to the events of eating and drinking. The meanings of βρῶσις and πόσις ({D:5.6}) would then be classified under Domain 23 Physiological Processes and States, Subdomain A Eat, Drink.

The term βρῶσις is included at this point since it is essentially similar in meaning to κατιόομαι ({D:2.61}) and is probably to be understood as a figurative extension of meaning of βρῶσις ‘eating’ ({D:23.3}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to consume solid food
a meal whether simple or elaborate
LEXSenses.Comments: Though ἄριστον[a], δεῖπνον[a], and βρῶσις[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of {S:04100602100020} that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as {S:04000601100004} as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering {S:04200400400022} (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of {S:04200400400022} is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any type of solid food, particularly meat
the process of producing rust or tarnish by oxidation{N:003}
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:04000601900022} βρῶσις has been generally understood to mean ‘corrosion,’ it might actually refer to a type of insect, as it does in the Septuagint of Malachi {D:3.11}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause to go down into water or other liquid substance
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:βυθίζω<SDBG:βυθίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to cause to sink,’ {D:15.115}) to cause someone to experience serious consequences
the relatively deep area of the sea or ocean sufficiently far from land as to be beyond the range of any protection from the seacoast
LEXSenses.Comments: In order to designate the high sea or the ocean, it may be necessary in some instances to speak of ‘the sea far from land’ or ‘the sea out of sight of land.’ People who live near the ocean and are seafaring frequently have quite distinct terms for different conditions of the sea, whether, for example, it is stormy, moderately rough, or relatively calm. Languages may also use different terms in speaking of different areas of the sea or ocean. Note, for example, in English the use of China Sea, North Sea, Bering Sea, in contrast with Indian Ocean, Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean. In English this contrast is relatively fixed, but it does reflect a gradation of size, since sea is used normally in speaking of smaller areas than is the case with ocean.

Notes.Content: It is possible that βυρσεύς in {S:04400904300022} should be interpreted as the surname of Simon, a Christian in Joppa, that is to say, the name of Simon would be Simon Berseus or Simon Tanner.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who tans hides to make leather

Notes.Content: From the context of {S:06601801200022} it is impossible to determine whether the referents of βύσσινον ({D:6.167}), σιρικόν ({D:6.168}), and πορφύρα ({D:6.169}) are cloth or garments made of linen, silk, and purple cloth respectively.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:βύσσος<SDBG:βύσσος:000000>} ‘fine linen,’ {D:6.166}) cloth consisting of fine linen

Notes.Content: It would be possible to treat λίνον[a] linen cloth ({D:6.165}) and βύσσος fine linen ({D:6.166}) as meaning linen garments and fine linen garments respectively. However, there is no need for setting up such a separate meaning for NT usage, especially since in both {S:06601500600030} and {S:04201601900020} the semantic element of garment or clothing is a significant compound of the verb meaning to dress, and thus the referents would naturally be garments. The same applies to πορφύρα ({D:6.169}) in {S:04201601900020}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: high quality cloth made from the stems of the flax plant; known for its strength and coolness{N:001}
an altar with a base or pedestal; for offering sacrifices to a god
LEXSenses.Comments: In this only reference in the NT in which βωμός occurs, the altar to the Unknown God may be spoken of as ‘a place for offerings to a god whom people do not know’ or ‘… god whose name is not known.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: third in a series involving either time, space, or set
LEXSenses.Comments: Occurring only in titles of NT writings: Ἰωάννου γ ‘Third Letter of John.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the Aramaic name for a paved area outside the residence of Pontius Pilate and the setting for the public trial of Jesus; see {D:7.71}
an archangel
a disease involving severe inflammation and possibly a cancerous spread of ulcers which eat away the flesh and bones
a son of Jacob and ancestor of an Israelite tribe
(derivative of Γάδαρα ‘Gadara,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who lives in or is a native of Gadara
a number of possessions and valuables constituting an important and official asset of a political entity
a city in southwest Palestine on a principal road to Egypt
an alternative form of {L:Γαδαρηνός<SDBG:Γαδαρηνός:000000>}, {D:93.438} ({S:04000802800022}, apparatus)
a room in the Temple used as a treasury
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that in {S:04300802000014} γαζοφυλάκιον designates the offering boxes rather than the treasury itself (see γαζοφυλάκιον[b], {D:6.141}). If one interprets γαζοφυλάκιον in {S:04300802000014} as the offering boxes, then one may translate ‘he spoke these words near where the offering boxes were.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a large box in which offerings were placed
LEXSenses.Comments: The offering box in the Temple was also referred to as {L:δῶρον<SDBG:δῶρον:000001>}[b] ({D:6.142}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Macedonian companion of Paul
a Christian from Derbe
a man from Corinth who was baptized by Paul
the recipient of 3 John

Notes.Content: The meanings of ᾠόν ‘egg’ ({D:5.18}) and γάλα ‘milk’ ({D:5.19}) could be classified under Body Products in Domain 8, but in the NT contexts the focus is upon these products as food and not upon the physiological processes involved in producing such products.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: white fluid secreted by women and female mammals for nourishment of their young; also used as food for humans
LEXSenses.Comments: The term γάλα may refer to any type of milk, whether produced by humans or by certain domesticated animals, for example, cow, sheep, goat, camel.|In a number of languages two distinct terms are used for milk, one identifying the human milk and another term specifying milk from animals. In the context of {S:04600300200002} it is probably the latter reference which is important, though the passage is highly figurative and the emphasis is upon food for babies.{N:001}

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:Γαλατία<SDBG:Γαλατία:000000>} ‘Galatia,’ {D:93.442}) a person who is a native of Galatia
a district in the Roman province of Asia
(derivative of {L:Γαλατία<SDBG:Γαλατία:000000>} ‘Galatia,’ {D:93.442}) pertaining to Galatia

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a calm or unruffled surface of a body of water
Glosses: a calm (in contrast with a storm over water)
LEXSenses.Comments: A calm after a storm may be referred to figuratively in some languages as ‘the water lay down’ or ‘the waves sank down again’ or ‘the water became like a table top.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a district in the northern part of Palestine
the Lake of Galilee, also called Tiberias and Gennesaret
(derivative of {L:Γαλιλαία<SDBG:Γαλιλαία:000000>} ‘Galilee,’ {D:93.444}) a person who is a native of Galilee

LEXSenses.Comments: The Greek term γέεννα is derived from a Hebrew phrase meaning ‘Valley of Hinnom,’ a ravine running along the south side of Jerusalem and a place where the rubbish from the city was constantly being burned. According to late Jewish popular belief, the last judgment was to take place in this valley, and hence the figurative extension of meaning from ‘Valley of Hinnom’ to ‘hell.’ In most languages γέεννα is rendered as ‘place of punishment’ or ‘place where the dead suffer’ or ‘place where the dead suffer because of their sins.’

A number of languages distinguish clearly between various types of laughter: (1) laughter directed against some person as a form of ridicule; (2) laughter resulting from seeing some humorous event or as the result of listening to a humorous account; and (3) laughter which reflects happiness and joy. In {S:04200602100024} and {S:05900400900014} it is this third type of laughter which is relevant to the contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: people living at the same time and belonging to the same reproductive age-class
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘the people of this generation’ may also be expressed as ‘the people living now’ or ‘the people of this time.’ Successive generations may be spoken of as ‘groups of people who live one after the other’ or ‘successions of parents and children.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an ethnic group exhibiting cultural similarities
LEXSenses.Comments: Compare {L:γενεά<SDBG:γενεά:000000>}[a] those of the same time ({D:11.4}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
LEXSenses.Comments: In the case of γενεά[c], {L:τέκνον<SDBG:τέκνον:000001>}[b], and {L:σπέρμα<SDBG:σπέρμα:000001>}[b] ({D:10.29}), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

Notes.Content: See {D:33.38}, where {S:04000100100004} is the illustrative example for βίβλος[c] ‘written statement,’ ‘record.’ See {D:23.46} for γένεσις[a] ‘birth.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: coming into existence by birth
LEXSenses.Comments: A literal translation of {S:04000101800012} as ‘this is the way that Jesus Christ was born’ might be misleading, since it would imply a description of the actual process of his birth rather than an account of those circumstances and events which took place in connection with his birth. It may, therefore, be better to translate {S:04000101800012} as ‘this is what happened when Jesus Christ was born’ or ‘these things happened at the time of Jesus Christ’s birth.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: persons of successive generations who are related by birth
LEXSenses.Comments: In biblical times the reckoning of a lineage was somewhat complex in view of certain distinctions between legal and biological relations. The focus of meaning in γένεσις[b], {L:οἶκος<SDBG:οἶκος:000002>}[c], and {L:πατριά<SDBG:πατριά:000000>}[a] is not, however, the list of ancestors, but the lineage of successively related persons to which the reference person belongs. Some scholars, however, interpret γένεσις in {S:04000100100004} as being part of what is essentially a title for the book of Matthew and thus would render the introductory phrase as ‘the book of the history of Jesus Christ’ (see γένεσις[c] ‘history,’ {D:33.19}).|In some languages a successive series of ancestors is called ‘the forefathers’ or ‘those to whom one looks back’ or ‘those who have gone ahead.’ In other languages a lineage is referred to as ‘a person’s root’ or ‘a man’s trunk’ (referring to the trunk of a tree).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an account of the origin and life of someone
LEXSenses.Comments: For the most part, scholars understand the phrase βίβλος γενέσεως in {S:04000100100004} as referring to the list of ancestors which immediately follows. Therefore, βίβλος γενέσεως is more often interpreted as ‘the record of the ancestors’ or ‘the birth record of …’ (see {D:10.24}).{N:001}

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of existence
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05900102300034} the term γένεσις is largely redundant, for the reference could only be to a person’s own face.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: coming into existence by birth

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the male role in causing the conception and birth of a child
to give birth to a child{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.|γεννάω also occurs together with ἐξ αἱμάτων ({S:04300101300032}) and ἐκ τῆς σαρκός ({S:04300300600004}) in reference to physical birth. In {S:04300300500020}, γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has likewise been interpreted by some scholars as referring to physical birth (compare {S:04300300600004}), but others understand this as referring to baptism. Certainly the occurrence of γεννηθῇ with πνεύματος in {S:04300300500020} is a reference to religious rebirth, in which case γεννάω would involve a radical change of state (see {D:13.56}). The use of the same word with two different meanings or referents is typical of the style of the Gospel of John.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γεννάω<SDBG:γεννάω:000001>}[b] ‘to give birth,’ {D:23.52}) to cause to experience a radical change, with the implication of involvement of the total personality
LEXSenses.Comments: The phrase γεννηθῇ ἐξ ὕδατος has been interpreted by some as a literal reference to physical birth (see {D:23.52}). Others, however, interpret this phrase as referring to baptism by water. In a parallel fashion, the expression γεννηθῇ ἐξ … πνεύματος would refer to baptism by the Spirit or rebirth made possible by the Spirit.

In {S:04300300300026}, however, Nicodemus understood {L:ἄνωθεν<SDBG:ἄνωθεν:000000>} as meaning ‘again’ (see {D:67.55}) and γεννάω as ‘physical birth’ (see {D:23.52}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:γεννάω<SDBG:γεννάω:000001>}[b] ‘to give birth,’ {D:23.52}) that which has been produced or born of a living creature
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be possible to translate this phrase in {S:04000300700030} more or less literally, for example, ‘the offspring of vipers,’ in which ‘vipers’ means poisonous snakes, but in other languages this would be impossible, and one must therefore use ‘little snakes.’ For another interpretation of γέννημα in {S:04000300700030}, see {D:58.26}.

It is for that reason that γεννητοῖς γυναικῶν may be rendered in some instances as ‘of all those persons who have ever lived.’ However, this reference to the preeminence of John the Baptist is difficult, and the implications of it go far beyond the matter of translational equivalence.

Notes.Content: πατριά[a] and φυλή[b] nation, people ({D:11.56}) focus attention upon a particular people as a socially functioning unit, while the feature of biological descent is largely secondary. But in the case of γένος[b] and σάρξ[e], the feature of biological descent is focal, while group functioning is largely secondary.

LEXSenses.Comments: It may be difficult in some languages to clearly distinguish between culture and race as in {S:04100702600016}. Sometimes this difference can be indicated by saying ‘the woman lived like a Greek, but she was a Syrophoenician’ or ‘… her parents were from Syrophoenicia.’ In translating ‘people of my own race’ in {S:04501101400012}, it may be necessary to say ‘all my fellow Jews’ or ‘all those people of whom I am a part’ or ‘those people who are my roots’ or ‘… my trunk,’ based on the analogy of a tree trunk and branches.

Notes.Content: Though γερουσία and πρεσβυτέριον[a] refer to the same council of the Jews as the term συνέδριον[b] ({D:11.80}), this does not mean that the three terms are completely identical in meaning. The focus upon maturity of age and judgment as well as presumed social standing are more significant factors in γερουσία and πρεσβυτέριον[a] than in συνέδριον[b].

to consume solid food
