Notes.Content: The occurrences of γῆ[a], οἰκουμένη[a], and κόσμος[b] relate specifically to the known inhabited areas of the earth, which in the NT period included the countries bordering on the Mediterranean, the Fertile Crescent as far as the Indus Valley, and as far north in Europe as England and Scandinavia. This was the total known earth or world. Such a restriction to a known area of the earth is also true of terms used in some receptor languages, though the referents are obviously different. What is important is not the particular area of the earth, but the corresponding concept of the surface of the earth as the place of human habitation. It is possible that οἰκουμένη[a] differs slightly in meaning from γῆ[a] and κόσμος[b] in view of a somewhat greater emphasis or focus upon the civilized part of earth.

Although in the NT γῆ does not occur as a reference to all solid substances in contrast with fire, air, and water, it does so occur in Classical and Hellenistic Greek. This generic meaning of γῆ as an element is thus not part of the lexical inventory of the NT, but γῆ[b], a designation for soil, ground, does occur.

The overlapping features of meaning in γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμα, ὅριον, and μέρος[c] may be readily illustrated by the comparable overlapping of English terms such as region, territory, and land. For example, in the case of {S:04001502100018} it would be possible to speak of the region of Tyre and Sidon, the territory of Tyre and Sidon, the land of Tyre and Sidon, and even the district of Tyre and Sidon. The English terms region, territory, land, and district do differ in certain nuances of meaning reflecting primarily supplementary components which are largely connotative.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the surface of the earth as the dwelling place of mankind, in contrast with the heavens above and the world below{N:001}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Land in Contrast With the Sea

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: dry land, in contrast with the sea
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between terms which designate land in contrast with water and those which designate cultivated land. Even in English the normal term for land close to water is ‘shore’ or ‘coast,’ and therefore one may translate {S:04001402400018} as ‘the boat was already far away from the shore.’ Similarly, in {S:04402702700042} one may translate ‘we were getting close to shore.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the loose top layer of earth in which plants grow, usually black, brown, or reddish in color and made of organic matter and mineral particles{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: The meaning of γῆ[c] may be expressed in some instances as soil for planting or ground for plants.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:003}
Glosses: land (and even district, though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
LEXSenses.Comments: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:γῆ<SDBG:γῆ:000000>}[a] ‘earth,’ {D:1.39}) all people who dwell on the earth
a more or less fixed phrase: the heavens and the earth, equivalent to a single lexical item: the totality of God’s creation
LEXSenses.Comments: There may be certain complications involved in rendering ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ as ‘heaven and earth,’ since ‘heaven’ might be interpreted in some languages as referring only to the dwelling place of God himself. The referents in this passage are ‘the sky and the earth,’ in other words, all of physical existence, but not the dwelling place of God, for the latter would not be included in what is destined to pass away.

Notes.Content: The meanings of terms in {D:67.152}-{D:67.158} could almost be treated equally well in Physiological Processes and States (Domain 23), since these could be regarded as simply derivatives of physiological states. However, the focus of meaning in the respective contexts seems to be more upon a particular period of time rather than upon a physiological state or condition.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the period of advanced age, normally of a person beyond his or her prime{N:001}

Notes.Content: It is also possible to treat γηράσκω in Domain 23 Physiological Processes and States, but the focus in {S:04302101800032} seems to be more upon duration of time than upon a physiological state.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to become old in age (referring to living beings)

Notes.Content: This meaning of γίνομαι and ἐπιγίνομαι reflects only a slight shift of focus from the meaning of γίνομαι in {D:13.48}, in which the focus is upon the change.

It would also be possible to classify the meaning of γίνομαι[f] and ὑπάρχω[d] as belonging to the domain of Relations (89), especially if one regards the occurrence of the dative of the possessor with γίνομαι[f] and ὑπάρχω[d] as being an integral element in the meaning.
Of all the meanings in Domain 41 (Behavior and Related States), Subdomain A Behavior, Conduct, γίνομαι[g] is undoubtedly the most generic and implies the widest possible scope of conduct.

ἐγένετο δέ and καὶ ἐγένετο occur frequently in the Gospels, especially in Luke, as markers of transition, and in a number of languages they are equivalent to a new paragraph. Note the following passages especially: {S:04200500100000}, {S:04200501200000}, {S:04200501700000}; {S:04200500100000}, {S:04200600600000}, {S:04200601200000}; {S:04200701100000}; {S:04200800100000}, {S:04200802200000}; {S:04200901800000}, {S:04200902800000}, {S:04200903700000}, {S:04200905100000}.

γίνομαι γνώμης is similar to τίθημι ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ and τίθεμαι ἐν τῷ πνεύματι ({D:30.76}). All relate to the process of decision making, but it is possible that the idioms in {D:30.76} indicate greater initiative and purpose.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to come into existence
to possess certain characteristics, with the implication of their having been acquired
to come to acquire or experience a state
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages there is no convenient lexical item meaning simply ‘to become,’ but in all instances there are certain paraphrastic expressions which may be employed, for example, ‘to arrive at being’ or ‘to cease being one thing and be another’ or ‘to change to be.’ One must, however, beware in the case of {S:04300101400010} not to employ some expression which would suggest that Christ had lost his divine nature in becoming a person or that he only appeared to be human (docetism).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to happen, with the implication that what happens is different from a previous state{N:001}
to make a change of location in space (a highly generic meaning)
LEXSenses.Comments: Though the meaning of γίνομαι is often given as ‘to become,’ it is clear that in contexts such as {S:04402501500006} and {S:04402700700016} it would be impossible to render γίνομαι by traditional expressions such as ‘to become.’ In these contexts movement is clearly indicated, and therefore one must frequently employ an expression such as ‘to come to,’ ‘to arrive at,’ or even ‘to travel to.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to belong to someone{N:002}
to exist and to conduct oneself, with the particular manner specified by the context{N:003}
to be in a place, with the possible implication of having come to be in such a place
to come to be in a place
a marker of new information, either concerning participants in an episode or concerning the episode itself (occurring normally in the formulas ἐγένετο δέ or καὶ ἐγένετο{N:004}
LEXSenses.Comments: Often left untranslated.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to become to a man) to become married to a man
(an idiom, literally: to become of a mind) to make up one’s mind, with emphasis upon the process of coming to such a decision{N:005}

Notes.Content: In {S:04300803200004} (γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειανκαὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς ‘you will know the truth and the truth will make you free’), it is also possible to understand γινώσκω as ‘to find out’ or ‘to learn’ ({D:27.2}).

It is possible that ἐπιγινώσκω[b] differs somewhat in meaning from γινώσκω[d] in focusing attention on what is understood or indicating that the process of understanding is somewhat more emphatic, but such a distinction cannot be determined from existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to possess information about
to acquire information by whatever means, but often with the implication of personal involvement or experience
to learn to know a person through direct personal experience, implying a continuity of relationship
LEXSenses.Comments: In translating γινώσκω in {S:04301700300016}, it is important to avoid an expression which will mean merely ‘to learn about.’ Here the emphasis must be on the interpersonal relationship which is experienced.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to come to an understanding as the result of ability to experience and learn{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>} in {S:04001301100018} as meaning ‘to know about’ (see {D:28.1}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to indicate that one does know
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that in {S:04600800300016} {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>} means only ‘to know’ ({D:28.1}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>}[a] to know, {D:28.1})
LEXSenses.Comments: In almost all languages there are euphemistic ways of speaking about sexual intercourse, and the use of γινώσκω[f] and συνέρχομαι[c] is illustrative of this in the Greek NT. It is possible to translate γινώσκω in {S:04200103400026} as simply for I am not married to a man, and likewise, συνέρχομαι in {S:04000101800036} may be rendered as ‘before they were married.’ In some languages one may use such expressions as ‘before they were joined’ or ‘before they slept together’ or ‘before they discovered one another.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a new, sweet wine in process of fermentation
pertaining to being sweet in contrast with being bitter or salty
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it would be somewhat misleading to speak of ‘sweet water,’ since this would suggest water to which sugar or some other sweet substance had been added. The equivalent in {S:05900301100020} may be ‘fresh water’ or ‘good water’ in contrast with ‘bad water’ or ‘not bitter water’ in contrast with ‘bitter water.’

Notes.Content: In this subdomain (Human Beings) a number of expressions referring to people are based upon metonymies involving terms for parts or aspects of persons. Such metonymic figures of speech are involved in σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα ({D:9.14}), γόνυ[b] ({D:9.16}), χείρ[b] ({D:9.17}), γλῶσσα[g] ({D:9.18}), ὄνομα[b] ({D:9.19}), and ψυχή[c] ({D:9.20}).

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: organ in the mouth used for speaking and eating
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:05900300500008} the tongue is referred to as a part of the body, it is used essentially as a symbol for speech, and since in some languages the tongue is not regarded as an organ of speech, but simply as a part of the mouth, it may be necessary to change the expression to read ‘the mouth is a small member of the body’ or ‘speaking is only a small part of one’s life.’ It is obviously not the tongue as an organ which corrupts the whole person, but the capacity for speech which has such a corrupting effect.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a language, with the possible implication of its distinctive form
LEXSenses.Comments: The miracle described in {S:04400200400020} may have been a miracle of speaking or a miracle of hearing, but at any rate people understood fully, and therefore it seems appropriate in this context to speak of ‘languages’ in contrast with {S:04601400200008}, in which case people required an interpreter if they were to receive the presumed content of the speech (see {D:33.3}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an utterance having the form of language but requiring an inspired interpreter for an understanding of the content
LEXSenses.Comments: Most scholars assume that the phenomena described in {S:04400200400000} (see {D:33.2}) and in {S:04601400200000} are significantly different in that in one instance people understood in their own regional language or dialect and in the other instance an interpreter was required. It is for that reason that many interpret γλῶσσα in {S:04601400200008} as ecstatic speech, which was also an element in Hellenistic religions and constituted a symbol of divine inspiration.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) to communicate orally
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) the faculty or capacity for speech
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04200106400018} στόμα and γλῶσσα appear to have the same referent and therefore may be regarded as essentially synonymous.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which has been spoken or uttered
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γλῶσσα<SDBG:γλῶσσα:000000>}[a] ‘tongue,’ {D:8.21}) a person as one who utters something{N:001}
a box in which money was kept
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be useful, however, in rendering {S:04301302900012} to say simply ‘Judas had charge of the money’ or ‘Judas was the treasurer of the group,’ since the Greek expression may be understood as an idiom.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who cards, cleans, and/or bleaches cloth
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04100900300020} the reference is obviously to the process of bleaching, but a γναφεύς also was engaged in the cleaning of cloth as well as carding it, a process by which the nap of cloth was somewhat raised and made soft by being combed with bristles.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
pertaining to possessing purported good character or quality
a condition resulting from the partial or complete absence of light (see {D:14.36})
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is impossible to speak of ‘darkness’ as being an agent in the sense of {S:04202304400016} ‘darkness covered the whole country.’ Accordingly, one must say ‘throughout the whole country it was dark’ or ‘it darkened over the whole country.’ In some languages darkness may be characterized as being a quality of the night, for example, ‘it was like night.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Intend, To Purpose, To Plan

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which is purposed or intended, with the implication of judgment or resolve

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which is regarded or considered to be the case
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to under stand γνώμη in {S:05700101400010} as ‘agreement’ or ‘consent’ (see {D:31.14}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: agreement based on knowledge
LEXSenses.Comments: This interpretation of γνώμη in {S:05700101400010} is less likely than the meaning of γνώμη as ‘opinion’ (see {D:31.3}).

Notes.Content: It would also be possible to treat γνωρίζω in {S:04301501500054} as a matter of communication (Domain 33), but the focal component of meaning in γνωρίζω[b], as in this context, would seem to be upon the resulting knowledge, not upon the communicative process.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to possess information about
to cause information to be known by someone
possessing information about
the content of what is known
esoteric knowledge (primarily philosophical and religious), with the implication of its being heretical and contrary to the gospel
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05400602000028}, ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως may be rendered as ‘that which is falsely called knowledge’ or ‘knowledge which people think is true but is really false.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: coming to an understanding as the result of ability to experience and learn{N:001}
(derivative of {L:γινώσκω<SDBG:γινώσκω:000000>}[a] ‘to know,’ {D:28.1}) one who knows, with the usual implication of to know well
pertaining to that which is known
pertaining to being well known or well acquainted with
LEXSenses.Comments: It may also be possible to understand γνωστός in {S:04200204400038} as meaning ‘friend’ (see {D:34.17}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being well known or famous because of some outstanding quality
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of γνωστός in {S:04400401600020}, see {L:γνωστός<SDBG:γνωστός:000005>}[f] {D:58.55}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being able to be known
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the phrase ‘can be known,’ expressing a capacity relating to a passive state, must be restructured in an active form. This may often be done by rendering {S:04500101900006} as ‘because what people can know about God is clearly evident to these persons’ or ‘they can clearly comprehend what they can know about God’ or ‘because they can clearly see what people can know about God.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being a friend or acquaintance of someone, and thus enjoying certain privileges as a result of such a relation
LEXSenses.Comments: It is clear that in {S:04301801500030} γνωστός implies much more than simply being ‘well known by.’ To have been simply well known by the High Priest could have been a source of danger for the disciple. It was the fact of a relationship of friendship which made it possible for the disciple to view the proceedings.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which is unusual in the sense of being extraordinary
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of γνωστός in {S:04400401600020}, see γνωστός[c] {D:28.32}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to express one’s discontent
to express one’s discontent
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be necessary to restructure ‘complaint’ as a verb rather than as a noun, and therefore this expression in {S:04400600100020} may be rendered as ‘Greek-speaking Jews complained against what the local Jews were doing.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:γογγύζω<SDBG:γογγύζω:000000>} ‘to complain,’ {D:33.382}) one who has a habit of complaining or grumbling

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who habitually fools or deceives people through pretense
the Aramaic name of a hill near Jerusalem where executions took place; see also {D:8.11}
a city located at the southern part of the Dead Sea and destroyed because of its evil
(derivative of γέμω ‘to be laden,’ not occurring in the NT) a relatively heavy object which is carried
biological or legal parents

Notes.Content: In this subdomain (Human Beings) a number of expressions referring to people are based upon metonymies involving terms for parts or aspects of persons. Such metonymic figures of speech are involved in σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα ({D:9.14}), γόνυ[b] ({D:9.16}), χείρ[b] ({D:9.17}), γλῶσσα[g] ({D:9.18}), ὄνομα[b] ({D:9.19}), and ψυχή[c] ({D:9.20}).

One may also interpret the idiom κάμπτω τὸ γόνυ as consisting of a metonymy in the case of τὸ γόνυ (in other words, knee as a substitute for person). Accordingly, κάμπτω to bend or to bow could then be interpreted as meaning simply to worship.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: central hinge joint of the leg where the thigh is joined to the lower leg
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04200500800014} the phrase ‘fell on his knees before Jesus’ should normally not be rendered literally since it might imply accidental stumbling. A more satisfactory equivalent may be ‘knelt down before,’ as a sign of worship or gratitude.|The term γόνυ occurs in a number of idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, in {S:05801201200016} the command ‘to strengthen the weak knees’ should normally not be translated literally, but by an expression meaning ‘to strengthen determination’ or ‘to give courage to’ (see {D:25.152}). The ‘bending of the knees’ in {S:04101501900026} was a sign of mock respect, and in such a context the term for ‘knee’ is often semantically absorbed into an expression meaning literally ‘bow down before’ (see {D:53.61}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γόνυ<SDBG:γόνυ:000000>}[a] ‘knee,’ {D:8.47}) a person in the attitude or position of one worshiping or submitting to authority{N:001}
(a Semitic idiom, literally: the knee bends, or: the knee bows) to bend or bow the knee as a symbol of religious devotion{N:002}
(an idiom, literally: straighten paralyzed knees) to gain encouragement by a strong resolve
LEXSenses.Comments: See discussion at {D:23.170}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

LEXDomains.Domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

Notes.Content: α, β, and γ, the first three letters of the Greek alphabet, are used as ordinal numbers (first, second, and third) in connection with the titles of books of the NT. See Domain 60 Number.
γράμμα[c] may also be classified as a derivative of γράφω to write ({D:33.61}) and mean anything that is written; see {D:33.50}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a letter of the Greek alphabet{N:001}
any kind of written document, whether in book or manuscript form, with focus upon the content

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an object containing writing addressed to one or more persons, normally written on papyrus{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be necessary to try to distinguish between a letter as an object and a letter as content or message. In {S:04402303300018} the focus seems to be upon the letter as an object, not necessarily upon the contents of the document. In most contexts, however, it is impossible to distinguish between a letter as a material object and a letter as a message (see {D:33.48}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a written statement of financial accounts, especially of debts
LEXSenses.Comments: In place of the expression ‘here is your account,’ one may say ‘here is a list of what you owe.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (pl; των n) the body of information acquired in school or from the study of writings
LEXSenses.Comments: For a discussion of problems involved in translating {S:04300701500016}, see {L:μανθάνω<SDBG:μανθάνω:000000>}[a] ({D:27.12}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a recognized expert in Jewish law (including both canonical and traditional laws and regulations)
Glosses: one who is learned in the Law
expert in the Law of Moses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person who has acquired a high level of education in a certain body of literature or discipline
LEXSenses.Comments: In traditional translations γραμματεύς in contexts such as {S:04600102000008} and {S:04001305200016} has been rendered as ‘scribe,’ but this generally is misleading since the term ‘scribe’ is usually restricted in meaning to one who writes or copies documents. A γραμματεύς in Jewish life of Bible times would have been an expert in the Law or a scholar in the Holy Scriptures and not a mere copier of manuscripts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a city official with responsibility for the records of a town or city and apparently certain responsibilities for maintaining law and order
pertaining to being written

Notes.Content: γραφή[a] in {D:33.10} differs significantly in meaning from γραφή[b] ({D:33.53}) in that the latter denotes specifically some OT Scripture passage, while γραφή[a] is a more generic reference to any unit of discourse, though in {S:04200402100020} it happens to refer to an OT section.
For γραφή in the more generic sense, see {D:33.10} and footnote.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a particular portion or unit of discourse{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering τόπος[b], περιοχή, or γραφή[a], it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. In other instances one may wish to use a term meaning the words. Accordingly, {S:04200402100020} may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a particular passage of the OT{N:002}
(pl; ῶν f) the sacred writings of the OT
LEXSenses.Comments: Some translators have mistakenly attempted to use the rendering ‘Bible’ when translating αἱ γραφαί ‘the Scriptures’ in the NT. The reference is to the OT and not to the entire Bible, including both New and Old Testaments. It is also a mistake to translate αἱ γραφαί as ‘God’s writings,’ for this would give the impression that God himself wrote the words.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to make the marks that form words on a surface (paper or other material), using a marking instrument (such as a pen)
LEXSenses.Comments: Since the knowledge of writing is almost universal, there is usually no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for writing. In some instances in which languages are only now being reduced to writing, a phrase is often employed, for example, ‘to make marks on paper’ or ‘to talk with lines’ or ‘to speak with paper.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (pass. form of the verb) what is written, referring to Scripture
(derivative of γραῦς ‘old woman,’ not occurring in the NT) characteristic of old women
to remain awake because of the need to continue alert
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages γρηγορέω in {S:04002404300028} may be rendered as ‘his eyes would be open’ or ‘he would surely see what was happening.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Be Ready To Learn, Pay Attention

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γρηγορέω<SDBG:γρηγορέω:000000>}[a] ‘to stay awake,’ {D:23.72}) to be in continuous readiness and alertness to learn
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γρηγορέω<SDBG:γρηγορέω:000000>}[a] ‘to stay awake,’ {D:23.72}) to remain fully alive and alert
an alternative form of {L:Τρωγύλλιον<SDBG:Τρωγύλλιον:000000>}, {D:93.600} ({S:04402001500031}, apparatus)

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to control oneself by thorough discipline
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘to discipline oneself’ is literally ‘to make oneself obey.’ This may sometimes be expressed idiomatically as ‘to command one’s heart.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to experience vigorous training and control, with the implication of increased physical and/or moral strength
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering γυμνάζω in {S:05801201100042} it may be important in some languages to translate ‘those who have learned by such punishment’ or ‘those whose ways have been made right by such punishment’ or ‘those who because of punishment have learned how they must act.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to engage in physical exercise as a way of improving the body
to dress in worn-out, ragged clothing
pertaining to wearing no clothing or being very scantily clothed
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:γυμνός<SDBG:γυμνός:000000>}[a] ‘naked,’ {D:49.22}) easily able to be known in view of the fact that nothing is hidden
LEXSenses.Comments: It is rare that one can employ in translating γυμνός b a term which literally means ‘naked,’ but it is possible to retain something of the metaphorical value by using a phrase such as ‘with nothing to cover’ or ‘with nothing which can be used to hide.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of being naked or only scantily clothed
LEXSenses.Comments: In the context of {S:04500803500034} ‘nakedness’ refers to poverty.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a diminutive, pejorative derivative of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>}[a] ‘woman,’ {D:9.34}) an adult woman of foolish and/or frivolous charter
(derivative of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>}[a] ‘woman,’ {D:9.34}) pertaining to being a woman
an adult female person of marriageable age
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be awkward to speak of ‘arresting men and women,’ since it is normal in such languages to speak of ‘men and women’ simply as ‘people.’ However, where the distinction of ‘men and women’ can be employed, it should be done, since the arresting of women for presumed heresy in NT times would seem far less justified than the arresting of men, who were supposed to take a more active part in new movements and thus were more likely to be arraigned before authorities.|As a form of address, γυνή was used in Koine Greek in speaking politely to a female person: ὦ γύναι, μεγάλη σου ἡ πίστις ‘Lady, your faith is great’ {S:04001502800016}. In {S:04300200400020} Jesus uses γυνή to address his mother courteously.|In a number of languages it would be totally impossible to have Jesus address his mother merely as ‘woman.’ To do so in some languages would imply that Jesus was denying that Mary was his mother. In other languages, such an expression would imply that Jesus was calling his mother a prostitute or evil person. Accordingly, in a number of languages there is simply no other way in which Jesus could address his mother than as ‘mother’ or ‘my mother.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a woman who is married to a man
LEXSenses.Comments: The distinctions in meaning of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>}[a] woman ({D:9.34}) and γυνή[b] wife parallel those involving {L:ἀνήρ<SDBG:ἀνήρ:000002>}[c] and {L:ἄνθρωπος<SDBG:ἄνθρωπος:000002>}[c] (see {D:10.53}). A number of languages, however, employ essentially the same usage as Greek in that a wife is simply called his woman, my woman, etc. The contexts normally indicate clearly which meaning of {L:γυνή<SDBG:γυνή:000000>} is involved.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to touch a woman) to marry a woman
LEXSenses.Comments: It is important to note that this expression in the second part of {S:04600700100014} may be either a statement by Paul or a quotation from a letter from the church of Corinth. This fact should be clearly noted in the margin.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to take a woman) to marry a woman
(an idiom, literally: to have a woman) to be married to a woman
a cryptic name to designate an enemy to be conquered by the Messiah
the corner of an area or construction, either an inside corner or an outside corner
an alternative form of {L:Θαδδαῖος<SDBG:Θαδδαῖος:000000>}, {D:93.150} ({S:04100301800034}, apparatus)
(derivative of {L:δαιμόνιον<SDBG:δαιμόνιον:000000>}[a] ‘demon,’ {D:12.37}) to be possessed by a demon
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages one cannot speak of a person ‘being possessed by a demon.’ A more appropriate expression may be ‘the person possesses a demon.’ In other instances an idiomatic phrase is employed, ‘the demon rides the person’ or ‘the demon commands the person’ or even ‘the demon is the person.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an evil supernatural being or spirit
LEXSenses.Comments: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a supernatural being of somewhat lesser status than {L:θεός<SDBG:θεός:000001>}[b] ‘god’ ({D:12.22})
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘foreign gods’ ({S:04401701800048}) may be rendered as ‘gods whom the foreigners worshiped’ or ‘gods of the foreigners.’ It would be wrong to render ‘foreign gods’ by a phrase which would mean ‘the gods are foreigners.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:δαιμόνιον<SDBG:δαιμόνιον:000000>}[a] ‘demon,’ {D:12.37}) pertaining to a demon
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages δαιμονιώδης may be rendered as ‘typical of the way a demon acts’ or ‘the way in which demons behave.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an evil supernatural being or spirit
LEXSenses.Comments: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of δάκνω ‘to bite,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause personal harm to someone

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the watery fluid which flows from the eye
to weep, with the clear implication of shedding tears
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between weeping which results from sorrow and grief and weeping caused by physical suffering. Without careful attention to such a distinction, a translator may seriously distort the meaning of the text.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a ring for the finger, normally made of gold or silver and usually containing the signet of the owner by which he could mark ownership and seal documents

Notes.Content: It is possible that χείρ[c], βραχίων, and δάκτυλος[b] in the figurative sense of power of an individual differ somewhat in meaning one from the other, but it is impossible to determine this on the basis of existing contexts.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one of the five long and slender projections of the human hand, used for writing, pointing, grasping, and other activities
LEXSenses.Comments: Though it may seem quite logical to speak of ‘writing with the finger’ ({S:04300800600032}), in some languages one is required to speak of ‘writing with the hand.’ Similarly, in {S:04002300400034} the idiom ‘to lift a finger’ is more satisfactorily expressed as ‘to lift a hand.’ Expressions such as ‘to lift the hand’ and ‘to lift the finger’ must be carefully studied for their idiomatic significance, for ‘to lift the hand’ may mean ‘to release something,’ while ‘to lift the finger’ may be a lewd gesture.|In a number of languages the expression ‘to lift a finger’ ({S:04002300400034}) may be best rendered as ‘to do a thing to help’ or ‘to help in any way.’ For δάκτυλος θεοῦ ‘the finger of God’ ({S:04201102000008}), see {D:76.3}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a place of uncertain location near the western shore of the Lake of Galilee
the southern part of Illyricum
to bring under control and to continue to restrain
LEXSenses.Comments: In many languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘bringing a person under control.’ It may therefore be more appropriate to use some such phrase as ‘not allow a person to do just what he wants’ or ‘make a person behave’ or ‘make a person obey.’ In speaking of animals, one may render {S:05900300700028} as ‘all kinds of wild animals … can be made to obey a person.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the young female of cattle
LEXSenses.Comments: A δάμαλις ‘heifer’ would be older and bigger than a calf but younger than a cow, since ‘heifer’ refers to a cow before she has been impregnated or given birth to her first calf.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an Athenian woman converted by Paul
(derivative of {L:Δαμασκός<SDBG:Δαμασκός:000000>} ‘Damascus,’ {D:93.459}) a person who lives in or is a native of Damascus
the capital of Syria
(derivative of δανείζω ‘to lend money,’ {D:57.209}) that which has been loaned
to lend money, normally with the expectation of receiving the same amount in return plus interest
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04200603400030} it is possible that no interest payment is involved, in which case the meaning is similar to that of {L:κίχρημι<SDBG:κίχρημι:000000>} ‘to lend’ ({D:57.214}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to borrow money, normally with the implication of interest to be paid
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible, however, that in {S:04000504200020} interest on the loan is not involved.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a major OT prophet
(derivative of δανείζω ‘to lend money,’ {D:57.209}) a person whose business it is to lend money to others at an interest rate
to pay out money (or other assets) as a means of obtaining benefits or in payment for benefits
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of δαπανάω in {S:04701201500008}, see δαπανάω[c] {D:42.27}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to spend completely, with the implication of uselessly, and therefore, to waste
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages ‘to waste’ may be expressed as ‘to use up and to get no benefit’ or ‘to have, but for no purpose.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:δαπανάω<SDBG:δαπανάω:000000>}[a] ‘‘to spend,’ {D:57.146}) to exert great effort in doing something
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible, however, that δαπανάω in {S:04701201500008} should be understood in the literal sense and hence rendered ‘I will be glad to spend all I have on your behalf’ (see {L:δαπανάω<SDBG:δαπανάω:000000>}[a] {D:57.146}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:δαπανάω<SDBG:δαπανάω:000000>}[a] ‘to spend,’ {D:57.146}) the amount spent or to be spent in procuring some object or benefit
a king of Israel and an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus
a marker of an additive relation, but with the possible implication of some contrast
marker of a sequence of closely related events
a marker of contrast
a marker of two or more items which are additively related and thematically parallel
a marker of sets of items in contrast with one another

Notes.Content: Though δέησις basically means ‘that which is asked for urgently,’ in the NT it occurs only in connection with pleas made to God, and therefore it is properly translated as ‘prayer.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:δέομαι<SDBG:δέομαι:000000>} ‘to plead, to beg,’ {D:33.170}) that which is asked with urgency based on presumed need{N:001}
to be that which must necessarily take place, often with the implication of inevitability
LEXSenses.Comments: It is impossible to tell in a context such as {S:04101300700020} whether δεῖ implies mere inevitability of an event or whether the events are somehow part of the plan and purpose of God. The latter interpretation could only be derived from broader theological implications and not from the meaning of δεῖ itself.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to be something which should be done as the result of compulsion, whether internal (as a matter of duty) or external (law, custom, and circumstances)
(derivative of {L:δείκνυμι<SDBG:δείκνυμι:000000>}[a] ‘to make known,’ {D:28.47}) the means by which the nature of something is made known, particularly as an example of what is to be avoided
Glosses: means by which something is known

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to suffer public disgrace or shame
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘to disgrace in public’ may be rendered in some languages as ‘to cause everyone to think bad about’ or ‘to cause everyone to speak in whispers about.’

Notes.Content: It is possible that ὑποδείκνυμι[a] is somewhat more emphatic or intensive in connotation than δείκνυμι[a], but this cannot be shown from existing contexts.
There may very well be a slight difference of meaning between δείκνυμι[b] and ὑποδείκνυμι[b], but this cannot be determined from existing contexts.

The ‘more excellent way’ referred to in {S:04601203100026} consists of a verbal statement occurring in 1 Cor 13, so that in this context δείκνυμι refers to an oral communication, but the content of 1 Cor 13 involves far more than oral communication, so that in the context of {S:04601203100026}, one is perfectly justified in analyzing the meaning as being essentially ‘causing to know.’ It is obviously very difficult to determine in the case of δείκνυμι[b] and ὑποδείκνυμι[b] whether the focus is upon the act of communication or upon the resulting knowledge or understanding of the receptors. The same type of difficulty occurs in the meanings listed in {D:33.151}-{D:33.154}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to make known the character or significance of something by visual, auditory, gestural, or linguistic means{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in {S:04601203100026}, see δείκνυμι[b] {D:33.150}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to explain the meaning or significance of something by demonstration{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of δείκνυμι in {S:04601203100026}, see {L:δείκνυμι<SDBG:δείκνυμι:000000>}[a] {D:28.47}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a state of fear because of a lack of courage or moral strength
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘Cowardice’ is often rendered by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to have a fallen heart,’ ‘to have a soft heart,’ or ‘one’s heart has disappeared.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to be fearful and cowardly
pertaining to being cowardly
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages a ‘coward’ is ‘one who always runs’ or ‘one who runs away at nothing.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a reference to an entity which one cannot or does not wish to make explicit (in the NT only a reference to a man)
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in many translations δεῖνα is translated as ‘certain,’ this can give a wrong impression since it would imply that the individual is known to the parties involved or has been identified by the context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which is severe or hard, with the implication of fear
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἀλλὰ ἐγγίζει ἄλλα δεινά ‘but other severe (afflictions) are near’ {S:04101601400042} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an extreme point on a scale involving negative values
to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a meal whether simple or elaborate (this generic meaning of δεῖπνον is in contrast with the more specific meaning of δεῖπνον[b], {D:23.25})
LEXSenses.Comments: Though ἄριστον[a], δεῖπνον[a], and βρῶσις[b] are highly generic in this usage, it is not necessary to translate these terms by a corresponding generic term in another language, since a more specific term may fit the context more satisfactorily. In fact, a generic term might be quite inappropriate in that it would suggest in the case of {S:04100602100020} that Herod was quite stingy in simply providing an ordinary meal for his officials.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the principal meal of the day, usually in the evening
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in the so-called Western world there is a tendency to have three meals each day, breakfast, lunch, and dinner (or supper), in many parts of the world there are only two principal meals: one eaten around nine or ten o’clock in the morning, and another at four or five o’clock in the afternoon.|In some languages there is a very important distinction made between a more or less formal meal and the relatively informal times of eating which might be called ‘snacks.’ These would be occasions on which one would eat only one kind of food and possibly in relatively small quantities.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an elaborate meal
a set of beliefs concerning deity, with the implication of corresponding behavior
pertaining to being religious
LEXSenses.Comments: δεισιδαίμων may occur in either a good or a bad sense; that is to say, it may mean either ‘very religious’ or ‘superstitious,’ although the meaning of ‘superstitious’ is primarily a later development in the meaning of this word. In {S:04401702200032} there seems every reason to believe that Paul was using the term in a positive sense.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: cardinal number, where there are ten instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are eighteen instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are fifteen instances of a countable entity
a league of ten cities in a region east of the Jordan
cardinal number, where there are fourteen instances of a countable entity
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that δεκατέσσαρες in {S:04000101700058} has a symbolic meaning in view of its being equivalent to twice seven. Others have suggested that the number fourteen is derived from the value of the name David based on the numerical values of the consonants in the Hebrew form of the name. This may explain certain of the irregularities in the listing of the generations.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: tenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a tenth part of an object, series, or mass
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering ‘the tenth of the city fell’ in {S:06601101300022}, it may be necessary in some languages to say ‘for every ten buildings, one building fell’ or ‘every tenth building in the city collapsed.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (semantic derivative of {L:δέκατος<SDBG:δέκατος:000001>}[b] ‘tenth part,’ {D:60.65}) a tenth of a substance being offered for some distinctive purpose
to cause someone to pay a tenth
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are problems involved in speaking of ‘a tenth,’ and accordingly there are difficulties in formulating expressions about ‘tithing.’ In some languages one may speak of ‘a tenth’ as ‘one part of ten parts’ or ‘one part together with nine parts.’ ‘To tithe’ may be rendered as ‘from ten parts to pay one part’ or ‘to pay one part and to keep nine parts.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to give a tenth of one’s income
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05800700900024} it may be important to indicate clearly that it was not Levi himself who received the tenth but his descendants. Therefore, one may render the latter part of {S:05800700900024} as ‘Levi, whose descendants collect the tenth, also paid it.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to that which is pleasing in view of its being acceptable
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is necessary to restructure expressions containing ‘acceptable to’ or ‘pleasing to.’ For example, in {S:04401003500022} it may be necessary to translate ‘God accepts whoever worships him and does what is right’ or ‘God is pleased with whoever worships him and does what is right.’ Similarly, in {S:05400200300008} one may translate ‘this is good, and God our Savior likes it’ or ‘… is happy because of it.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being welcomed or acceptable
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering this expression in {S:04200402400018} it may be necessary to restructure the relationships somewhat radically, for example, ‘because people of a town do not wish to accept one of their fellow townsmen as a prophet.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being appropriate or fitting, with the implication of being favorable

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to lure or entice someone to sin (compare δέλεαρ ‘bait,’ not occurring in the NT)
LEXSenses.Comments: δελεάζω may often be translated as ‘to make sinning look attractive’ or ‘to make sin taste good’ or ‘to wave sin in front of a person’s nose.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of relatively large woody plant
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering δένδρον ‘tree’ it is important in a number of contexts to determine whether or not the trees in question produce edible fruit, since in a number of languages this distinction is reflected in the use of quite different terms.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: exact meaning unsure; a soldier other than heavily armed infantry or horsemen
pertaining to being to the right of some point of reference
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of δεξιός as part of an idiom in {S:04101003700022}, see {D:87.34}.

The right hand is often spoken of idiomatically as ‘the good hand’ or ‘the strong hand.’ Sometimes it is called ‘the mouth hand,’ that is to say, the hand which one uses in eating.|For δεξιά in the idiom δεξιὰς δίδωμι ‘to give the right hand’ ({S:04800200900034}), see {D:34.42}.

Furthermore, one must often make a distinction between a skin which still has the hair on it and that which does not. In {S:05801103700024} the likelihood is that these skins were tanned and still retained the hair as extra protection.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

to bind or tie on

LEXSenses.Comments: In translating {S:04401602600042} one may often use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘those things that bound them’ or ‘things with which they were tied.’ It is generally more satisfactory, however, to employ wherever possible a more specific referent, for example, ‘ropes,’ ‘chains’ or ‘fetters.’

LEXSenses.Comments: The state of being a prisoner is often expressed somewhat idiomatically, for example, ‘to be tied hand and foot,’ ‘to be chained like a dog,’ or ‘to look through iron bars.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000000>}[a] ‘bond,’ {D:6.14}) a state of physical incapacity or illness, usually as the result of some controlling supernatural force (in {S:04201301600040}, the result of the activity of Satan)
a person in charge of guarding a jail or prison
a place of detention
LEXSenses.Comments: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:δεσμός<SDBG:δεσμός:000001>}[b] ‘to be in prison,’ {D:37.115}) a person who is under custody in prison

Notes.Content: It would also be possible to classify δεσπότης[a] meaning ‘Lord’ along with κύριος[a] ({D:12.9}) in Domain 12 Supernatural Beings and Powers, Subdomain A, in which titles for supernatural beings are included, but δεσπότης in {S:04400402400024} appears to be more a descriptive appellative rather than a standardized title.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who holds complete power or authority over another

Notes.Content: δεῦρο[a] and δεῦτε may be regarded (particularly in their absolute usage) as semantic hybrids in that they are adverbial in form, but in certain contexts they involve not only extension toward a goal near the speaker but actual movement.
The implications of δεῦρο in {S:04500101300034} may reflect the spacial meaning of δεῦρο[a] here (see {D:84.24}).

Notes.Content: δεῦρο[a] and δεῦτε may be regarded (particularly in their absolute usage) as semantic hybrids in that they are adverbial in form, but in certain contexts they involve not only extension toward a goal near the speaker but actual movement.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: extension toward a goal at or near the speaker and implying movement{N:001}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to the second of two days
LEXSenses.Comments: Some persons have interpreted δευτεραῖος as a period of two days, so that one may translate ‘after two days we came to Puteoli.’ Though general Greek usage does not seem to substantiate this meaning for δευτεραῖος, the context of {S:04402801300024} may involve a span of two days.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a term of doubtful meaning, occurring only in {S:04200600100008} in manuscripts of the Byzantine tradition, and normally omitted in critical texts; one possible meaning is ‘the second after the first,’ but in relationship to the word σάββατον, the reference is uncertain

Notes.Content: There may be some subtle distinction in meaning between δέχομαι[a] on the one hand and λαμβάνω[c] and λῆμψις on the other, in that the latter set of meanings may imply more active participation on the part of the one who receives or takes the gift, but this cannot be determined from existing contexts.

There are no doubt certain contextual constraints involved in the choice of ἀναδέχομαι[a], ἀποδέχομαι[a], ἐπιδέχομαι[a], εἰσδέχομαι, ὑποδέχομαι, προσδέχομαι[b], and παραδέχομαι[b] in the sense that the spacial relationships involved in the welcoming of a guest can be reflected in the prepositional prefixes. For example, in {S:04200804000014} the use of ἀποδέχομαι may focus upon the particular source, while ἐπιδέχομαι in {S:06400101000044} may be relevant in view of the fact that the believers are coming to a particular point. προσδέχομαι in {S:04201500200026} may suggest a kind of reciprocal relationship which is established with outcasts, and παραδέχομαι in {S:04401500400010} may simply point to spacial proximity. However, it would be wrong to insist upon clear distinctions in meaning based on the very limited number of contexts involved. Some of these same distinctions in spacial relations may exist for the set προσλαμβάνω[e], παραλαμβάνω[d], ἀπολαμβάνω[d].
It is possible that δέχομαι in {S:04202201700004} may mean ‘to receive’ (see {D:57.125}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver, but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver{N:001}
to accept the presence of a person with friendliness{N:002}
to readily receive information and to regard it as true
to take hold of something or someone, with or without force
LEXSenses.Comments: A number of languages differ radically in terms for ‘taking hold of,’ depending upon whether force is employed, whether the object is a thing or an animate being, and whether the language incorporates into a verb of ‘taking hold of’ a classification as to the objects involved, for example, long and thin, round and flat, ball-like, angular, or lumpy.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to tie objects together, or tie something around something else
to confine someone by binding with ropes or chains
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘To imprison a person’ is often expressed in somewhat idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to be tied inside’ or ‘to be locked in the dark’ or even ‘to eat one’s food with rats.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to compel someone to act in a particular manner
LEXSenses.Comments: In some instances ἀναγκάζω and δέω[c] may be rendered as ‘to cause it to be necessary for.’ In other instances a simple causative seems to be the closest equivalent. For example, the last clause of {S:04800201400058} may be expressed as ‘how can you make Gentiles live like Jews,’ and in {S:04402002200008} one may translate ‘and now the Spirit makes me go to Jerusalem.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to be under the authority of someone or something else
to exercise authority over something on the basis that it is not legitimate
LEXSenses.Comments: There are a number of different interpretations of the implication of this statement in {S:04001601900034}, and translators should carefully review this passage in various commentaries.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause physical incapacity for someone
marker of relatively weak emphasis
Glosses: indeed or frequently not translated but possibly reflected in the word order

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being clearly and easily able to be known
to make something known by making evident what was either unknown before or what may have been difficult to understand
to make something evident or clear by explanation
Glosses: to make clear to make evident

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a companion of Paul

Notes.Content: It is possible that δημηγορέω implies somewhat greater formality than διαλέγομαι[b], but it is impossible to determine this on the basis of NT usage.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to speak in a somewhat formal setting and probably implying a more formal use of language{N:001}
a silversmith in Ephesus
a church leader
one who creates a construction, involving both design and building (often used in reference to divine activity)

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a group of citizens assembled for socio-political activities
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that in ἐκκλησία[c] there is somewhat more focus upon the people being together as a legal assembly, while in the case of δῆμος the emphasis is merely upon a meeting of citizens. But in the NT one cannot distinguish clearly between the meanings of these two words.|ἐκκλησία[c] and δῆμος may be rendered in some languages as ‘a meeting of the people who belonged to that place’ or ‘… who were inhabitants of that town’ or ‘… whose homes were in that town.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being able to be known by the public
LEXSenses.Comments: The rendering of διακατηλέγχετο in {S:04401802800012} provides the verbal correspondences ‘he … refuted … in … debate.’ The term δημοσίᾳ indicates that the debates took place in public so that everyone could know or did know what was said and proven. It is, of course, possible to understand δημοσίᾳ only in the sense of ‘public setting,’ but in {S:04401802800012} something more than mere setting seems to be implied.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Roman silver coin equivalent to a days wage of a common laborer
LEXSenses.Comments: The practice of translating terms for coins with specific monetary values has differed widely in different languages at different times and in different contexts. One of the most serious problems has been the recent rapid inflation which has taken place in many parts of the world and which has thus made traditional renderings relatively meaningless or even absurd. For a number of years the silver content in an ancient denarius was equivalent to twenty cents U.S., but the value of silver has changed appreciably within recent times, and therefore any calculation based upon the value of silver content in ancient coins is misleading. Furthermore, in ancient times silver coins had proportionately far more buying power than the equivalent amount of silver would have today. Therefore, a number of translators have attempted in some measure to relate coinage to buying power, or perhaps better, to earning power. For example, in {S:04100603700030} the reference to ‘two hundred denarii’ is sometimes translated as ‘the equivalent of 200 days’ wages’ or even ‘eight months of a laborer’s wages.’|In {S:04001802800030} the reference to ‘a hundred denarii’ is designed primarily to indicate the contrast between the enormous sum owed by one servant in contrast with the very small amount owed by the fellow servant. In this instance the contrast may be expressed in terms of ‘thousands of denarii’ in contrast with a ‘few denarii.’ In such a case the equivalent coinage may be turned into a local currency, for example, ‘thousands of dollars’ in contrast with a ‘few dollars.’ In a number of cases translators have attempted to avoid any specific reference to a particular coin and have simply spoken of ‘silver coins’ or ‘gold coins’ without indicating particular values. Under such circumstances a marginal note is sometimes employed in order to indicate the relative value of the currency.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time without Reference to Other Points of Time: Time, Occasion, Ever, Often

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an indefinite point of time or occasion
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο οἵῳ δήποτ᾽ οὖν κατείχετο νοσήματι ‘he was cured from whatever disease he ever had’ {S:04300500400018} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of somewhat greater emphasis (in comparison with {L:μέν<SDBG:μέν:000001>}[b], {L:γέ<SDBG:γέ:000000>}, and {L:δή<SDBG:δή:000000>}, {D:91.6})

Notes.Content: There are probably certain subtle distinctions between the use of διά[c] in contrast with εἰς[h] or ἐν[p] as markers of means, but this cannot be clearly determined from existing contexts.
It is possible to interpret διά in {S:04000802800054} as being a blend of two meanings, namely, extension along a path and passage through an area (see {D:84.29}).

The series of expressions indicating relative shortness of time may very well differ slightly, at least in connotative meaning, but on the basis of existing NT contexts it is not possible to determine significant denotative differences. The phrases in this series may be technically regarded as idioms, but functionally they are better classed as frozen phrases, which act essentially like morphological units.

LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04100601700028} Herodias clearly constituted the reason or cause for Herod putting John in prison, but there is a sense in which διὰ Ηρῳδιάδα may also indicate Herods purpose in trying to please Herodias, and therefore one may translate ‘for the sake of Herodias’ (see {L:διά<SDBG:διά:000003>}[d], {D:90.38}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: through days) a point of time subsequent to another point of time after an interval of a few days

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a relatively brief extent of time{N:003}
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be best to translate this phrase in {S:06000501200018} as ‘I have written a brief letter.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a title for the Devil, literally ‘slanderer’) the principal supernatural evil being{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there is a well known proper name for the Devil as the chief of all demons. In other instances, however, he is given a descriptive name, for example, ‘the ruler of the evil spirits,’ ‘the chief of the demons,’ ‘the truly bad one,’ ‘the left-handed one’ (as the one who is opposed to all which is right or correct), ‘the no-good one,’ ‘the avaricious one.’ In some instances a term for the Devil may be highly idiomatic as, for example, ‘the barking one,’ a reference to the Devil’s presumed activity in animal guise.|Some translators have attempted to construct a term for Devil on the basis of the meaning of the Greek term διάβολος as ‘slanderer.’ This, however, has rarely been advisable, largely because in practically all languages there is a far more relevant way of speaking about the Devil. Other translators have attempted to render the term Devil by simply borrowing the form of the word from a dominant language, but this may also introduce complications, since one cannot always control the manner in which such a term will be understood. In one language, for example, the borrowed term ‘devil’ was identified simply as a small spirit that spreads fever among people, while in another area the borrowed term ended up meaning only a spirit which induces insanity. In this latter instance, the translators finally used an expression for the Devil which meant literally ‘the lord of all sin.’|Some translators have employed for ‘Devil’ the proper name Satan, but this is often not a satisfactory solution. In one language in West Africa, for example, the term Satan had already been borrowed but was understood in the sense of the culture hero of the people and not as a designation for the chief of demons.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an evil supernatural being or spirit
LEXSenses.Comments: While in a number of languages the Devil may be spoken of as ‘the chief of the demons,’ sometimes the demons are simply called ‘the spirits of the Devil’ or ‘the servants of the Devil.’|In a number of languages the difficulty in terminology for demons is not the absence of a term, but the abundance of different terms for different kinds of demons, each one of which may be responsible for particular kinds of human behavior, for example, insanity, depression, epilepsy, sex perversion, and violent assault. Sometimes demons are classified as ‘those of the home’ and ‘those of the forest,’ in which case the latter are normally regarded as more violent and virulent. When there is an abundance of different terms for demons and no generic term for all types of demons, one can usually select a class of demons which parallels most closely the descriptions of demon activity in the NT and use such a term with appropriate contextual qualifications so as to suggest that such a term is to be understood in a general sense.|For another interpretation of διάβολος in {S:04300607000030}, see {D:88.124}.

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in the various terms listed here as meaning ‘food,’ but it is impossible to determine such distinctions in meaning from NT contexts. Perhaps τροφή and διατροφή are somewhat more generic in meaning and may suggest a greater emphasis upon nourishment (see footnote b). At the same time, βρῶσις[c] and βρῶμα[a] may imply solid substantive food, but it is difficult, if not impossible, to argue for such subtle connotative distinctions in meanings which are essentially generic.

It is possible that τροφή and διατροφή focus primarily upon the meaning of food as nourishment, and in {S:05400600800006} and {S:04001001000034} it would be perfectly appropriate to use a translation meaning ‘nourishment’ rather than merely ‘food.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as {S:04000601100004} as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering {S:04200400400022} (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of {S:04200400400022} is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

Notes.Content: In this meaning δίδωμι serves primarily as a so-called empty verb. The event is to be found in the so-called object of the verb.
δίδωμι seems to imply a benevolent purpose in the action of assigning someone to a role.

By setting up certain highly generic meanings for βλαστάνω, δίδωμι, ἀποδίδωμι, and ποιέω, it would be possible to treat the phrase compounds in this series as being semantically endocentric. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. In contexts such as {S:04002202000012} an equivalent translation may be simply ‘a picture,’ but in {S:04500102300020} and {S:04400704300030} one may use the same expression as is employed to render {L:εἴδωλον<SDBG:εἴδωλον:000000>}[a] ‘idol’ ({D:6.97}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Same or Equivalent Kind or Class

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which has the same form as something else
LEXSenses.Comments: Since the expressions τοῦ χοϊκοῦ and τοῦ ἐπουρανίου refer to individuals, it is much more satisfactory to translate {S:04601504900022} as ‘just as we have the likeness of the man made of earth, so we will have the likeness of the Man from heaven.’|In {S:04601504900022} εἰκών designates similarity in class or kind, while in {S:04500102300020} εἰκών indicates a fashioned object (see {D:6.96}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which represents something else in terms of basic form and features

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

Notes.Content: It is possible that in {S:05000101000018} εἰλικρινής is to be understood in the sense of moral purity and hence ‘with clean lives’ or ‘without fault.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being sincere in the sense of having pure motivation

Notes.Content: The ellipsis of εἰμί[a] in this type of construction may be regarded as a zero actualization, that is, a significant omission.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an emphatic marker of condition
to speak or talk, with apparent focus upon the content of what is said
to use an attribution in speaking of a person
LEXSenses.Comments: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in {S:04000102300022} the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to say something in order to explain more fully the implications or intent of what has been said

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Have an Opinion, Hold a View

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to speak to oneself) to think about something without communicating the content to others
Glosses: to say to oneself (often used to introduce a direct quotation of one’s thoughts)

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to live in peace with others
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ‘live in peace’ is a negation of fighting, for example, ‘do not fight’ or ‘do not constantly quarrel.’

Notes.Content: εἰρήνη in Domain 25 pertains to a psychological state and not to a set of circumstances which may lead to peace and tranquility (see {D:22.42}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a set of favorable circumstances involving peace and tranquility
LEXSenses.Comments: The meaning of ‘peace’ or ‘tranquility’ may be expressed in some languages in a negative form, for example, ‘to be without trouble’ or ‘to have no worries’ or ‘to sit down in one’s heart.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a state of freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘Peace’ in the sense of ‘freedom from worry’ is often expressed by means of an idiom, for example, ‘to sit down in the heart,’ ‘to rest in the liver,’ or ‘to be quiet in one’s inner self.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to freedom from anxiety and inner turmoil
to cause a state of peace or reconciliation between persons
LEXSenses.Comments: εἰρηνοποιέω is closely related in meaning to the series in {D:40.1} in that the making of peace or reestablishing peace between persons is a distinctive feature of reconciliation, but the focus in εἰρηνοποιέω seems to be upon the resulting state rather than upon the process.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:εἰρηνοποιέω<SDBG:εἰρηνοποιέω:000000>} ‘to make peace,’ {D:40.4}) a person who restores peace between people
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:04000500900006} the cessation of war is by no means excluded, the focus of meaning of εἰρηνοποιός is reconciliation between persons and not primarily to cause wars to cease.

Notes.Content: In the meaning of extension toward a goal, εἰς[a] ({D:84.16}) and ἐπί[e] ({D:84.17}) overlap considerably. It is, of course, possible to argue that ἐπί implies being on or at a point, while εἰς defines entering into an area related to some point, but such a distinction would seem to be arbitrary.
In contexts where an accompanying expression designates movement into an area, ἐν[a] and εἰς[d] may be rendered as ‘into,’

There are no doubt certain subtle distinctions in the meanings of the terms in {D:83.9}. For example, πρός[d] may suggest some kind of interaction or response and παρά[b] may focus upon association, but it is difficult, if not impossible, on the basis of existing contexts to define precisely the differences in meaning.
There are probably certain subtle distinctions between the use of διά[c] in contrast with εἰς[h] or ἐν[p] as markers of means, but this cannot be clearly determined from existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: extension toward a special goal{N:001}
extension toward a goal which is inside an area

LEXSubDomains.Domain: On, Upon, On the Surface Of

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a position on the surface of an area
a position defined as being within certain limits{N:002}
a position within an area determined by other objects and distributed among such objects{N:003}
a marker of intent, often with the implication of expected result
a marker of result, with the probable implication of a preceding process
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret εἰς in this construction of {S:05300100500014} as purpose (see εἰς[f], {D:89.57}).|It would be possible to interpret εἰς … ἄγω in {S:04500200400040} as being purely an expression of cause since ἄγω[g] (see {D:36.1}) also involves a component of cause, and therefore one may interpret the expression εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει as ‘it causes you to repent.’ In either case, however, εἰς marks a resulting event or state.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of the means by which one event makes another event possible{N:004}
(with the accusative) a marker of content as a means of specifying a particular referent

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a degree extending to a particular point as marked by the context
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04701001500046} περισσείαν itself indicates a superabundant degree of something (see {D:78.31}), while εἰς marks a degree up to such a point. One may say, therefore, that semantically εἰς serves to reinforce the meaning of περισσείαν.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of a change of state
a marker of an involved experiencer
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible to translate {S:06000101100030} as ‘trying to find out when the time would be and how it would come’ by interpreting εἰς in {S:06000101100030} as εἰς[i] ({D:90.23}) and ποῖον as {L:ποῖος<SDBG:ποῖος:000001>}[b] ({D:58.30}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (with the accusative) a marker of persons benefited by an event, with the implication of something directed to them
LEXSenses.Comments: In both {S:04601600100012} and {S:04700800400028} there is clearly an ellipsis of an event of ‘sending’ such help to and on behalf of God’s people.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (with the dative) a marker of objects which serve as symbolic substitutes for supernatural persons or powers presumed to act as guarantors of compliance with oaths

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
