LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04301000900008} θύρα[b] is used figuratively to refer to Jesus as the means of access to salvation: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα δἰ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθω σωθήσεται ‘I am the door; whoever comes in by me will be saved.’ In {S:04301000900008} the emphasis is upon the door as a passageway and not as an object closing off an entrance. Literal translations of ‘I am the door’ may often lead to misinterpretation, since the term used for ‘door’ is likely to refer to a literal door rather than to the entranceway, thus suggesting that Jesus Christ functions primarily to prevent passage rather than making entrance possible.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time subsequent to another point of time and indicating imminence, that is to say, the subsequent event is regarded as almost begun
a long, oblong shield; used to protect the entire body in battle; made of wood, metal, leather stretched over wood, or plaited strips of wood or reeds
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages ‘shield’ is described as ‘protection one carries when one fights’ or ‘protection carried to prevent blows from the enemy.’ The phrase ἀναλαβόντες τὸν θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως may thus be rendered as ‘take hold of faith as a protection against the enemy’ or ‘regard your faith as a protection to prevent the attacks of the enemy.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an opening in a wall for the entrance of light and air and for the purpose of seeing in or out
one who guards the door giving access to a house or building
that which is offered as a sacrifice

any type of altar or object where gifts may be placed and ritual observances carried out in honor of supernatural beings (in the NT θυσιαστήριον is employed to refer to a number of different types of altars; including the altar for burnt offerings in the Temple; the altar of incense; the altar which Abraham built; and the heavenly altar mentioned in the book of Revelation)
LEXSenses.Comments: A descriptive equivalent of ‘altar’ occurs in some languages as ‘a place where offerings are made to God’ or ‘a place where gifts are given to God.’ In some contexts it may be necessary to add phrases such as ‘where sacrifices are burned to God’ or ‘where incense is burned to honor God.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to slaughter an animal in a ritual manner as a sacrifice to deity
to slaughter, either animals or persons; in contexts referring to persons, the implication is of violence and mercilessness
one of the twelve apostles; see also {D:93.95}
a piece of armor covering the chest to protect it against blows and arrows

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the portion of the upper trunk covered by the breastplate
LEXSenses.Comments: Note, however, that in {S:06600900900006} it is possible to understand the first occurrence of {L:θώραξ<SDBG:θώραξ:000000>} in the sense of ‘breastplate,’ the meaning which it normally has in other biblical contexts (for example, {S:04900601400024} and {S:05200500800014}). The passage could then be translated as ‘their breastplates were iron breastplates’ (see {D:6.39}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a synagogue official
the patriarch Jacob, a son of Isaac
the father of {L:Ἰωσήφ<SDBG:Ἰωσήφ:000001>}[b] in the genealogy of Jesus
one of the twelve apostles and the son of Zebedee and brother of John
a brother of Jesus
the son of Alphaeus and one of the twelve apostles
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars consider Ἰάκωβος[c] and {L:Ἰάκωβος<SDBG:Ἰάκωβος:000003>}[d] to be the same person.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the son of {L:Mary<SDBG:Μαρία:000003>}[d] and called ‘the younger’ in {S:04101504000034}
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars consider {L:Ἰάκωβος<SDBG:Ἰάκωβος:000002>}[c] and Ἰάκωβος[d] to be the same person.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the father of Judas, one of the twelve apostles
a tax collector called ‘James’ rather than ‘Levi’ ({S:04100201400008}, apparatus)
(derivative of {L:ἰάομαι<SDBG:ἰάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to cause to be well again, to heal,’ {D:23.136}) the capacity to cause someone to become healed or cured
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be difficult to speak of ‘giving the power to heal.’ A more natural form of expression is ‘cause to be able to heal.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jannes opposed Moses before Pharaoh
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
an Egyptian sorcerer who together with Jambres opposed Moses before Pharaoh

Notes.Content: It is possible that διασῴζω is somewhat more emphatic in meaning than σῴζω. It is also possible that in a number of contexts σῴζω and διασῴζω may have the added implication of having rescued such persons from a state of illness.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to become well again after having been sick{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ἰάομαι<SDBG:ἰάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to heal,’ {D:23.136}) to cause something to change to an earlier, correct, or appropriate state
the father of Enoch in the genealogy of Jesus
to cause someone to become well again after having been sick
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are different terms for ‘healing’ depending upon the type of sickness or illness which is involved.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: jasper; probably green in color (see {D:2.29})
the host of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica
a person who sends greetings in {S:04501602100020}
one who causes someone to be healed

Notes.Content: τὰ ἴδια is a substantivized form of ἴδιος[a], occurring only in the neuter plural and meaning one’s own possessions, as in {S:04201802800018}, ἰδοὺ ἡμεῖς ἀφέντες τὰ ἴδια ἠκολουθήσαμέν σοι look, we have left all our possessions to follow you. Some scholars, however, interpret τὰ ἴδια in this passage to mean one’s own home. In {S:04300101100014}, εἰς τὰ ἴδια ἦλθεν he came into his own possessions, it is possible to understand τὰ ἴδια in the sense of his own nation.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being the exclusive property of someone{N:001}
pertaining to that which is peculiar or distinctive to some entity

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a reference to each one individually

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: persons who in some sense belong to a so-called reference person
(an idiom, literally: according to that which is private) pertaining to what occurs in a private context or setting, in the sense of not being made known publicly
a person who has not acquired systemic information or expertise in some field of knowledge or activity
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04601401600022} ἰδιώτης is used to refer to a class of persons who were neither unbelievers nor fully instructed Christians, but who were inquirers or catechumens. In such a context, ἰδιώτης may be rendered as ‘ordinary, uninitiated’ (ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς ἐν πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ ‘when you give thanks to God in spirit only, how can an ordinary, uninitiated person taking part in the meeting say “Amen” to your prayer of thanksgiving’).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a mountainous region south of Judea (Edom of the OT)

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the watery fluid excreted through the pores of the skin
King Ahabs notorious queen
a city in Phrygia
the role of being a priest
the role of being a priest
to serve as a priest in the performance of religious rites and duties
LEXSenses.Comments: In contrast with the prophet who speaks to people on behalf of God, the priest is often defined as one who represents the people before God. In reality, however, the priest is one who is primarily engaged in religious ritual and ceremony in contrast with the prophet, whose primary activity is involved in proclaiming a message. In societies in which there is no organized priesthood and where there are only medicine men or shamans, it has often been possible to translate ἱερουργέω and ἱερατεύω as simply ‘to be God’s shaman.’ Whether such an expression can be used depends very largely upon the connotations associated with shamanism.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a major OT prophet
(derivative of {L:ἱερουργέω<SDBG:ἱερουργέω:000000>} or {L:ἱερατεύω<SDBG:ἱερατεύω:000000>} ‘to serve as a priest,’ {D:53.85}) one who performs religious rites and duties on behalf of others
a city in Judea, not far from the north end of the Dead Sea
pertaining to being sacrificed to a deity
Glosses: having been sacrificed to a deity
LEXSenses.Comments: In some cultures sacrificing is not practiced, and even the idea of killing an animal as a gift to a deity seems not only strange but even abhorrent. In such languages no special term is to be found for sacrifice, and it may therefore be necessary to use a phrase such as ‘to kill an animal and give it to God’ or ‘to kill an animal in honor of God.’ In such cases, however, it is obviously necessary to have some kind of supplementary note or glossary statement which will attempt to explain the significance and function of sacrifice in the Bible.

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in this series, but it is difficult to define these distinctions on the basis of existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being devoted to a proper expression of religious beliefs{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the concept of ‘living a godly life’ may be best expressed as ‘to live as God would have one live’ or ‘to live like one should who believes in God’ or ‘to always do what God requires.’ In some languages, however, the only equivalent is ‘to live a good life’ or ‘to live always doing good to others.’ The shift from the focus upon religious belief to good living or being good to others results from the fact that in some religious systems there is little or no connection between religious beliefs and moral behavior.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being appropriate for the expression of worship and reverence
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04600901300012} the reference of the expression οἱ τὰ ἱερὰ ἐργαζόμενοι is the activities in the Temple involving the performance of various rituals.|In a number of languages, however, it is difficult to speak of ‘holy writings’ or ‘holy activities.’ In some instances one may use an expression which refers to positive taboo, that is to say, something which has been dedicated exclusively to the service of God, but in other languages it may be necessary to use some phrase which identifies objects or activities as being ‘appropriate for worship’ or ‘characteristic of worship’ or ‘involved in worship.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a temple or sanctuary ({L:ναός<SDBG:ναός:000000>}[a], {D:7.15}) and the surrounding consecrated area
LEXSenses.Comments: With the exception of ἱερόν in {S:04401902700038} (a reference to the temple of Artemis in Ephesus), ἱερόν in the NT refers to the Temple in Jerusalem, including the entire Temple precinct with its buildings, courts, and storerooms.|In a number of languages ἱερόν is rendered normally as ‘the house of God,’ or, as in {S:04401902700038}, ‘the house of the goddess Artemis.’ In a number of languages, however, there are technical terms for ‘temple,’ and these are often carefully distinguished from an expression designating a central sanctuary in which the deity is thought to dwell (ναός[a]).|Though in a number of contexts it is not necessary to distinguish between ἱερόν and ναός, in {S:04002101200032} (and parallel passages: {S:04101101500038}, {S:04201904500010}, and {S:04300201400010}) it is important to indicate this distinction, so as not to leave the impression that sacrificial animals were actually being sold inside the central sanctuary.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the city of Jerusalem, including its inhabitants
the heavenly Jerusalem of the future
(derivative of Ιεροσόλυμα ‘Jerusalem,’ {D:93.480}) an inhabitant of Jerusalem
to take by force or stealth objects from a temple
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret ἱεροσυλέω in {S:04500202200020} as meaning ‘to commit sacrilege,’ in the sense of doing harm or damage to sacred objects in temples (see {D:53.104}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to commit sacrilege by doing harm or damage to sacred objects in temples
LEXSenses.Comments: In biblical times the damaging of valuable objects in a temple was more than simply a criminal act, since it involved a serious breach of respect for supernatural beings. LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to serve as a priest in the performance of religious rites and duties
LEXSenses.Comments: In contrast with the prophet who speaks to people on behalf of God, the priest is often defined as one who represents the people before God. In reality, however, the priest is one who is primarily engaged in religious ritual and ceremony in contrast with the prophet, whose primary activity is involved in proclaiming a message. In societies in which there is no organized priesthood and where there are only medicine men or shamans, it has often been possible to translate ἱερουργέω and ἱερατεύω as simply ‘to be God’s shaman.’ Whether such an expression can be used depends very largely upon the connotations associated with shamanism.

Since leprosy was regarded as a defilement and hence made a person ritually unacceptable, it also meant excommunication from normal social life. The removal of leprosy was regarded as an important religious matter, and the healing had to be verified by the priests before an individual was regarded as ritually cleansed. In a number of languages, however, it is quite impossible to speak of ‘cleansing a leper,’ for this would mean only ‘giving a bath to a leper.’ Accordingly, it may be essential to say ‘to heal a leper’ or ‘to cure a leper’ or even ‘to make a person’s leprosy disappear.’ In such instances it is usually essential to have some kind of marginal note or glossary explanation so as to indicate the religious implications of leprosy and the resulting ritual defilement.

Notes.Content: There are certain technical problems involved in treating the series καθέζομαι, κάθημαι[a], καθίζω[a] ({D:17.12}) and συγκάθημαι, συγκαθίζω[a] ({D:17.13}), since there appears to be an alternation in meaning between (1) being in a position and (2) assuming such a position. It would be possible to set up two distinct meanings or to assume that the respective forms are essentially ambiguous. In general, however, the participial forms indicate a state of being, while the non-participial forms imply assuming a particular position of being seated. However, there are certain subtle differences in the tenses of the participial forms, and hence one cannot determine precisely what are the referential distinctions.

In the first place, it is important to translate the phrase ‘garment of camel’s hair’ in such a way as to indicate that the garment was made of cloth woven out of camel’s hair and did not consist of the entire skin nor of camel’s hair stuck onto John the Baptist’s body. Notes.Content: κατά[e] differs in meaning from μέσος[a], ἀνὰ μέσον[a],ἐντός[a], εν[b], μετά[h], εἰς[e], ἐπί[c], πρός[d], and παρά[b] ({D:83.9}) in that the focus of meaning is upon distribution rather than upon inclusion within any defined area or set.
It is possible that κατά in {S:04402700500010} refers to a position parallel with the coast and possibly involving a type of extension.

The difference in meaning between the set κατά[g], ἐπί[s], ἐν[s], ἐκ[k], and καθώς[d] and the set πότε, ποτέ[b], ὁπότε, ὅτε[a], and ὅταν[b] ({D:67.30}) is largely a matter of class meanings, but there may be certain subtle rhetorical differences as well.

It would seem that the meanings of items in subdomains {D:70.1}-{D:70.4} (ὅλως[b], ὄντως, ἀληθής[b], ἀληθινός[a], ἀληθῶς, and idioms with ἀλήθεια) do reflect certain subtle differences, but it is not at all easy to determine precisely how they differ.

It is possible to interpret κατ ἰδίαν as being primarily an element of setting, that is to say, without the presence of other persons, but in some contexts the focus seems to shift from setting to the fact that such events take place without the general knowledge of the public. Depending therefore upon the context, one may render κατ ἰδίαν by such expressions as without others knowing or without other people being present.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a pointed stick used in driving draft animals
LEXSenses.Comments: In the NT κέντρον[b] occurs only in the idiom πρὸς κέντρον λακτίζειν 'to kick against the goad;' meaning to hurt oneself by active resistance.{N:001} See {D:39.19}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κέντρον<SDBG:κέντρον:000000>}[a] ‘sting,’ {D:8.45}) the power or ability to kill or destroy
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κέντρον in {S:04601505500020}, see {D:24.86}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κέντρον<SDBG:κέντρον:000000>}[a] ‘sting,’ {D:8.45}) the means or capacity to cause severe suffering
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κέντρον in {S:04601505500020}, see {D:20.69}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Roman officer in command of about one hundred men
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages, centurion can very readily be rendered by a phrase such as ‘a commander of a hundred soldiers,’ but in many instances the closest natural equivalent is simply ‘captain.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being totally without purpose
a part of a letter of the alphabet
LEXSenses.Comments: The reference of {L:ἰῶτα<SDBG:ἰῶτα:000000>} ({D:33.36}) and κεραία is to the small details of the Law, and therefore it may be appropriate in many languages to translate {S:04000501800034} as ‘not one of the smallest parts of the Law will be done away with’ or ‘… will become null and void.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κεράμιον<SDBG:κεράμιον:000000>} ‘earthenware vessel,’ {D:6.128}) one who makes earthenware vessels
(derivative of {L:κέραμος<SDBG:κέραμος:000000>} ‘potter’s clay,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to being made of potter’s clay
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may seem unduly repetitious to speak of ‘clay pots’ in {S:06600202700022} since a term for pot may refer only to objects made of clay. In biblical times, however, some σκεύη were of metal and others were of stone and wood. It may be possible to translate this expression in {S:06600202700022} as ‘they shall be broken like pots’ or ‘… like dishes.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an earthenware container for storing or carrying liquids
a thin slab or bent piece of baked clay; used to cover a roof
to mix substances, normally liquids
LEXSenses.Comments: Note that in the process of mixing, the various substances become a single mass, and the constituent parts are indistinguishable. For another interpretation of κεράννυμι in {S:06601401000024}, see {D:47.3}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to pour something out
LEXSenses.Comments: Since κεράννυμι normally means ‘to mix,’ it is possible to interpret the participial form κεκερασμένου in {S:06601401000024} as meaning ‘to be mixed’ (see {D:63.9}), but this would seem to contradict in some measure the following adjective {L:ἄκρατος<SDBG:ἄκρατος:000000>} ‘full strength, pure’ ({D:79.99}).

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the hard bony outgrowth on the heads of certain animals
LEXSenses.Comments: Finding a term for ‘horn’ is usually not at all difficult. The problem arises when a term for ‘horn’ is already employed in a receptor language as a euphemistic expression for the male genital organ. It may therefore be necessary in {S:06600500600042} to speak of ‘a lamb with seven horns on his head.’|In speaking of the horn-shaped corners of the altar ({S:06600901300026}), it is often better not to use a term meaning literally horn, since this might imply that the altar had the horns of animals stuck on to the corners. One can normally say ‘corners of the altar shaped like horns’ or ‘… looking like horns or projections on the corners of the altar.’ See {D:79.105}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a projection at the corner of an object
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κέρας<SDBG:κέρας:000000>}[a] ‘horn,’ {D:8.17}) power of unusual significance
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04200106900006} the reference of the phrase κέρας σωτηρίας is to the role of the Messiah, and accordingly one may often best render this phrase as ‘mighty Savior’ or ‘powerful Savior.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a diminutive derivative of {L:κέρας<SDBG:κέρας:000000>}[a] ‘horn,’ {D:8.17}) the pod of the carob tree (which closely resembles a small horn)
LEXSenses.Comments: Carob pods were commonly used for fattening swine and were employed as an article of food by poor people. In translating {S:04201501600012} it is not necessary, however, to identify specifically carob pods. In most languages some such expression as ‘edible pods’ is probably more satisfactory, since carob trees are unlikely to be known.

Notes.Content: κερδαίνω normally has the meaning of to gain or to make a profit (see κερδαίνω[a], {D:57.189}); however, the avoidance of a loss may also be regarded as a gain.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to gain by means of one’s activity or investment
to cause a loss not to happen{N:001}
(derivative of {L:κερδαίνω<SDBG:κερδαίνω:000000>}[a] ‘to earn, to gain,’ {D:57.189}) that which is gained or earned
LEXSenses.Comments: κέρδος in the sense of ‘gain’ is not restricted, however, to monetary gain or profit. It may refer to any kind of benefit or advantage, for example, ἐμοὶ γὰρ τὸ ζῆν Χριστὸς καὶ τὸ ἀποθανεῖν κέρδος ‘for me life is Christ, and death is a gain’ {S:05000102100018}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: coins of lesser value
one who exchanges currency, either in terms of different types of currency or different values of the same currency
a brief statement of the main point of a previously given discourse
a sum of money

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: uppermost part of the human body, or the front or upper part of the body of an animal, typically separated from the rest of the body by a neck, and containing the brain, mouth, and sense organs; associated with the entire person, that person’s life and responsibilities
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be necessary to distinguish clearly between the head which is still a part of a body and a severed head. It is this latter meaning which is obviously involved in {S:04100602500038}.|In rendering {S:04601100400022}, πᾶς ἀνὴρ προσευχόμενος ἢ προφητεύων κατὰ κεφαλῆς ἔχων ‘any man who prays or prophesies with his head covered,’ it may be important to indicate that the covering is not one which is designed to cover the entire head including the face, but only the top of the head. The same applies, of course, to {S:04601100500024} and {S:04601100700016}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κεφαλή<SDBG:κεφαλή:000000>}[a] ‘head,’ {D:8.10}) one who is of supreme or pre-eminent status, in view of authority to order or command
Glosses: one who is the head of

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a set phrase, literally: head of the corner) the cornerstone or capstone of a building, essential to its construction (κεφαλὴ γωνίας occurs in the NT only figuratively in reference to Christ)
LEXSenses.Comments: Though some scholars have thought that κεφαλὴ γωνίας refers to a keystone of an arch or the lintel stone over a door, it is highly probable that κεφαλὴ γωνίας has essentially the same meaning as ἀκρογωνιαῖος.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
LEXSenses.Comments: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’ {S:04000802000050}, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In {S:04301903000026} this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see {D:16.16}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to have down on the head) to wear a covering over one’s head
to beat someone on the head, implying repeated blows

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Instruments Used in Marking and Writing

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: section of a scroll or of a long composition
LEXSenses.Comments: Long compositions often involved several scrolls, and a κεφαλίς would form one section or scroll of such a composition.|In the case of practically all terms for documents (for example, ‘letter,’ ‘book,’ ‘scroll’) the meaning involves not only the object on which the writing was done, but also the contents of the writing. In some languages a distinction must be made between these two aspects of such objects, and one must make certain that the particular expression used in a receptor language will at least include the contents and not refer merely to the materials on which the words may have been written.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to put something over or around the mouths of animals so as to prevent them from eating
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it may be necessary to employ some type of descriptive equivalent of ‘to muzzle,’ for example, ‘do not tie the mouth of the ox so that it cannot eat’ or ‘do not cover the mouth of the ox so that it cannot eat.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a borrowing from Latin) a tax paid by each adult male to the government
LEXSenses.Comments: See discussion at {D:57.179}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a field used for the cultivation of herbs, fruits, flowers, or vegetables
one who takes care of a garden or orchard

LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: οἱ δὲ ἐπέδωκαν αὐτῷ … ἀπὸ μελισσίου κηρίου ‘and they gave him … some honeycomb’ {S:04202404200014} (apparatus); see {D:4.50}. In rendering κηρίον it is important to employ an expression which will include both the honey and the comb. A literal rendering of ‘honeycomb’ might refer only to the wax container without the honey, but for many languages a term meaning simply ‘honey’ also refers to the honeycomb.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κηρύσσω<SDBG:κηρύσσω:000002>}[c] ‘to preach,’ {D:33.256}) the content of what is preached
(derivative of {L:κηρύσσω<SDBG:κηρύσσω:000002>}[c] ‘to preach,’ {D:33.256}) a person who preaches

Notes.Content: The referent of κηρύσσω[c] ({D:33.256}) is essentially similar to that of εὐαγγελίζω ({D:33.215}), for both expressions may refer to the content of the gospel. This does not mean, however, that the meaning of the two expressions is precisely identical.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to announce in a formal or official manner by means of a herald or one who functions as a herald
to announce extensively and publicly
to publicly announce religious truths and principles while urging acceptance and compliance{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate κηρύσσω[c] without indicating the content of what is preached. Accordingly, one may have such expressions as to preach about the good news or to preach about God.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any large sea creature
the Aramaic equivalent of the Greek name {L:Πέτρος<SDBG:Πέτρος:000000>} ‘Peter’ ({D:93.296})
a large box-like structure (the vessel built by Noah)
LEXSenses.Comments: The central meaning of κιβωτός is ‘box’ or ‘chest,’ but it was apparently applied to Noah’s ark in view of the type of construction and the fact that Noah’s ark resembled more a barge than a seagoing vessel. However, in view of the size of Noah’s ark, it is probably best in most languages to speak of it as a ‘ship.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any box-like container, whether plain or elaborate; here, refers to the box used to hold the tablets of the Law
LEXSenses.Comments: In the NT κιβωτός[b] occurs only in the phrase κιβωτὸς τῆς διαθήκης ‘the box of the covenant,’ which was placed in the Holy of Holies of the Temple in Jerusalem and referred to also as being in the heavenly temple ({S:06601101900028}).|In the case of English some persons object to speaking of the so-called ‘ark of the Covenant’ as ‘the Covenant Box,’ since they assume that the English word ‘ark’ has some special meaning equivalent to the corresponding Greek or Hebrew terms. However, the term ‘ark’ in Old English and Middle English is simply a borrowing of Latin arca meaning ‘box, chest, coffer.’ In present-day English the term ark is known primarily from the context of ‘Noah’s ark.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a small stringed harp-like instrument held in the hands and plucked
LEXSenses.Comments: The closest equivalent to a κιθάρα is in most instances a small harp.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κιθάρα<SDBG:κιθάρα:000000>} lyre, harp, {D:6.83}) to play a lyre, a small stringed harp-like instrument held in the hands and plucked
(derivative of {L:κιθαρίζω<SDBG:κιθαρίζω:000000>} ‘to play a lyre,’ {D:6.84}) one who plays the lyre, a small stringed harp-like instrument held in the hands and plucked
a province in the southeast corner of Asia Minor
to be in dangerous circumstances
to expose oneself to danger
a state of dangerous and threatening circumstances
to make a change of location in space (a highly generic meaning)
LEXSenses.Comments: A strictly literal translation of κινέω in {S:04401702800012} might imply merely moving from one place to another. The meaning, however, is generalized movement and activity; therefore, it may be possible to translate κινούμεθα as ‘we come and go’ or ‘we move about’ or even ‘we do what we do.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to be moved from a place
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to translate κινέω in {S:06600200500036} as ‘I will take away.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to set something in motion, with the nature of the movement dependent upon the object in question
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04101502900012} the shaking of the head signifies derision and scorn, but in some languages this meaning is expressed by quite different gestures, for example, pointing with the finger, throwing back the head, or shrugging the shoulders. In fact, in some languages shaking the head from side to side means assent, while nodding shows opposition.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause people to riot against

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Agent in a Causative Role Marked by Verbs

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a marker of a causative relation, with the implication of significant activity
the motion of a solid or mass, without indication of movement in space
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἐκδεχομένων τὴν τοῦ ὕδατος κίνησιν ‘waiting for the water to move’ {S:04300500300018} (apparatus).|In a number of languages it may be necessary to indicate clearly the kind of motion which would be implied in {S:04300500300018}. Perhaps the most satisfactory rendering would involve the kind of motion resulting from the bubbling up of water, but not with the implication of being caused by heat. It would be inappropriate to use a term meaning merely ‘to shake,’ since this might suggest an earthquake.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a type of spice derived from the bark of certain aromatic plants
LEXSenses.Comments: In most languages κιννάμωμον is simply borrowed in a transliterated form. However, it is also possible to use a type of descriptive phrase, for example, ‘good-tasting bark’ or ‘flavoring bark.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the father of King Saul
to give something to someone for use, with the expectation that the same or its equivalent will be returned
a secondary woody stem arising from the trunk or bough of a tree or shrub
Glosses: branch (of a tree or woody shrub)
LEXSenses.Comments: Some languages distinguish carefully between two major types of branches those which are essentially leaves (as in the case of palms) and those which have a number of buds or potential branches. Other languages may make a distinction between branches of a plant which is woody (a perennial) and those which are relatively soft and flexible, typical of an annual plant.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04000201800020} κλαίω occurs with a so-called ‘direct object,’ for example, Ραχὴλ κλαίουσα τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς … ὅτι οὐκ εἰσίν ‘Rachel weeps for her children … because they are all dead.’ The so-called direct object is, however, the cause of the weeping, and the so-called transitive usage of κλαίω does not alter the meaning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κλάω<SDBG:κλάω:000000>} ‘to break,’ {D:19.34}) a fragment or piece resulting from the action of breaking
alternative forms of {L:Καῦδα<SDBG:Καῦδα:000000>}, {D:93.497} ({S:04402701600012}, apparatus)
a Christian woman who sent greetings in {S:05500402100026}
Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus (compare {D:93.359}), a Roman emperor, who ruled from 41 A.D. to 54 A.D.
Claudius Lysias, a Roman officer in Jerusalem
to weep or wail, with emphasis upon the noise accompanying the weeping
to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to break bread) to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.|The implication of ‘eating together’ comes from the total context. ἐν δὲ τῇ μιᾷ τῶν σαββάτων συνηγμένων ἡμῶν κλάσαι ἄρτον ‘on the first day of the week we gathered together for a meal’ {S:04402000700018}. No doubt the reference in {S:04402000700018} is to the ‘fellowship meal,’ called ‘agape,’ which constituted the early Christian form of the ‘Lord’s Supper.’ See {D:23.28}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an instrument used for locking and unlocking doors and gates
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering {S:06600900100040} it may not be possible to speak of ‘the key to the abyss,’ but rather ‘the key to the entrance to the abyss’ or ‘the key used in opening or closing the gate to the abyss.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κλείς<SDBG:κλείς:000000>}[a] ‘key,’ {D:6.220}) a means of acquiring something
LEXSenses.Comments: One may also translate this expression in {S:04201105200016} as ‘you have kept to yourselves the key to knowledge’ or ‘… the means by which one may gain understanding.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to be shut
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of this expression in {S:04400502300012} would be ‘we found the jail securely locked.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to close the bowels) to refuse to show compassion
to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
a believer whom Jesus met on the road to Emmaus

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a good reputation as an index of status
(derivative of {L:κλέπτω<SDBG:κλέπτω:000000>} ‘to steal,’ {D:57.232}) a person who steals
to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else
a more or less tender, flexible branch, as of a vine
a member of the church at Philippi
to receive something of considerable value which has not been earned
to receive a possession or benefit as a gift from someone who has died, generally a parent
Glosses: to receive from a deceased parent
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the process of inheritance must be made rather explicit, so that ‘he will inherit the property’ must be expressed as ‘he will become owner of the property which his father said he should have.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000000>}[a] ‘to gain as a possession,’ {D:57.131}) a valuable possession which has been received
(derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000001>}[b] ‘to inherit,’ {D:57.138}) that which is received from a deceased person
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04201201300034} it may also be possible to render κληρονομία as ‘the property our father left us’ or ‘the property which our father said should be given to us.’

Notes.Content: It is possible to interpret κληρονόμος in {S:05900200500034} (and particularly in {S:05600300700012}) as identifying essentially a future experiencer, but with the additional components of the experience being valuable and not having been worked for. In this respect κληρονόμος overlaps between Subdomain I, Receive, in Domain 57 Possess, Transfer, Exchange, and Domain 90 Case.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000000>}[a] ‘to gain as a possession,’ {D:57.131}) one who receives something as a gift
Glosses: one who comes into possession of

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κληρονομέω<SDBG:κληρονομέω:000001>}[b] ‘to inherit,’ {D:57.138}) the person who inherits possessions
a specially marked pebble, piece of pottery, or stick employed in making decisions based upon chance
LEXSenses.Comments: Both in form as well as in function, the closest equivalent of κλῆρος[a] is frequently a term which refers to dice. In {S:04202303400038} a term for dice would be particularly appropriate.|It is not possible to know the particular method employed in ‘choosing by lot,’ for evidently various devices were used. In {S:04400102600006} (ἔδωκαν κλήρους αὐτοῖς ‘they drew lots,’ literally ‘they gave them lots’), it is probable that small sticks were handed out. See also footnote under {L:κληρόω<SDBG:κληρόω>}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which is given as a rightful possession (often in the sense of an inheritance)

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Assign to a Role or Function

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a responsibility, function, or ministry which has been assigned to a person
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in {S:04400101700018}, see {D:63.18}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: what has been assigned as someone’s responsibility to take care of
a share or portion which has been assigned or granted
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κλῆρος in {S:04400101700018}, see {D:37.101}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: the lot falls upon someone) the process of choosing, with the probable implication of discerning God’s will in this manner
LEXSenses.Comments: In some societies the closest natural equivalents of deciding by lot are procedures involving ‘drawing straws’ or ‘throwing dice’ or ‘throwing down sticks’ or ‘dropping pebbles.’

Notes.Content: The phrases δίδωμι κλήρους in {S:04400102600006} and βάλλω κλήρους in {S:04202303400038} (βάλλω κλῆρον in {S:04002703500018}) refer to choosing someone by means of casting lots, but these expressions may be interpreted in a strictly literal sense and thus are not treated here as idioms (see {D:6.219}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of κληρόω ‘to be chosen by lot,’ not occurring in the NT) to choose, with the implication of supernatural or divine intervention or guidance{N:001}
Glosses: to choose in accordance with the will of God

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to urgently invite someone to accept responsibilities for a particular task, implying a new relationship to the one who does the calling
LEXSenses.Comments: It is rare that one can translate {L:καλέω<SDBG:καλέω:000003>}[d], κλῆσις[a], and {L:προσκαλέω<SDBG:προσκαλέω:000001>}[b] as simply ‘to call’ in the sense of ‘to speak to someone at a distance and tell them to come.’ For example, in {S:05300201400008} it may be necessary to render the above clause as ‘through the good news we preached, which summoned you to do this.’ Similarly, in {S:04401601000026} one may translate ‘because God has urgently invited us to preach the good news to the people there.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of having been called to a particular task and/or relation
LEXSenses.Comments: As in the case of {L:καλέω<SDBG:καλέω:000003>}[d], {L:κλῆσις<SDBG:κλῆσις:000000>}[a], and {L:προσκαλέω<SDBG:προσκαλέω:000001>}[b] ({D:33.312}), it may be entirely impossible to use a term in a receptor language which means literally ‘to call.’ Therefore, it may be necessary to translate {S:04900400100024} as ‘I ask you then … live worthy of the responsibility which God has urgently invited you to accept’ or ‘… live worthy of the task which God has given you to do.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the station in life or social role which one has
LEXSenses.Comments: In this context, κλῆσις refers to the status or role of being either a slave or a free person. In a number of languages this expression in {S:04600702000008} can be best translated as ‘everyone should continue to be the same kind of person that he was when he was called.’ Such an expression must, of course, refer to one’s position in society and in the total social structure, not to particular aspects of moral or immoral behavior.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to having been called
LEXSenses.Comments: As in the case of the translation of meanings in {D:33.312} and {D:33.313}, it may be necessary likewise to make certain semantic adjustments in the translation of κλητός[a] . For example, the phrase in {S:04500100100010} may be rendered as ‘urgently invited to be an apostle’ or even ‘summoned and commissioned to be an apostle.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to having been invited
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that this expression in {S:04002201400008} was a common popular saying, namely, an adage. There are certain problems in the understanding of this adage in {S:04002201400008}, for it would seem as though many persons are invited to do something, but few are permitted to do it. Perhaps this should be understood in the sense of ‘many are invited to apply, but few are selected.’ In this context, of course, both the invitation and the selection would be by God.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a dome-like structure made of clay, in which wood and dried grass were burned, and then after being heated, was used for baking bread
LEXSenses.Comments: The function of κλίβανος may be described as ‘a place heated for baking bread,’ and it may be useful in some instances to employ a more extensive description of a κλίβανος in a glossary, but this is rarely necessary since function is far more important than form.

Notes.Content: The overlapping features of meaning in γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμα, ὅριον, and μέρος[c] may be readily illustrated by the comparable overlapping of English terms such as region, territory, and land. For example, in the case of {S:04001502100018} it would be possible to speak of the region of Tyre and Sidon, the territory of Tyre and Sidon, the land of Tyre and Sidon, and even the district of Tyre and Sidon. The English terms region, territory, land, and district do differ in certain nuances of meaning reflecting primarily supplementary components which are largely connotative.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: region or regions of the earth, normally in relation to some ethnic group or geographical center, but not necessarily constituting a unit of governmental administration{N:001}
Glosses: district (though this might imply too precisely a governmental area)
LEXSenses.Comments: The meanings of γῆ[d], χώρα[b], κλίμαὅριον, and μέρος[c] are not to be regarded as completely synonymous, but in certain of their NT usages they are largely overlapping in reference.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any piece of furniture employed for reclining or lying on
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04000900200014} a rendering such as ‘stretcher’ or ‘cot’ is certainly more advisable than the traditional rendering ‘bed,’ which might imply a large piece of furniture. In each passage one must employ a term which is most likely to identify the type of object which fits the context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively small and often temporary type of object on which a person may lie or recline; made of reeds or cloth; thin and light for carrying
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of contexts the terms κλινίδιον, κλινάριον, and κράβαττος refer to cots or stretchers on which sick or convalescent persons might be resting or on which they could be transported. There is no NT context in which these terms refer to couches on which people reclined while eating.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to incline
LEXSenses.Comments: See also {D:23.83}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause to flee or run away from

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κλίνω in {S:04200901200010}, see {D:68.51}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to begin to come to an end, with particular reference to the period of a day (a figurative meaning dependent upon the position of the sun)
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κλίνω in {S:04200901200010}, see {D:67.118}.

LEXDomains.Domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication

LEXCollocations: κλίνω τὸ πρόσωπον εἰς τὴν γῆν

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to incline the face to the ground) to prostrate oneself before someone as an act of reverence, fear, or supplication
(an idiom, literally: to lay down the head) to experience the rest which comes from sleep
LEXSenses.Comments: ὁ δὲ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου οὐκ ἔχει ποῦ τὴν κεφαλὴν κλίνω ‘the Son of Man has no place to lie down to rest’ {S:04000802000052}, implies that Jesus possessed no permanent home. In {S:04301903000022} this same expression must be understood not as an idiom but as a case of literally bowing the head (see {D:16.16}).

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a group of persons engaged in eating together
LEXSenses.Comments: Note that Luke employs κλισίας in essentially the same type of context in which Mark uses συμπόσια.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to take secretly and without permission the property of someone else

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a moving ridge or succession of swells on the surface of a body of water
to be tossed back and forth by the motion of waves
Glosses: to be tossed about by waves
LEXSenses.Comments: The imagery in {S:04900401400010} is based upon a person in a boat being tossed about by the waves. It may, therefore, be necessary to introduce a boat or ship in the context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the husband of Μαρία 5, one of the women at the crucifixion

Notes.Content: The idiom κνήθομαι τὴν ἀκοήν involves two quite distinct semantic features. One is the desire to be pleased, and the second is the means of such gratification, namely, what is heard. It would be possible to classify this idiom either under Sensory Events and States (Domain 24) or in the domain of Attitudes and Emotions. Since in {S:05500400300036} the latter seems the more focal feature of meaning, the idiom is included in the domain of Attitudes and Emotions.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to itch with respect to hearing) to have one’s ears tickled by what is heard{N:001}
Glosses: to desire to hear what one wants to hear

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a peninsula on the southwest coast of Asia Minor
a Roman copper coin worth 1/4 of an assarion ({S:04001002900008}) or 1/64 of a denarius ({S:04202002400006})

Notes.Content: It would be possible to treat σπλάγχνα[b], κοιλία[c], and νεφρός in this figurative sense in Domain 25 Attitudes and Emotions, but these meanings have been assigned to this domain of Psychological Faculties since the meanings involve aspects of personality which function as agents or presumed locations of psychological dispositions.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the entire digestive apparatus, including stomach and intestines

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the uterus
(figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοιλία<SDBG:κοιλία:000000>}[a] ‘belly,’ {D:8.67}) the psychological faculty of desire, intent, and feeling{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Though some persons have attempted to distinguish between {L:σπλάγχνον<SDBG:σπλάγχνον:000001>}[b], κοιλία[c], and {L:νεφρός<SDBG:νεφρός:000000>}, it is extremely doubtful whether this is really possible or practical. The semantic focus in the use of these terms is clearly the deeper and more intimate feelings and emotions. In some languages one can use a term which literally means ‘belly’ or ‘bowels,’ but more often than not, these emotions are associated with some particular organ of the body such as heart, spleen, liver, etc. Rather, however, than attempting to employ a figurative expression which may or may not be fully equivalent, it is often preferable to refer to the emotional content by using terms such as ‘feelings,’ ‘intents,’ ‘desires,’ or ‘compassion,’ depending upon the context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: desire for gratification of the body
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that κοιλία in {S:04501601800026} refers to Jewish dietary laws and regulations.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: the womb carries) to experience the process of pregnancy
LEXSenses.Comments: It may, however, be necessary in some languages to render {S:04201102700038} as ‘fortunate is the woman who gave you birth,’ since a literal reference to carrying in the womb may seem unduly crude.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of being asleep
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοιμάομαι<SDBG:κοιμάομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to sleep,’ {D:23.66}) to sleep, as a euphemistic expression for the state of being dead
LEXSenses.Comments: Some translators have attempted to preserve the figure of speech in {L:καθεύδω<SDBG:καθεύδω:000001>}[b] and κοιμάομαι[b] by translating ‘to sleep’ rather than ‘to have died’ or ‘to be dead.’ Such a practice, however, has resulted in misunderstanding in a number of instances and has sometimes led to the doctrine of so-called ‘soul-sleep.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of being asleep
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’|In {S:04301101300030} κοίμησις is combined with {L:ὕπνος<SDBG:ὕπνος:000000>} apparently to stress the fact that the sleep was an ordinary or natural sleep.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to sharing with someone else in a possession or a relationship implying mutual interest
LEXSenses.Comments: Since the emphasis in {S:05600100400010} is upon the fact that Paul and Titus have the same faith, one may also translate as ‘… the faith that you and I have’ or ‘… the faith we both believe in.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being ritually unacceptable, either as the result of defilement or because of the very nature of the object itself (for example, ritually unacceptable animals)
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that there is some subtle distinction in meaning, particularly on a connotative level, between κοινός[b] and ἀκάθαρτος in {S:04401001400022}, but it is difficult to determine the precise differences of meaning on the basis of existing contexts. The two terms are probably used in {S:04401001400022} primarily for the sake of emphasis.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being of little value, in view of being ordinary and common
pertaining to being in common between two or more persons
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand κοινός in {S:06500100300018} as {L:κοινός<SDBG:κοινός:000000>}[a] ‘shared, mutual’ (see {D:57.9}).

Notes.Content: βεβηλόω may differ significantly from κοινόω[a] in denoting a more serious degree of defilement, but this cannot be readily determined from existing contexts.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to become unclean, profane, or ritually unacceptable{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is quite impossible to translate literally the concept of unclean, for physical cleanliness and ritual acceptability are completely unrelated. In some languages it is necessary to translate κοινόω[a] or βεβηλόω as to take away its holiness or to make something unacceptable to God. In many cultures one must express this concept as involving so-called negative taboo.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to call or to regard something as common or defiled
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
to join with others in some activity
(an idiom, literally: to share blood and flesh) to have the characteristics and nature of a human being
an association involving close mutual relations and involvement
to share one’s possessions, with the implication of some kind of joint participation and mutual interest
(derivative of {L:κοινωνέω<SDBG:κοινωνέω:000000>}[a] ‘to share,’ {D:57.98}) that which is readily shared
(derivative of {L:κοινωνέω<SDBG:κοινωνέω:000000>}[a] ‘to share,’ {D:57.98}) pertaining to willing and ready sharing

Notes.Content: It is possible that συγκοινωνός[a] is somewhat more emphatic than κοινωνός in focusing upon the joint nature of participation.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who participates with another in some enterprise or matter of joint concern{N:001}

Notes.Content: κοίτη[c] sexual immorality is a peripheral extension of meaning of κοίτη[b] sexual relations (see {D:23.62}). This is due to a process of semantic narrowing.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a piece of furniture used for sleeping
LEXSenses.Comments: It is not necessary to understand {S:04201100700042} to mean that the children were in the same bed with the man, but it is, of course, possible that the reference here is to a relatively humble house in which all the members of the family would sleep on a single raised platform. See also {D:10.37}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοίτη<SDBG:κοίτη:000000>}[a] ‘bed,’ {D:6.108}) to have sexual relations
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages one may speak of ‘sexual life’ as ‘the way one lives with one’s wife’ or ‘how one treats one’s wife.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to engage in immoral sexual excess{N:001}
(an idiom, literally: to have bed, though in combination with ἔχω, κοίτη early acquired the metonymic meaning of sexual relations) to be in a state of pregnancy
LEXSenses.Comments: This expression contrasts with the meaning of {L:συλλαμβάνω<SDBG:συλλαμβάνω:000001>}[b], {D:23.49}, in that it seems to focus more upon the state of pregnancy rather than the event of conception.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a room in a house for sleeping
LEXSenses.Comments: It would be wrong to render the expression ‘who was in charge of the king’s bedroom’ in {S:04401202000036} as meaning simply one who kept the bedroom clean. A person such as Blastus would have been a highly respected person with considerable responsibility for the king’s living quarters and personal affairs. The expression may be adequately rendered in {S:04401202000036} by speaking of Blastus as ‘a high official.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a dye obtained from egg-clusters of a cochineal, collected from the leaves of Quercus coccifera
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04002702800010} ‘scarlet robe’ may have implied high military rank.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a reddish-purple cloth dyed with a substance obtained from the murex shellfish; expensive to produce; associated with wealth and royalty
the kernel part of fruit, usually grain
LEXSenses.Comments: A number of languages make distinctions between two quite different types of seed: (1) those produced by grasses (that is to say, grains) and (2) those produced by other types of plants, for example, beans, squash, apples, etc. In all passages employing the Greek terms in this subdomain (κόκκος, {L:σπέρμα<SDBG:σπέρμα:000000>}[a], {L:σπόρος<SDBG:σπόρος:000000>}), it is best to use some expression referring to ‘grain.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: praise as a means of gratifying someone’s vanity
to punish, with the implication of resulting severe suffering
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages punishment is often expressed as a causative of suffering, that is to say, ‘to cause to suffer’ or ‘to cause to endure harm.’ In some languages, however, there are a number of different types of punishment, and clear distinctions must be made between various degrees of punishment as well as between physical versus mental punishment.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to strike or beat with the fist, either once or repeatedly
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κολαφίζω<SDBG:κολαφίζω:000000>}[a] ‘to beat with the fist,’ {D:19.7}) to cause injury or weakness or possibly a circumstantial difficulty
LEXSenses.Comments: Though differences of interpretation exist concerning the meaning of ‘a thorn in my flesh’ ({S:04701200700038}), especially since some scholars have felt that this must refer to some kind of physical disability, it seems more likely to assume that it refers to some special personal circumstance such as the opposition Paul encountered in preaching the gospel, a reference suggested by {S:04701201000000} (see also {D:22.20}).|Without some clear understanding of the reference of ‘a thorn in my flesh,’ it is difficult to determine precisely how κολαφίζω is to be interpreted in {S:04701200700038}.

Notes.Content: προσκολλάομαι may very well differ from κολλάομαι[a] by suggesting a more permanent association, with focus upon reciprocal relations.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to begin an association with someone, whether temporary or permanent{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Though the Greek text of {S:04400802900018} says literally ‘join this carriage,’ in reality, of course, the association is not directly with the carriage, but with the man riding in the carriage. It is therefore necessary in a number of languages to translate κολλήθητι τῷ ἅρματι τούτῳ as ‘join the man riding in this carriage.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to stick or cling to something
(an idiom, literally: to cling to heaven) to increase enormously the number of something, with the implication of reaching the attention of God
an ointment for the eyes
LEXSenses.Comments: κολλούριον may often be rendered simply as ‘a medicine for the eyes.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who exchanges currency, either in terms of different types of currency or different values of the same currency
to cause something to be reduced in number or extent
LEXSenses.Comments: There may be difficulties involved in a strictly literal rendering of ‘those days will be shortened,’ for it might appear that each day would become shorter rather than that the number of days would be decreased. Therefore, one must render this expression in {S:04002402200034} in a number of languages as ‘those days will be fewer.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a city in Phrygia in Asia Minor

Notes.Content: According to ancient Jewish tradition, the end of the age would be characterized by a heavenly feast to be enjoyed by the righteous. This would be presided over by Abraham, and therefore to go to Abrahams bosom would be equivalent to being an honored guest at this celestial banquet.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the region of the body extending from the breast to the legs, especially when a person is in a seated position
LEXSenses.Comments: The term κόλπος occurs in several idiomatic phrases in the NT. For example, the expression ‘who was in the bosom of the Father’ in {S:04300101800022} denotes an association of intimacy and affection (see {D:34.18}). In a context referring to the position of a person at a meal (as in {S:04301302300020}), κόλπος indicates an honored place (see {D:17.25}). In {S:04201602200028} κόλπος Ἀβραάμ signifies the heavenly abode (see {D:1.16}).

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the fold of a garment forming a type of pocket or container
a part of the sea which is partially enclosed by land
LEXSenses.Comments: A ‘bay’ may be described as ‘a protected area of the sea’ or ‘a part of the sea protected by land.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: Abraham’s bosom) the heavenly abode, with the implication of close interpersonal relations
LEXSenses.Comments: A literal rendering of κόλπος Ἀβραάμ as ‘the bosom of Abraham’ or ‘the lap of Abraham’ is often misleading. In some languages it may even suggest homosexuality, and in other cases it implies that Lazarus was either a baby or was changed into a baby in heaven. Since κόλπος Ἀβραάμ is generally interpreted as a reference to the eschatological heavenly feast,{N:001} one may be justified in rendering {S:04201602200028} as in TEV ‘the poor man died and was carried by the angels to sit beside Abraham at the feast in heaven.’ In some languages κόλπος Ἀβραάμ in this context is translated as ‘he was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side’ or ‘… to be with Abraham.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: movement through water by the use of limbs
LEXSenses.Comments: A number of languages have several different terms for ‘swim’ depending on whether it is a person, an animal, a fish, or an eel (or a snake). Care must be exercised in choosing the appropriate term for this context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively large construction for collecting water
LEXSenses.Comments: The term κολυμβήθρα occurs in the NT only in {S:04300500200018}, and refers to a pool having five porches, one on each of four sides and another porch which went across the middle of the pool

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a city or town with special privileges in that the inhabitants of such a town were regarded as Roman citizens (such towns were originally colonized by citizens of Rome)
LEXSenses.Comments: A translational equivalent of ‘colony’ is frequently a phrase, for example, ‘a city where people were Romans’ or ‘a city of people who regarded Rome as their hometown.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to wear long hair as part of one’s attire
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it may be necessary to translate κομάω as ‘to let one’s hair grow long’ or ‘not to cut one’s hair.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: hair of the head of human beings
to carry or bring something to someone, usually implying a transfer
to cause someone to experience something on the basis of what that person has already done
Glosses: to cause to experience in return
to cause to experience in proportion to

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to receive as a type of compensation
to receive back something which one has previously possessed or its equivalent
the state of being in better health after a previous state of relative lack of health
to apply whitewash to a surface
LEXSenses.Comments: For many languages the closest equivalent of the phrase ‘whitewashed tombs’ is simply ‘tombs that have been painted white.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: whitewashed wall) one who pretends to be one thing, while in reality he is something quite different
dust, soil (see also {D:2.16})
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘Shake the dust from your feet’ may be expressed as ‘kick the dust from your feet.’ In some instances, however, the more appropriate equivalent would be ‘get rid of the dust from your feet’ or even ‘remove the dust from your feet and leave it there.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cease, in reference to some type of movement
LEXSenses.Comments: Languages may differ considerably in expressions relating to the ceasing of wind, for example, ‘the wind died,’ ‘the wind stood still,’ ‘the wind refused to move,’ or ‘the wind could not be felt.’

Notes.Content: The meanings of κόπτομαι and κοπετός in Domain 52 differ from related meanings in Domain 23 Physiological Processes and States and Domain 25 Attitudes and Emotions, since the expressions of grief in {S:04200805200010} and {S:04400800200018} reflect a form of ritualized and institutionalized mourning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: beating the breast and lamenting as an expression of sorrow{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a violent and extensive slaughter, especially associated with armed conflicts
to engage in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
to be tired or weary, as the result of hard or difficult endeavor
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret κοπιάω in {S:04001102800012} as {L:κοπιάω<SDBG:κοπιάω:000000>}[a] ‘to work hard’ (see {D:42.47}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:κοπιάω<SDBG:κοπιάω:000001>}[b] ‘to be tired,’ {D:23.78}) to become emotionally fatigued and discouraged
act of engaging in hard work, implying difficulties and trouble
a state characterized by troubling circumstances

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:κόπριον<SDBG:κόπριον:000000>} ‘manure,’ {D:8.76}) a pile or heap of manure

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: fecal matter used as agricultural fertilizer

Notes.Content: The meanings of κόπτομαι and κοπετός in Domain 52 differ from related meanings in Domain 23 Physiological Processes and States and Domain 25 Attitudes and Emotions, since the expressions of grief in {S:04200805200010} and {S:04400800200018} reflect a form of ritualized and institutionalized mourning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cut, by means of a sharp-edged instrument (for example, knife, sword, or ax)
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages important distinctions are made for various types of cutting. For example, terms referring to the cutting of flesh may be different from those involving wood or stone. Similarly, important distinctions may be made as to whether there is simply an incision by cutting or whether a particular object is cut in two or cut off.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to beat the breast and lament as an expression of sorrow{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is entirely impossible to use an expression such as ‘to beat the breast’ in referring to mourning or grief, since ‘to beat the breast’ is often employed as a gesture of self-congratulation or pride in accomplishment. In a number of instances the closest equivalent of ‘to beat the breast’ is ‘to beat the head’ or even ‘to pull out the hair.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: large black bird with thick strong beak, and fairly short legs; highly intelligent; Corvus family; crows and ravens belong to the same family of birds but differ in size, ravens being somewhat larger and being more inclined to feed on dead bodies
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages one must be especially sensitive to connotations relating to terms for ‘crow’ or ‘raven,’ since these birds may be either particularly disliked or may be regarded as symbols of death and sickness. If such is the case, it may be preferable to simply use a more generic term for birds.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a diminutive derivative of κόρη ‘girl,’ not occurring in the NT, but seemingly having lost the diminutive feature of meaning) a girl about the age of puberty
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04100504100030} κοράσιον is equated in meaning with the Aramaic term ταλιθα (see {D:9.48}), and in {S:04100504200010} this girl is identified as being twelve years of age. Compare also ἠνέχθη ἡ κεφαλὴ αὐτοῦ ἐπὶ πίνακι καὶ ἐδόθη τῷ κορασίῳ ‘his head was brought in on a plate and given to the girl’ ({S:04001401100022}). It is impossible to determine the age of Herodias’ daughter, but in view of her role as an attractive dancer, she was probably of the age of puberty.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a borrowing from Hebrew) that which has been set aside as a gift to be given later to God, but which is still at the disposal of the owner
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages it is important to translate ‘corban’ as ‘what I have promised to later give to God.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a room in the Temple used as a treasury
the leader of a rebellion against Moses
to be happy or content with what one has, with the implication of its being abundant
LEXSenses.Comments: Note that in this statement in {S:04600400800004} there is evidently a significant element of irony, and it is for that reason that some translations employ a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ For another interpretation of κορέννυμι in {S:04600400800004}, see {D:57.22}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to have enough, often with the implication of even more than enough
LEXSenses.Comments: This first statement in {S:04600400800004} is probably to be understood ironically, and therefore it may be readily translated as a question, for example, ‘do you already have everything you need?’ or as a statement referring to what the people of Corinth evidently presumed, for example, ‘you think you already have all you need.’ For another interpretation of {L:κορέννυμι<SDBG:κορέννυμι:000000>} in {S:04600400800004}, see {D:25.80}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:Κόρινθος<SDBG:Κόρινθος:000000>} ‘Corinth,’ {D:93.506}) a person who lives in or is a native of Corinth
a city in Greece
a Roman centurion to whom Peter ministered

Notes.Content: Though in the Greek text of {S:04201600700024} the number of cors is given as a hundred, it may not be particularly important to preserve the numeral as in the previous item ({S:04201600600010} in {D:81.20}), for at least in English the expression ‘a thousand’ may have a similar symbolic significance of a huge amount.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Hebrew dry measure for grain, flour, etc., of between ten and twelve bushels or about 390 liters
to cause something to be beautiful by decorating
pertaining to the earth
(derivative of {L:κόσμος<SDBG:κόσμος:000002>}[c] ‘world system,’ {D:41.38}) pertaining to the system or standards of the world
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05600201200018} τὰς κοσμικὰς ἐπιθυμίας may also be rendered as ‘the desires which people in this world have,’ but in this context the term ἐπιθυμίας should imply wrong desires.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being modest in the sense of moderate and wellordered
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of κόσμιος in {S:05400200900012}, see {D:66.10}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being proper or suitable in terms of being attractive
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of {L:κόσμιος<SDBG:κόσμιος:000000>} in {S:05400200900012}, see {D:88.48}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who rules over the whole world
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression ‘world ruler’ should not be understood in terms of merely ruling over the earth as a physical object but of ‘ruling over those who are on the earth.’ Most scholars, however, interpret κοσμοκράτωρ in {S:04900601200040} as meaning a supernatural power (see {D:12.44}), though it is possible to understand κοσμοκράτωρ in this context as meaning a human ruler.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
LEXSenses.Comments: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of {S:04900102100006} some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

Notes.Content: The occurrences of γῆ[a], οἰκουμένη[a], and κόσμος[b] relate specifically to the known inhabited areas of the earth, which in the NT period included the countries bordering on the Mediterranean, the Fertile Crescent as far as the Indus Valley, and as far north in Europe as England and Scandinavia. This was the total known earth or world. Such a restriction to a known area of the earth is also true of terms used in some receptor languages, though the referents are obviously different. What is important is not the particular area of the earth, but the corresponding concept of the surface of the earth as the place of human habitation. It is possible that οἰκουμένη[a] differs slightly in meaning from γῆ[a] and κόσμος[b] in view of a somewhat greater emphasis or focus upon the civilized part of earth.

It is possible to understand κόσμος in {S:04600600200016} as referring to all mankind, but in view of certain contrasts which are implied in this context, it seems more satisfactory to understand κόσμος in a more limited sense of ‘people of the world.’

κόσμος[f] may be regarded as a highly generic term for any and all kinds of decorations and adornments; or it may be considered as the process whereby people may adorn themselves (see {D:79.12}). κόσμος[f] is semantically complex, since it involves not only certain artifacts and the use of such artifacts, but also an abstract component of attractive appearance.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the universe as an ordered structure
LEXSenses.Comments: In many languages there is no specific term for the universe. The closest equivalent may simply be ‘all that exists.’ In other instances one may use a phrase such as ‘the world and all that is above it’ or ‘the sky and the earth.’ The concept of the totality of the universe may be expressed in some languages only as ‘everything that is on the earth and in the sky.’
