LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being in a wretched state, either mentally or physically
pertaining to weighing a talent or 125 Roman pounds of twelve ounces each or approximately ninety pounds (English weight) or forty kilograms
LEXSenses.Comments: It may, however, be better to use in {S:06601602100010} an expression with a more general sense, for example, ‘great stones of hail weighing almost a hundred pounds’ or ‘… forty kilos.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Greek monetary unit (also a unit of weight) with a value which fluctuated, depending upon the particular monetary system which prevailed at a particular period of time (a silver talent was worth approximately six thousand denarii with gold talents worth at least thirty times that much)
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04002501500012} what is important is the relative number of talents or sums of money. In a number of translations the respective amounts are stated in terms of local currency. For example, in English one may speak of five thousand dollars as equivalent to five talents, though in terms of buying power, five talents would be worth much more than five thousand dollars. What is important, however, in this story is not the precise sums of money but the relative amount which was given to the different servants.|The ‘ten thousand talents’ referred to in {S:04001802400020} would be equivalent to millions of denarii. The sum in this parable is perhaps greatly exaggerated, precisely in order to emphasize the vast differences between the two debts. It is also true, of course, that in ancient times persons with extensive mercantile businesses sometimes became slaves as a result of defeat in war, and they were purchased by business syndicates together with their business enterprises, which they would continue to manage.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an Aramaic word in an emphatic form) the designation for a little girl, probably implying affectionate concern
a room in the interior of a house, normally without windows opening to the outside
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04201200300040} the emphasis is upon the strictly private location of the inner room. In such a context one may translate ‘a strictly private room’ or ‘a small room in the center of the house.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a room for the storage of valuables
LEXSenses.Comments: ταμεῖον[b] and θησαυρός[a] may often be rendered by descriptive phrases, for example, ‘a room where valuable things are kept’ or ‘a place where valuables are stored.’|In {S:04001203500014} θησαυρός[a] is used figuratively (ὁ ἀγαθὸς ἄνθρωπος ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ ἐκβάλλει ἀγαθά ‘a good man draws good things from his good storehouse,’ meaning ‘… storehouse of good things’) to describe the heart as a kind of storehouse or treasure.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an ordered or arranged sequence
a proper and correct order
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:05100200500036} τάξις may refer to the orderly manner in which the church at Colossae conducted its affairs or carried on its worship.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: kind or type of entity, implying a contrast-comparison to other similar entities
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that τάξις in {S:05800500600026} refers to a kind of priest on the basis of being in a particular grouping or order of priests, but there seems to be no reference to any higher rank or position.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (compare ταπεινός[c] ‘of low status,’ {D:87.61}) pertaining to being discouraged and lacking in hope, with the possible implication of some association with low social status

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being unpretentious in one’s behavior
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the expression ‘humble in spirit’ or ‘humble in heart’ may be expressed as ‘speaking only soft words’ or ‘without shouting at others.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to having low and humble status

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being meek, with the implication of low status

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the quality of humility
LEXSenses.Comments: The rendering of ταπεινοφροσύνη in {S:05100201800012} as ‘false humility’ is justified in terms of the context, but there is nothing in the word ταπεινοφροσύνη itself which means ‘false.’ It would be possible to render ταπεινοφροσύνη in {S:05100201800012} as ‘subjection to,’ and one might render the entire expression as ‘in abject worship of angels.’ In other languages ‘false humility’ may be rendered as ‘just pretending to be humble’ or ‘appearing to be humble but really being proud.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to having the attitude of humility
to cause something to become low in height
LEXSenses.Comments: For another (probably preferred) interpretation of {S:04200300500018}, see {D:79.87}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause something to become level
LEXSenses.Comments: One might argue that {L:ταπεινόω<SDBG:ταπεινόω:000000>} in {S:04200300500018} is to be understood as ‘to be brought low,’ but in contrast with πληρωθήσεται, which refers to filling up valleys, ταπεινωθήσεται should perhaps be understood as referring to ‘leveling off’ mountains and hills. For this other interpretation of {L:ταπεινόω<SDBG:ταπεινόω:000000>} in {S:04200300500018}, see {D:81.7}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to be in a low status

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:ταπεινός<SDBG:ταπεινός:000001>}[b] ‘humble,’ {D:88.52}) to cause someone to be or to become humble
LEXSenses.Comments: A strictly literal rendering of ‘he who humbles himself’ could be misunderstood as ‘one who despises himself’ or ‘one who has no regard for himself.’ In the context of {S:04001800400006} it is often important to use an idiomatic expression which will adequately convey the meaning, for example, ‘one who causes his heart to bow down’ or even ‘one who makes his heart small.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to become disgraced and humiliated, with the implication of embarrassment and shame

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to live in circumstances regarded as characteristic of low status
Glosses: to live like those of low status
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages ταπεινόομαι in {S:05000401200006} may be rendered as ‘to live like poor people.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the quality of unpretentious behavior, suggesting a total lack of arrogance or pride
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages humility is expressed indirectly by an idiomatic phrase, for example, ‘to live without strutting’ or ‘to walk without wanting to be noticed.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Low Status or Rank [including persons of low status]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the state of low status, with the probable implication of humility
to cause movement, usually as the result of shaking or stirring
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: ἄγγελος γὰρ κυρίου κατὰ καιρὸν κατέβαινεν ἐν τῇ κολυμβήθρᾳ καὶ ἐταράσσετο τὸ ὕδωρ ‘from time to time an angel of the Lord would come down in the pool and cause the water to move’ {S:04300500400000} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:ταράσσω<SDBG:ταράσσω:000000>}[a] ‘to stir up,’ {D:16.3}) to cause acute emotional distress or turbulence
to cause people to riot against
the motion resulting from a mass being stirred up or shaken
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: ὁ οὖν πρῶτος ἐμβὰς μετὰ τὴν ταραχὴν τοῦ ὕδατος ὑγιὴς ἐγίνετο ‘the first person to go into (the pool) after the water had been moved was healed’ {S:04300500400000} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: disorderly behavior of people in violent opposition to authority
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: λιμοὶ καὶ ταραχαί ‘famines and riots’ {S:04101300800030} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a serious disturbance
a state of acute distress and great anxiety, with the additional possible implications of dismay and confusion
LEXSenses.Comments: Since τάραχος refers to the type of extreme anxiety which borders on fear, it may be possible in some languages to use a double expression, ‘were greatly distressed and afraid.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:Ταρσός<SDBG:Ταρσός:000000>} ‘Tarsus,’ {D:93.596}) a person who lives in or is a native of Tarsus
the capital of Cilicia in southeast Asia Minor

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of τάρταρος ‘Tartarus,’ ‘hell,’ as a place of torture or torment, not occurring in the NT) to cast into or to cause to remain in Tartarus
LEXSenses.Comments: In many cases it is confusing to add still another term for a designation of hell by transliterating the Greek τάρταρος, and so most translators have preferred to render ταρταρόω as either ‘to cast into hell’ or ‘to keep in hell,’ thus using for ‘hell’ the same term as is employed for a rendering of the Greek term {L:γέεννα<SDBG:γέεννα:000000>} ({D:1.21}).

Notes.Content: The meanings of τάσσω[c], συντάσσω, προστάσσω[a], ἐπιτάσσω, and διατάσσω[a] no doubt differ somewhat, particularly in connotation, but it is not possible to determine this from existing contexts.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Assign to a Role or Function

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
LEXSenses.Comments: Though τάσσω in {S:04401304800032} has sometimes been interpreted as meaning ‘to choose,’ there seems to be far more involved than merely a matter of selection, since a relationship is specifically assigned.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause someone to be in a state involving an order or arrangement
to give detailed instructions as to what must be done{N:001}
to propose something to someone
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand τάσσω in {S:04402802300002} as meaning ‘to arrange,’ but in {S:04402802300002} it would seem that τάσσω implies not only proposing a date but obtaining an agreement.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to do something with devotion, with the possible implication of systematic, regular activity
male bovine; large ruminant animal with horns and cloven hoofs; used for sacrifice and for meat, as a beast of burden, or for pulling a cart or a plow
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘bull’ is simply a generic term for cattle to which is added a specific designation such as ‘male.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a place for burying
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand ταφή in the context of {S:04002700700024} as a reference to the process of burial, and one may therefore translate {S:04002700700024} as ‘they used the money to buy the Potter’s Field to bury foreigners.’

Notes.Content: It is possible that μνῆμα and μνημεῖον[a] differ in meaning from τάφος in that they contain a semantic component of memorial, that is, a reminder to people of someone who has died.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a construction for the burial of the dead; often a natural cave or hewn out of bedrock{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between a grave (a hole in the ground in which a corpse is placed) and a tomb (a construction built above the surface of the ground for housing a corpse). In some contexts, however, it may be better to use a more generic expression, for example, ‘places where people are buried’ or ‘places where corpses are placed.’ In {S:04100500200024} it is important to avoid a term which would designate merely graves, for the demoniac who met Jesus was not living down in graves in the ground, but had found some habitation either in burial caves or in tombs constructed above ground.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a low probability of occurrence

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a very short extent of time
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04800100600008} ταχέως refers clearly to the relatively brief period of time before the Galatians abandoned their earlier convictions.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a very short extent of time
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:06100200100052} ταχινός may refer to the swift nature of the destruction or to the fact that destruction comes after a relatively brief period of time.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a very brief period of time
Glosses: quickly (in combination with the preposition ἐν)
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04402201800020} τάχος evidently refers to a brief period of time before fulfilling the admonition to leave Jerusalem.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a very short extent of time
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04301102900012} ταχύ probably refers to the short period of time between Mary‘s hearing about Jesus and her getting up to go out to meet him. It is, of course, also possible to interpret ταχύ in {S:04301102900012} as referring to the rapidity of Mary‘s movement in getting up and going out to meet Jesus.|Again, in {S:04301302700038} the emphasis is upon the brief period of time before Judas is to do what he had set out to do.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a point of time subsequent to another point of time (either an event in the discourse or the time of the discourse itself), with emphasis upon the relatively brief interval between the two points of time
a marker of a close relationship between coordinate, nonsequential items
a marker of a close relationship between sequential events or states
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a totality of two closely related elements
a marker of a closely related coordinate set
a particularly strong permanent wall, primarily the wall built around a city for its protection
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a translator must make a clear distinction between a wall of a house and a city wall. The wall of a house may be called ‘a side of a house’ and an inner wall ‘a partition in a house,’ while a city wall is often related to terms such as ‘barricade’ or ‘fence.’ Hence, a city wall may be called ‘a fortified fence around a city.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: that which causes something to be known as verified or confirmed
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages ‘convincing proof’ is rendered as ‘that which causes one to know for sure’ or ‘… with certainty.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (extension of meaning of {L:τέκνον<SDBG:τέκνον:000000>}[a] ‘child, offspring,’ {D:10.36}) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
LEXSenses.Comments: It may be impossible to translate τεκνία literally as ‘my children’ in  {S:06200300700002} since this might suggest a kinship relationship between the author of 1 John and the people to whom he is addressing his letter. A more satisfactory equivalent in some languages is often ‘my dear friends’ or ‘my dear ones.’

Notes.Content: It is possible that τεκνογονέω and τεκνογονία differ somewhat in connotation from τίκτω[a] and γεννάω[b] in being stylistically more formal, but there seems to be no significant denotative distinction in meaning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to give birth to a child{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

Notes.Content: It is possible that τεκνογονέω and τεκνογονία differ somewhat in connotation from τίκτω[a] and γεννάω[b] in being stylistically more formal, but there seems to be no significant denotative distinction in meaning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to give birth to a child{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one’s immediate offspring, but without specific reference to sex or age
LEXSenses.Comments: In languages in which there is no generic term for ‘child’ or ‘offspring,’ one may use ‘son’ or ‘daughter’ or ‘son and daughter,’ singular or plural, depending upon the context.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: successive following generations of those who are biologically related to a reference person
LEXSenses.Comments: In the case of {L:γενεά<SDBG:γενεά:000002>}[c], τέκνον[b], and {L:σπέρμα<SDBG:σπέρμα:000001>}[b] ({D:10.29}), the reference is not to one’s immediate descendants or offspring (that is to say, to one’s sons or daughters) but to a successive series of such persons, one’s descendants. In some languages such descendants may be called merely ‘the children of one’s children,’ and in other languages one may refer to descendants as ‘those who follow one’ or ‘those who come later.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child,’ {D:10.36}) inhabitants of a particular place
LEXSenses.Comments: Only rarely can one preserve the figurative significance of τέκνον[c] as a designation of the inhabitants of an area. Readers are too likely to understand such a reference as applicable only to children who live in a particular place. Even the use of a simile does not assist appreciably, since it would be interpreted as likening the inhabitants of an area to children, probably in the sense of their being immature or incapable. For example, the expression the people of Jerusalem like children would probably lead to serious misunderstanding.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Persons For Whom There Is Affectionate Concern

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (extension of meaning of τέκνον[a] ‘child, offspring,’ {D:10.36}) a person of any age for whom there is a special relationship of endearment and association
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is impossible to translate τέκνον in {S:04000900200040} as ‘child,’ since this might immediately suggest that Jesus was declaring himself to be the father of this man. Furthermore, the paralytic was evidently an adult male. A more satisfactory equivalent would be ‘my dear man’ or ‘my dear fellow.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person who looks to another as being, so to speak, a father in the faith and thus becomes a disciple of that person
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible that τέκνον in {S:06400100400020} is to be understood simply as an affectionate way of talking about persons who in one way or another are in a dependent relationship to someone (see {D:9.46}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a kind or class of persons, with the implication of possessing certain derived characteristics
Glosses: one who has the characteristics of

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: children of light) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also {D:9.4} and {D:12.15}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’

Notes.Content: There may very well be subtle differences of meaning in the series in {D:35.51}, but there is no direct contextual evidence to support significant distinctions in meaning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who uses various materials (wood, stone, and metal) in building
LEXSenses.Comments: There is every reason to believe that in biblical times one who was regarded as a τέκτων would be skilled in the use of wood and stone and possibly even metal.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being perfect in the sense of not lacking any moral quality
LEXSenses.Comments: Compare the meaning of τέλειος[e] mature in {D:88.100}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being truly and completely genuine
pertaining to having no defect whatsoever
pertaining to that which is fully accomplished or finished

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being mature in one’s behavior
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret τέλειος in {S:04900401300038} as meaning ‘perfect’ (see {D:88.36}).|In {S:04000504800008} it is possible that τέλειος also means maturity of behavior, but it is usually interpreted as ‘being perfect,’ since the comparison is made with God (see {D:88.36}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to an adult human being
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in {S:05800501400002} τέλειος is to be understood in a literal sense, the context as a whole is figurative.

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who is initiated into a religious community of faith (a meaning which reflects the occurrence of τέλειος as a technical term for persons initiated into the mystery religions)
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages ‘initiated’ ({S:05000301500006 05100102800036}) may be best expressed as ‘to become a member of’ or ‘to become a believer in.’ It is possible, however, to interpret τέλειος in {S:05000301500006} and {S:05100102800036} as mature spirituality or a state of being spiritually mature (see {D:88.100}).

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: maturity in thought and behavior

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a state of perfection, implying some process of maturity

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle distinctions, particularly of emphasis, in the series τελέω, ἐκτελέω[a], ἀποτελέω, ἐπιτελέω[a], συντελέω[a], and τελειόω[c], but it is not possible to determine with precision the particular distinctions on the basis of existing contexts, though possibly ἐκτελέω and ἀποτελέω emphasize more finality, while ἐπιτελέω[a] may focus upon the resulting purpose.

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to make perfect in the moral sense
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of τελειόω in {S:06200200500030}, see {D:73.7}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause to be truly and completely genuine
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of {L:τελειόω<SDBG:τελειόω:000000>} in {S:06200200500030}, see {D:88.38}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to bring an activity to a successful finish{N:001}
to be completely successful in accomplishing some goal or attaining some state
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of τελειόω in {S:05000301200014}, see {D:53.50}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to admit into or initiate into faith (possibly based on technical usage in the mystery religions)
LEXSenses.Comments: It is important that in {S:05000301200014} τελειόω is to be understood in the sense of a functional stage of religious attainment: ‘I have already become an initiate.’ For another interpretation of τελειόω in {S:05000301200014}, see {D:68.31}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause to happen for some end result
to attain a state as a goal
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to make perfect in the moral sense
to cause to happen for some end result
one who makes possible the successful completion of something
to produce completely mature fruit
(figurative extension of meaning of τελευτάω ‘to end,’ not occurring in the NT) to come to the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death
(figurative extension of meaning of τελευτή ‘end,’ not occurring in the NT) the end of one’s life, as a euphemistic expression for death

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle distinctions, particularly of emphasis, in the series τελέω, ἐκτελέω[a], ἀποτελέω, ἐπιτελέω[a], συντελέω[a], and τελειόω[c], but it is not possible to determine with precision the particular distinctions on the basis of existing contexts, though possibly ἐκτελέω and ἀποτελέω emphasize more finality, while ἐπιτελέω[a] may focus upon the resulting purpose.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to bring an activity to a successful finish{N:001}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:τέλος<SDBG:τέλος:000000>}[a] ‘end,’ {D:67.66}) to occur or happen at the end of a duration
to cause to happen for some end result
to obey as a means of fulfilling the purpose of a rule or standard
LEXSenses.Comments: The phrase ‘to obey the Law’ in {S:04500202700018} may be rendered simply as ‘to do what the Law says one must do.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to pay tax or tribute (used absolutely or with a noun complement meaning ‘tax’ or ‘tribute’)

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time marking the end of a duration
LEXSenses.Comments: There are serious problems involved in rendering τέλος[a] in {S:04002401400042} and in similar contexts. In a number of languages one simply cannot say ‘the end will come’; rather, it may be necessary to say ‘that is the finish’ or ‘everything is finished.’ In the context of {S:04002401400042}, however, it may be best to translate ‘God will finish everything.’ The phrase εἰς τέλος in {S:05200201600044} may also be understood as an idiomatic expression involving a degree of completeness (see {D:78.47}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the result of an event or process, with special focus upon the final state or condition
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages τέλος in {S:04002605800044} may be rendered simply as ‘what would happen’ or ‘what would finally happen.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the purpose of an event or state, viewed in terms of its result
a degree of completeness, with the possible implication of purpose or result
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to understand the phrase ἕως τέλους in the temporal sense of ‘to the end’ (see {D:67.66}).|It is also possible to understand τέλος in the expression εἰς τέλος in {S:05200201600044} as a temporal expression, with εἰς ({D:67.117}) as a marker of an extent of time, so that this passage may be rendered as ‘and in the end wrath has come down on them’ or ‘and wrath has at last come down on them’ (see {D:67.66}). In this context ὀργή may very well be translated as ‘punishment’ ({D:38.10}), and in many languages it is necessary to indicate the agent of such punishment. The same ambiguity with εἰς τέλος occurs in {S:04301300100064} in the clause εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς, meaning ‘he loved them completely’ or ‘he loved them to the end’ (see {D:67.119}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: payments customarily due a governmental authority
LEXSenses.Comments: The term τέλος[e] differs from {L:κῆνσος<SDBG:κῆνσος:000000>} ({D:57.180}) in being somewhat more generic in meaning. In certain contexts τέλος[e] may refer to various kinds of direct taxes, customs duties, and tribute money, but in contexts such as {S:04001702500048} in which {L:κῆνσος<SDBG:κῆνσος:000000>} also occurs, τέλος probably refers primarily to customs duties, while {L:κῆνσος<SDBG:κῆνσος:000000>} refers to a direct poll tax upon all adult males.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: the end) a marker of a conclusion to what has preceded, but not necessarily the conclusion of a text
(derivative of {L:τελέω<SDBG:τελέω:000004>}[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ {D:57.178}) one who collects taxes for the government
LEXSenses.Comments: Since Jews who farmed the taxes for the Romans (that is to say, who paid Roman authorities for the privilege of collecting taxes) were considered traitors to their own people, the term τελώνης has strongly negative connotations in the NT. In any translation of the Gospels it may be especially important to have an adequate marginal note designed to explain the basis for the hostility which many people had toward tax collectors.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:τελέω<SDBG:τελέω:000004>}[e] ‘to pay taxes,’ {D:57.178}) a place where taxes or revenue was collected from those entering a town to sell produce
LEXSenses.Comments: In the ancient world taxes were primarily of two types: (1) a head tax on each individual (which was relatively small) and (2) revenue or tribute paid for goods and produce brought into an area for sale. The latter was essentially a kind of ‘sales tax,’ but paid by the seller who obviously increased the prices of goods accordingly.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an unusual sign, especially one in the heavens, serving to foretell impending events
LEXSenses.Comments: In ancient times a portent might consist of a particular arrangement of the planets, an unusual display of northern lights, a conspicuous comet, or a cluster of falling stars. For a discussion of {L:σημεῖον<SDBG:σημεῖον:000000>} ‘sign,’ see {D:33.477}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a person who sends greetings in {S:04501602200008}
an attorney who accused Paul before Felix
cardinal number, where there are four instances of a countable entity
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘from the four winds’ or ‘from the four directions’ is simply ‘from every direction.’ The Greek expression does not mean from only four specific directions, but rather from every direction.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: fourteenth in a series involving either time, space, or set
cardinal number, where there are forty instances of a countable entity

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a very long period of time
LEXSenses.Comments: Though most translations render ἔτη τεσσεράκοντα as ‘forty years,’ the expression probably is to be understood as meaning an unusually long period of time. See also discussion at {D:67.93}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (literally: forty days and forty nights) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
LEXSenses.Comments: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (shortened form of [c] literally, forty days) possibly a symbolic temporal expression denoting a relatively long period of time
LEXSenses.Comments: Most translations render ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα as either ‘forty days and forty nights’ or ‘forty days,’ though it is possible, in view of the symbolic meaning of the number ‘forty,’ that this expression is to be understood as meaning a long period of time.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a period of forty years

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to the fourth in a series of days
fourth in a series involving either time, space, or set
a fourth part of an object, series, or mass
LEXSenses.Comments: For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved, see {D:60.63}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to function as a tetrarch (see {D:37.78})
Glosses: to be the governor of a region

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a ruler with rank and authority lower than that of a king and one who ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities
pertaining to having four equal sides and four right angles
a detachment of four soldiers
cardinal number, where there are four thousand instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are four hundred instances of a countable entity

Notes.Content: For both items {D:67.175} and {D:67.176} it is, of course, also possible to speak of months as moons. Compare {D:67.174}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a period of four months{N:001}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Double, Four Times As Much, Etc. [Multiples]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: four times as much in quantity
any four-footed animal, either wild or domesticated
LEXSenses.Comments: A high percentage of languages appear to have no generic term to identify all kinds of quadrupeds whether wild or domesticated. Rather, they tend to make quite clear distinctions between wild and domesticated animals, and therefore it may be necessary to indicate both types in those contexts where the reference is to both wild as well as domesticated animals. For example, one may sometimes speak of ‘animals of the grass and animals of the forest’ or ‘animals of the barn and animals of the mountains.’|In {S:04401001200012} the reference is primarily to wild animals, since for the most part wild animals would be those designated as unclean. However, swine were also regarded as unclean, and they were domesticated.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of τέφρα ‘ashes,’ not occurring in the NT) to destroy by reducing something to ashes
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible to render ‘to reduce to ashes’ as ‘to burn up completely’ or ‘to destroy by fire and leave only ashes.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an activity involving specialized training and skill
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there is no special term for ‘craft,’ but an equivalent of this clause in {S:04401800300030} may be rendered as ‘for their work was making tents’ or ‘they earned money making tents’ or ‘they customarily made tents.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: one who customarily engages in a particular craft or occupation
to become liquid, either by melting or condensation
pertaining to a particularly clear or plain visual image
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04100802500032} both διέβλεψεν ({D:24.35}) and ἐνέβλεπεν ({D:24.9}) occur. Some scholars assume that the two expressions are essentially equivalent in meaning, but others believe that διέβλεψεν is to be understood as ‘to look intently’ or ‘to focus one’s eyes upon.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a reference to the size of something (occurring rarely in an absolute sense)
a degree which is comparable to some other expression of degree
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the closest equivalent of this expression in {S:06601601800044} may be ‘that earthquake was indeed very great.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause a state to continue
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04600703700052} the reference to ‘girl’ may be either a man’s daughter or a man’s fiancée. Because of the ambiguity of this statement in {S:04600703700052} and in view of the cultural complications involved, especially because of differences of customs in different parts of the world, it is important that translators add a note at this point explaining the difference of interpretation and some of the cultural implications.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to continue to hold in custody
LEXSenses.Comments: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to continue to obey orders or commandments
to continue to hold in custody
LEXSenses.Comments: The act of holding someone in custody or guarding an individual may be expressed as ‘standing guard to see that someone will not escape’ or ‘watching carefully so that one cannot run off’ or ‘tying someone up so that he cannot leave.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a place of detention
LEXSenses.Comments: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to continue to obey orders or commandments
a city on the west shore of the Lake of Galilee
the Lake of Tiberias, also known as the Lake of Galilee
the Roman emperor Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus, who ruled from 14 A.D. to 37 A.D.; compare {D:93.214a}

Notes.Content: In this subdomain τίθημι[a] is by far the most generic expression.
This seemingly unusual use of τίθημι with τὰ ἱμάτια in {S:04301300400012} parallels the use of λαμβάνω in the sense of ‘putting on a garment’ in {S:04301301200016} (see {D:49.10}).

Any meaning involving ‘to cause to be’ implies some change in state, and therefore one could classify these meanings under Subdomain B Change of State in Domain 13 Be, Become, Exist, Happen. However, the focus seems to be primarily upon the changed state rather than upon the process of moving from one state to another. The fact that a change of state has taken place seems to be semantically incidental.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to put or place in a particular location{N:001}

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Assign to a Role or Function

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to assign someone to a particular task, function, or role
to remove or take off clothing
to explain something, presumably by putting forward additional or different information
to deposit money with a banker, with the intent of earning interest
to cause a state to be{N:003}
to cause someone to experience, with the implication of subjecting a person to something
(an idiom, literally: to put a plan) to suggest a plan of action
(an idiom, literally: to put into the ears) to listen carefully to, with the implication of not forgetting
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of this idiom in {S:04200904400002}, see {D:29.5}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to place in the ears) to continue to bear something in mind
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of the idiom τίθεμαι εἰς τὰ ὦτα in {S:04200904400002}, see {D:24.64}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to place in the heart) to store information in the mind, with the implication of its being valuable
Glosses: to treasure up in the heart
to store in the mind as valuable

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (idioms, literally: to place in the heart, and: to place in the mind) to engage in the process of deciding
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret the phrase ἐν τῷ πνεύματι in {S:04401902100010} as being a reference to the Holy Spirit and accordingly, the passage may be translated as ‘Paul, led by the Spirit, decided to travel through Macedonia.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (idioms, literally: to put at someone’s feet) to present something to someone who is reckoned as having superior status or position

LEXDomains.Domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to place the knees, a Latinism) to kneel down before, with the implication of an act of reverence or of supplication
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of cultures, kneeling does not imply either reverence or an act of supplication. In some instances translators have used a functional substitute involving a similar type of stance, namely, ‘to bow low before,’ but it may be necessary to use a more or less literal description of ‘kneeling before’ and then to place in a marginal note an indication of the implications of such an act.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to lay down one’s life) to die, with the implication of voluntary or willing action
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in English the phrases ‘to lay down one’s life’ or ‘to give one’s life’ do suggest a voluntary dying, a literal rendering of such expressions in other languages would not necessarily imply the same. It may therefore be necessary to use such expressions as ‘to die willingly’ or ‘to die without resisting.’ In some languages ‘willingly’ is expressed primarily as a negation of objecting, for example, ‘I will not object to dying.’

Notes.Content: It is possible that τεκνογονέω and τεκνογονία differ somewhat in connotation from τίκτω[a] and γεννάω[b] in being stylistically more formal, but there seems to be no significant denotative distinction in meaning.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to give birth to a child{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: All languages have expressions for human birth, though these are frequently in idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to drop a child’ or ‘to cause a baby to pass between the legs.’ A number of languages have a variety of terms referring to giving birth, and some of these may involve unfortunate connotations. One must therefore be careful about the selection of appropriate expressions.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to cause the growth and production of plants
to pluck or pick by pulling off or out of
the father of Bartimaeus

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to attribute high status to someone by honoring
to determine an amount to be used in paying for something
LEXSenses.Comments: It would also be possible to translate ‘the price set on him by the people of Israel’ as ‘the amount the people of Israel had agreed to pay for him.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to provide aid or financial assistance, with the implication that this is an appropriate means of showing respect
Glosses: to provide for the needs of as a sign of respect

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: honor as an element in the assignment of status to a person
the worth or merit of some object, event, or state
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the equivalent of ‘value’ is almost always in terms of ‘importance.’ This is particularly true if one is speaking of objects which are normally not bought and sold. Accordingly, one may render this particular expression in {S:04601202300018} as ‘those parts of the body which we think of as not being so important, to these we grant particular importance’ or ‘… we consider as being very important.’|It is also possible to interpret τιμή in {S:04601202300018} as a degree of honor or appreciation (see {L:τιμή<SDBG:τιμή:000000>}[a], {D:87.4}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the amount of money or property regarded as representing the value or price of something
LEXSenses.Comments: It would be wrong to assume that τιμή in {S:04600702300002} necessarily means ‘a high price.’ The notion ‘high’ comes from the contextual reference to the death of Christ. In {S:04600702300002}, however, the implication is that a price was set and that the payment has been made. If the passive expression in {S:04600702300002} must be made active, one may translate as ‘Christ bought you with a price’ or ‘Christ paid for you.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: compensation given for special service, with the implication that this is a way by which honor or respect may be shown
LEXSenses.Comments: τιμή[d] in the sense of compensation is related in meaning to {L:τιμάω<SDBG:τιμάω:000002>}[c] to support, to provide for ({D:57.117}) and τιμή[c] cost ({D:57.161}), but in {S:05400501700012} it is also possible to understand τιμή in the sense of τιμή[a] honor, respect ({D:87.4}), and therefore one may speak of the elders as receiving double honor.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being of considerable value or worth
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible to interpret λίθους τιμίους in {S:04600301200022} as a unit which means ‘precious stones’ (see {D:2.29}), but in this figurative context of a foundation, the reference may very well be more general.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to high status, involving both honor and respect
(derivative of {L:τίμιος<SDBG:τίμιος:000000>}[a] ‘valuable, precious,’ {D:65.2}) a large quantity of costly, valuable possessions
LEXSenses.Comments: ‘Wealth’ may usually be rendered by ‘the many valuable possessions.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a friend and coworker of Paul
one of the seven helpers in the church in Jerusalem
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
to punish, with the implication of causing people to suffer what they deserve
to experience something bad, often in retribution for some wrongdoing

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an interrogative reference to someone or something

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an interrogative reference to reason
LEXSenses.Comments: The expression τί ἐμοὶ καὶ σοί (literally ‘what for me and you?’) in {S:04300200400012} is an adage meaning ‘for what reason are you saying or doing this to me?’ In some languages it may be preferable to translate {S:04300200400012} as ‘why do you ask me this?’ In {S:04100102400026} one may translate ‘what do you want with us?’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a reference to someone or something indefinite, spoken or written about

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (occurring only in a predicate position) a reference to someone or something of prominence or distinction
LEXSenses.Comments: For a treatment of τις[b] as part of an idiom in {S:04400503600020}, see {D:87.49}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Jewish proselyte in Corinth whose additional name was Justus; see {D:93.179}
a brief notice used primarily for identification
a friend and companion of Paul
an alternative form of {L:Τίτιος<SDBG:Τίτιος:000000>}, {D:93.363} ({S:04401800700018}, apparatus)
an emphatic marker of result, often associated with exhortation
an emphatic marker of result, often associated with exhortation
pertaining to being of such a kind, often with the implication of a degree of uniqueness or distinctiveness

Notes.Content: In {S:04101301900020} τοιαύτη serves to make more emphatic the comparison already stated in οἵα.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being like some identified entity or event
a reference to that which is of such a kind as is identified in the context
Glosses: of a kind such as this

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: wall of a house or enclosure
LEXSenses.Comments: A literal translation of the phrase ‘whitewashed wall’ is rarely meaningful. Sometimes one can use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a dirty wall which is made to look white’ or ‘… to look clean.’ In other instances one may wish to focus upon the function suggested by the idiom ‘whitewashed wall’ and employ a phrase such as ‘one who has been made to look good but really isn’t.’

LEXDomains.Domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: whitewashed wall) one who pretends to be one thing, while in reality he is something quite different
the interest on money that has been loaned
to be so bold as to challenge or defy possible danger or opposition
(comparative adverb of τολμηρός ‘bold, daring,’ not occurring in the NT) pertaining to an activity involving unusual boldness or daring
one who is particularly bold and daring
pertaining to having the capacity to cut efficiently
an arc made of wood or other flexible material and bent by a string attached to its two ends; for propelling an arrow; weapon of war

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: topaz, usually yellow in color (see {D:2.29})

Notes.Content: It is possible that in the case of such meanings as τόπος[f] ({D:11.59}), πόλις[c] ({D:11.61}), κώμη[b] ({D:11.62}), and χώρα[e] ({D:11.64}) one should count on certain more or less automatic semantic rules by which the meaning of inhabitants could be derived by metonymy from expressions of place. Since, however, such metonymic developments are far from universal, the distinct meanings are listed here as a practical guide to translators. The same type of problem occurs with Ιεροσόλυμα ‘Jerusalem,’  Ἰουδαία ‘Judea,’ and περίχωρος ‘region’ in {S:04000300500000}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an area of any size, regarded in certain contexts as a point in space
LEXSenses.Comments: In {S:04301104800036} the expression τὸν τόπον refers to the Temple in Jerusalem.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a particular portion or unit of discourse
LEXSenses.Comments: In rendering τόπος[b], περιοχή, or γραφή[a], it is often possible to use a rather general term such as the place or the part. In other instances one may wish to use a term meaning the words. Accordingly, {S:04200402100020} may be rendered as ‘these words have come true today as you have heard them being read.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a role involving activity and responsibility
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages the latter part of this expression in {S:04400102500006} may be rendered as ‘helping in this way and being an apostle’ or ‘helping in this way as an apostle.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in {S:04400102500006}, see {D:87.1}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the position of a person within a group, implying a particular role or type of activity
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages the equivalent of this expression in {S:04400102500006} may be simply ‘to undertake the work of an apostle’ or ‘to be an apostle in serving.’ For another interpretation of τόπος in {S:04400102500006}, involving a shift in focus, see {D:42.21}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the possibility of some occasion or opportunity

LEXDomains.Domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the inhabitants of a place{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages it is impossible to use a term meaning ‘place’ as a reference to the people of such a place.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Land in Contrast With the Sea

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a bar or reef produced in an area where two currents meet
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible to understand τόπος {L:διθάλασσος<SDBG:διθάλασσος:000000>} in {S:04402704100010} as a place of crosscurrents; see {D:14.32}. In some languages it may be necessary to construct a descriptive equivalent for ‘sandbank,’ for example, ‘a hill of sand just beneath the surface of the water’ or ‘a ridge of sand hidden by the water.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to a quantity of objects or events considerably beyond normal expectations
pertaining to a quantity considerably beyond normal expectations

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a degree of correlative extent
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to render this portion of {S:06601800700002} as ‘to the degree that she glorified herself and lived in luxury, to that same degree give her torment and sorrow.’|Expressions involving correspondence of degrees must often be rather considerably restructured. For example, in the first part of {S:06601800700002} one may translate in some languages ‘she honored herself very much and lived in great luxury, and so give her very much suffering and grief.’ In the case of {S:05800100400012}, one may translate ‘God gave his Son a name that was more important than the name of the angels; therefore, God’s Son is greater than the angels.’

LEXSubDomains.Domain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a point of time subsequent to another point of time
male goat (smaller domesticated four-footed animal with hooves; genus Capra; source of meat, hides, hair, and horns)
LEXSenses.Comments: A number of languages have special terms for ‘he-goat’ and ‘she-goat,’ and frequently there is no formal relationship between the respective terms any more than there is in English between billy and nanny or between the corresponding terms for sheep, namely, ram and ewe.

Notes.Content: It is not possible to determine on the basis of existing evidence whether the expression τραπέζης μετέχω is a genuine idiom or a phrase which is to be taken in a literal sense as referring to the ordinance of Holy Communion in contrast to banqueting in heathen temples.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a generic expression for any type of table
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:τράπεζα<SDBG:τράπεζα:000000>}[a] ‘table,’ {D:6.113}) a meal, with possible emphasis upon its being relatively bountiful
a place where money is kept or managed or where credit is established

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to share in a table) to belong to a particular religious group as evidenced by ceremonial eating{N:001}
Glosses: to eat at the table of

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to serve tables) to be responsible for financial aspects of an enterprise
LEXSenses.Comments: It is also possible to interpret the phrase διακονέω τραπέζαις not as an idiom but simply as ‘to wait on tables, to serve meals’ (see {D:23.26} and {D:46.13}), but even so the context relates to caring for needs.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:τράπεζα<SDBG:τράπεζα:000002>}[c] ‘bank,’ {D:57.215}) a person who manages or works in a bank

Notes.Content: These expressions for wound normally do not imply a mortal wound. It is possible, however, to speak of a mortal wound by the phrase ἡ πληγὴ τοῦ θανάτου as in {S:06601300300026}, {S:06601301200058}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the condition resulting from being severely hurt or wounded{N:001}
to hurt or wound, normally resulting in some mark or permanent scar on the body

(a figurative extension of meaning of τραχηλίζω ‘to have the neck of a sacrificial victim twisted and thus exposed for slaughter,’ not occurring in the NT) that which can readily be known as the result of being exposed

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.Comments: τράχηλος also occurs in the NT in certain idiomatic expressions, for example, ‘to fall on the neck of someone’ ({S:04201502000050} and {S:04402003700020}) in the sense of ‘to embrace’ ({D:34.64}), and ‘to put down their necks’ ({S:04501600400016}) meaning ‘to risk their lives’ ({D:21.8}). It is rare indeed that one can translate such idioms literally, since ‘to fall on the neck of someone’ may readily suggest a murderous attack, and ‘to risk one’s neck’ may be simply meaningless, since the custom of beheading as a means of execution may be relatively unknown.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to put down the neck) willingly and purposely to expose oneself to extreme danger and risk
LEXSenses.Comments: In some instances one can translate this expression in {S:04501600400016} as ‘who showed they were willing to die in order that I could live’ or ‘in order to help me continue to live, they almost died.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: pertaining to being uneven and rough, as of terrain
a district to the south of Damascus
cardinal number, where there are three instances of a countable entity

Notes.Content: It is possible to regard τρέμω[b] ({D:25.259}) and φρίσσω ({D:25.260}) as belonging simultaneously to two quite distinct semantic domains, the one being physiological, that is to say, a type of uncontrolled physical response because of fear or great awe, and a psychological experience of fear or terror. Since, however, it is the latter which gives rise to the former, one would seem to be more justified in treating these meanings as matters of emotive responses rather than as physiological events.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to shake or tremble, often with the implication of fear and/or consternation
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are two distinct terms for trembling, one relating to illness (as in the case of epileptic seizures or the chills and fever associated with malaria) and the other associated with fear.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:τρέμω<SDBG:τρέμω:000000>}[a] ‘to tremble,’ {D:16.6}) to be so afraid as to tremble, often with the implication of awe{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of τρέμω in {S:06100201000034}, see {D:87.14}.

LEXSubDomains.Domain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to have such awe or respect for a person as to involve a measure of fear
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are serious problems involved in speaking of ‘fearing God,’ for this might imply merely ‘to be scared of God’ as though God were some kind of bogeyman. If there is a term with the meaning of ‘awe’ (perhaps in a phrase such as ‘to stand in awe of’), this may be an adequate equivalent. In some instances awe is expressed idiomatically as ‘to stand with one’s heart in one’s throat’ or ‘to be in someone’s presence with one’s heart beating fast.’|For another interpretation of τρέμω in {S:06100201000034}, see {D:25.259}.

Notes.Content: It is possible that ἐκτρέφω[a] is somewhat more emphatic in meaning than τρέφω[a], but this cannot be determined from existing contexts.
There may very well be subtle differences of meaning in the series in {D:35.51}, but there is no direct contextual evidence to support significant distinctions in meaning.

to raise a child to maturity by providing for physical and psychological needs{N:002}
LEXSenses.Comments: To raise or bring up children may be expressed in a number of different ways, for example, ‘to give food to children,’ ‘to take care of children,’ ‘to be a parent to children,’ ‘to cause a child to become an adult,’ or ‘to make a child become like oneself.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to run, with emphasis upon relative speed in contrast with walking
LEXSenses.Comments: τρέχω[a] also occurs in figurative contexts: δι᾽ ὑπομονῆς τρέχωμεν τὸν προκείμενον ἡμῖν ἀγῶνα ‘let us run with determination the race that is before us’ {S:05801200100038}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to try to do something (employed in the absolute construction)
to make progress in one’s behavior or conduct
LEXSenses.Comments: It may also be possible to translate ἐτρέχετε καλῶς as ‘you were doing better and better.’

Notes.Content: The terms τρῆμα, τρύπημα, and τρυμαλιά actually belong theoretically to a domain of openings, holes, and apertures, but since these terms in the NT are associated so closely with a needle, it seems far more satisfactory to treat them together with ῥαφίς and βελόνη needle ({D:6.215}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a small opening{N:001} (used in the NT only with reference to the so-called ‘eye’ of a needle)
LEXSenses.Comments: The hole in a needle is variously referred to in different languages, for example, ‘the nostril of the needle,’ ‘the ear of the needle,’ ‘the mouth of the needle,’ and even ‘the anus of the needle.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: cardinal number, where there are thirty instances of a countable entity
cardinal number, where there are three hundred instances of a countable entity
any kind of plant with sharp projections on its stem and/or branches; regarded as useless; symbol of hardship
LEXSenses.Comments: Since plants having thorny projections are almost worldwide in distribution, there is no difficulty in obtaining a satisfactory term for such plants. In some instances, however, a descriptive equivalent may be necessary, for example, ‘plants with piercing points’ or ‘plants that stick into one’s flesh.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a well-worn path or thoroughfare

LEXSenses.Comments: The action of grinding one’s teeth in the case of an epileptic fit is so widespread that it is normally not difficult to find some way of expressing this type of action.

Notes.Content: For both items {D:67.175} and {D:67.176} it is, of course, also possible to speak of months as moons. Compare {D:67.174}.

Notes.Content: Though τὸ τρίτον functions in an adverbial sense, there seems to be no reason to set up a separate meaning of τρίτος as referring only to a temporal sequence. The interpretation of τρίτος in terms of time or space is a factor of the context. When objects are involved, ordinals simply mark position in a spacial sequence; when events are involved, ordinals simply mark position in a temporal sequence.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: third in a series involving either time, space, or set{N:001}
a third part of an object, series, or mass
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages a fractional part of something is referred to by means of ordinal numbers. For example, ‘a third of the trees’ would be rendered as ‘every third tree,’ and ‘a third of the earth was consumed by fire’ would be rendered as ‘the third part of the earth was consumed by fire’ or ‘having divided the earth into three parts, one part was destroyed by fire.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (derivative of {L:θρίξ<SDBG:θρίξ:000000>} ‘hair,’ {D:8.12}) pertaining to or consisting of hair
to shake or tremble, often with the implication of fear and/or consternation
LEXSenses.Comments: In a number of languages there are two distinct terms for trembling, one relating to illness (as in the case of epileptic seizures or the chills and fever associated with malaria) and the other associated with fear.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the process of turning, with the implication of variation and change
LEXSenses.Comments: It is difficult to know precisely the significance of the phrase τροπῆς ἀποσκίασμα. It probably had a technical sense which has been lost, but clearly it is parallel in meaning to {L:παραλλαγή<SDBG:παραλλαγή:000000>} ‘change, alteration’ ({D:58.44}). In some languages it may be best to translate this expression in {S:05900101700044} as ‘in whom there is no change or variation.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: the manner in which something is done
manner of life, often with focus upon customary acts
LEXSenses.Comments: One may also render this expression in {S:05801300500006} as ‘you should not be like people who always love money.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to put up with someone or something, implying extensive patience

Notes.Content: There are no doubt certain subtle differences of meaning in the various terms listed here as meaning ‘food,’ but it is impossible to determine such distinctions in meaning from NT contexts. Perhaps τροφή and διατροφή are somewhat more generic in meaning and may suggest a greater emphasis upon nourishment (see footnote b). At the same time, βρῶσις[c] and βρῶμα[a] may imply solid substantive food, but it is difficult, if not impossible, to argue for such subtle connotative distinctions in meanings which are essentially generic.

It is possible that τροφή and διατροφή focus primarily upon the meaning of food as nourishment, and in {S:04001001000034} and {S:05400600800006} it would be perfectly appropriate to use a translation meaning ‘nourishment’ rather than merely ‘food.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: any kind of food or nourishment{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Almost all languages have at least a few general terms for food, though these may be derived from verbal expressions meaning essentially ‘that which is eaten.’ In some instances a distinction may be made between ‘that which is chewed’ and ‘that which is drunk,’ and it may therefore be important in certain contexts to speak of food in general by a phrase meaning ‘that which is either chewed or drunk.’ If one fails to include both types of food, the reader might interpret a passage such as {S:04000601100004} as requesting only solid foods.|In the place of a general term or phrase such as ‘that which is eaten’ or ‘that which is consumed,’ some languages generalize the meaning of a particular term. For example, in certain parts of the Orient the term meaning specifically ‘rice’ also refers to ‘food’ in general. In fact, some persons will declare, ‘I have not eaten!’ if they have not had rice as part of a meal. A similar type of meaning has developed in English with respect to ‘bread.’ For example, in rendering {S:04200400400022} (οὐκ ἐπ’ ἄρτῳ μόνῳ ζήσεται ὁ ἄνθρωπος ‘man shall not live by bread alone’) it would be wrong to employ a strictly literal rendering, since this might mean simply that people should not live on a diet consisting solely of bread. The meaning of {S:04200400400022} is, of course, ‘to live means more than merely eating.’

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a Christian of Ephesus and companion of Paul
a person who functions as a substitute for a mother in the process of rearing children
Glosses: nurse (in the British, not American, sense)
LEXSenses.Comments: It is possible that in {S:05200200700032} τροφός may mean a mother nursing and rearing her children.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to take care of, with special reference to supplying necessary nourishment
LEXSenses.Comments: This word is found as a variant reading only: καὶ ὡς τεσσερακονταετῆ χρόνον ἐτροφοφόρησεν αὐτοὺς ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ ‘and for forty years he took care of them in the desert’ {S:04401301800010} (apparatus).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (an idiom, literally: to make straight wheel tracks for the feet) to live or behave in strict conformance to a predetermined model for behavior

Notes.Content: The expression τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως in {S:05900300600048} is similar in meaning to the lexical items found in Domain 41 Behavior and Related States, Subdomain B Custom, Tradition.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of τροχός ‘wheel,’ not occurring in the NT) an ordered series of events, involving repeated patterns
LEXSenses.Comments: For another interpretation of τροχός in {S:05900300600048}, see {D:67.83}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: (a figurative extension of meaning of τροχός ‘wheel,’ not occurring in the NT) a period of time of indefinite length, characterized by recurring events or patterns
LEXSenses.Comments: In some languages τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως may be best rendered as ‘the very way in which we live’ or ‘the manner of our life.’ For another interpretation of {L:τροχός<SDBG:τροχός:000000>} in {S:05900300600048}, see {D:61.5}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a relatively deep concave dish used for holding or cooking food or liquids; usually made of clay, but also metals
LEXSenses.Comments: In the two NT occurrences ({S:04002602300026}; {S:04101402000028}) τρύβλιον can be understood as a part of an idiom (literally ‘to dip one’s hands into the bowl with someone’) meaning ‘to share a meal with someone.’ If, however, the idiom is to be translated literally (and this is normally the case), there are certain difficulties involved, since a literal rendering of ‘to dip one’s hand into a bowl’ might mean literally putting one’s fingers or hand into a bowl rather than dipping in food which one holds in the hand. An idiomatic interpretation of ‘sharing a meal with someone’ or ‘eating together with’ may be preferable. But if one does translate the idiom somewhat literally, it is important in some languages to render this phrase as ‘to dip food into a bowl together with someone’ or ‘to jointly dip food into sauce.’

Notes.Content: In Greek usage τρυγάω seems to be an agricultural term in contrast with τίλλω ({D:18.9}) and συλλέγω ({D:18.10}).

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: to pick or gather ripe fruit (especially used of grapes){N:001}

Asiatic Rock dove: bird with a blue-gray color with a pinkish sheen to the neck feathers and a black tip on its tail; lives in large colonies and eats mainly seeds; courts, mates, and has nests several times a year; nests on rock ledges; Columba via; used as food and for sacrifices; regarded as swift, docile, and innocent
LEXSenses.Comments: Though in English a relatively clear distinction is made between ‘doves’ (which have pointed tails) and ‘pigeons’ (which have square off tails), there seems to be no such distinction in the use of περιστερά and τρυγών in the Greek of the New Testament.|There are, however, certain problems involved in the connotations of terms relating to pigeons or doves. According to ancient zoology, the dove was thought to have no bile, and consequently, therefore, to be a very peaceful and clean bird. It thus became a symbol of Christian virtue and of gentleness (as in {S:04001001600040}). In reality, however, doves and pigeons are quite aggressive, and a group of pigeons are frequently known to peck an injured bird to death. Therefore, in some societies pigeons or doves are not regarded as gentle or peaceful, but rather as wicked and harmful. In fact, in some cultures doves are thought to be symbols of death and of evil. Under such circumstances it is important, therefore, to have some marginal note so as to indicate clearly the symbolic significance of such birds in biblical contexts.

Notes.Content: Properly speaking, στίγμα[a] ({D:8.55}) and τύπος[a] ({D:8.56}) are not body parts, but may refer to features of the body which may result from some external force or object and could accordingly be classified in Domain 19 Physical Impact. They are, however, included at this point because they may refer to types of scars, which become a permanent feature of the body.

LEXDomains.Domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: a visible impression or trace made as the result of a blow or pressure{N:001}
LEXSenses.Comments: Though both {L:στίγμα<SDBG:στίγμα:000000>}[a] ({D:8.55}) and τύπος[a] may mean scars, there are significant differences in meaning. {L:στίγμα<SDBG:στίγμα:000000>}[a] bears the connotation of brand or mark of ownership, while τύπος[a] indicates a wound or scar resulting from the shape and form of some object, for example, nails in the case of {S:04302002500064}.

LEXSenses.DefinitionShort: an object (not necessarily three-dimensional) which has been formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
LEXSenses.Comments: In certain contexts the referents of {L:εἰκών<SDBG:εἰκών:000000>}[a], τύπος[b], and {L:χάραγμα<SDBG:χάραγμα:000001>}[b] may have special religious significance in that they may refer to idols, but the focal component for the translator is that of a likeness or resemblance. In contexts such as {S:04002202000012} an equivalent translation may be simply a picture, but in {S:04500102300020} and {S:04400704300030} one may use the same expression as is employed to render {L:εἴδωλον<SDBG:εἴδωλον:000000>}[a] idol ({D:6.97}).
